teile.einleitung: Petrol is a liquid fuel that most cars, motorbikes and lawnmowers run on. It is made from crude oil and burns in the engine, driving the vehicle. Petrol is very useful, but also catches fire easily and is bad for the climate.
wichtigste: Petrol is made from crude oil.
A car needs petrol for its engine.
You fill up with petrol at the petrol station and buy it in litres.
Petrol is dangerous because it burns very easily.
When petrol burns, exhaust gases are produced, which come out of the exhaust pipe.
Crude oil does not grow back, so petrol will one day become scarce.
An electric car fills up with electricity instead of petrol.

abschnitte.text: Petrol is obtained from **crude oil**, which formed millions of years ago from dead sea creatures. In a **refinery** the crude oil is heated and separated into different parts, rather like separating steam from water when cooking. The lighter parts become petrol, heavier ones diesel, heating oil or tar. In Switzerland there is a refinery in Cressier in the canton of Neuchâtel.

In the engine, petrol is mixed with air and squeezed together in a cylinder. A spark from the **spark plug** ignites the mixture, which burns explosively. The hot gases push a piston down, and this movement drives the wheels through shafts and gearwheels. Only part of the energy in the petrol becomes movement; the rest becomes heat.

Swiss petrol stations usually offer unleaded 95 and unleaded 98. The number is the **octane rating**; it tells you how well the petrol behaves under pressure without igniting too early. In the past lead, which is poisonous, was added to petrol; in Switzerland leaded petrol has been banned since 2000. At the petrol station: switch off the engine, no smoking and no naked flames.

Petrol evaporates quickly, and its vapours are heavier than air. Even a small spark can ignite them, which is why petrol is extremely dangerous. It may only be kept in approved **cans** and must never be in the hands of children. Petrol is also poisonous if you breathe it in or swallow it.

Burning one litre of petrol produces over two kilograms of **carbon dioxide**, which strengthens climate change. Exhaust gases also contain substances that pollute the air in towns, which is why cars have a catalytic converter. Because crude oil does not grow back and the climate needs protecting, more and more electric cars are on the roads. They fill up with electricity, a large part of which comes from hydropower in Switzerland.

begriffe.erklaerung: A dark raw material from the ground from which petrol, diesel and plastics are made.
A factory in which crude oil is separated into petrol and other products.
A number that tells you how resistant to knocking, that is how evenly burning, a petrol is.
The gases that come out of the exhaust pipe when fuel burns.

gewusst: On the first long-distance car journey in 1888, Bertha Benz bought her fuel at a chemist’s in Wiesloch, which is therefore regarded as the world’s first petrol station.
Before there were cars, petrol was a by-product left over from making lamp paraffin.

teile.einleitung: A paper clip is a small, bent piece of wire used to hold loose sheets together. It is an everyday object in which you can discover a lot of physics: spring force, friction and above all magnetism. Because most paper clips are made of steel, they are attracted by magnets.
wichtigste: Most paper clips are bent from steel wire.
They are used to hold sheets of paper together.
A magnet attracts steel clips, but not clips made entirely of plastic.
Colourful clips with a plastic coating are still attracted, because there is steel inside.
A clip hanging on a magnet becomes magnetic itself and can hold a second one.
With a magnet you can even move paper clips through glass.
Gravity pulls a clip held by a magnet downwards.

abschnitte.text: A paper clip consists of a piece of **steel wire** bent into two loops, one inside the other. When you slide it over the edge of sheets of paper, the wire presses the sheets together like a little spring. This **spring force** and friction hold the sheets in place. Paper clips also come in plastic or with a colourful plastic coating.

Steel contains iron and is therefore attracted by a **magnet**. Clips made entirely of plastic, on the other hand, are not attracted. Colourful clips have a plastic layer on the outside but steel inside, and so they still stick. With a magnet you can pick up scattered clips from the floor in a flash.

When a paper clip hangs on a magnet, it becomes magnetic itself for a short time. That is why a second clip can hang from it, a third from that, and so on. This process is called **magnetisation**. If you take the top clip off the magnet, the chain usually falls apart, because the magnetic force almost completely disappears.

If a paper clip lies in a glass of water, you can push it upwards with a magnet on the outside of the glass without getting wet fingers. The **magnetic force** works through glass, water, paper and wood. When a magnet lifts a clip, its force is fighting against **gravity**, which pulls the clip down. If you carefully lay a clip flat on water, it can even float thanks to surface tension.

The usual shape today, with two loops, appeared in England towards the end of the 19th century and is called “Gem” after a company. In Norway Johan Vaaler is regarded as the inventor of the paper clip, although his shape looked a little different. During the Second World War Norwegians wore paper clips on their clothes as a silent sign of **resistance** against the occupation. Today billions of paper clips are made worldwide every year.

begriffe.erklaerung: A hard material made mainly of iron.
An object made of iron becomes magnetic itself because of a magnet.
The force with which a bent wire wants to return to its shape.
A kind of thin skin on the surface of water that can carry light things.

gewusst: Near Oslo there is a giant paper clip as a monument to the Norwegian inventor Johan Vaaler.
A Canadian swapped a single red paper clip through many trades until he got a house for it.
If you bend a paper clip back and forth many times, it breaks, because the wire becomes hard and brittle.

teile.einleitung: Chemical energy is energy stored in the bonds between atoms. It is found in food, wood, petrol and batteries and is released when substances react with each other. Almost everything we do, from running to heating to charging a phone, has to do with chemical energy.
wichtigste: Chemical energy is stored in the bonds between atoms.
A burning candle turns chemical energy into heat and light.
Muscles turn the chemical energy of food into kinetic energy and heat.
In photosynthesis, radiant energy is turned into chemical energy.
A battery turns chemical energy into electrical energy; when a rechargeable battery is charged, it is the other way round.
A petrol engine uses the chemical energy of the fuel.
A reaction in which energy is released as heat is called exothermic.

abschnitte.text: Atoms in molecules are held together by **chemical bonds**. These bonds contain energy. In a chemical reaction bonds are broken and new ones are formed. If the new bonds are more stable, the difference is released as heat, light or electricity.

When something burns, a substance reacts with the **oxygen** in the air. In this way a candle turns wax into heat and light, and a wood fire warms a hut. In a **petrol engine** the chemical energy of the fuel first becomes heat and then movement. Reactions that release heat are called **exothermic**, and those that need heat are called endothermic.

Plants use sunlight to make sugar from water and carbon dioxide; this is **photosynthesis**. In the process radiant energy is turned into chemical energy and stored in the sugar. Animals and people eat plants or animals and use this energy in turn. Coal, crude oil and natural gas also contain chemical energy from plants and tiny organisms that lived millions of years ago.

Our food contains chemical energy, mainly in carbohydrates, fats and proteins. The body breaks them down step by step and gains energy in the process. **Muscles** turn it into kinetic energy and heat, which is why we get warm when doing sport. Packaging shows the energy content in kilojoules or **kilocalories**.

In a **battery** chemical reactions take place that supply electrical energy, for example for a torch. A **rechargeable battery** can be charged up again: when charging, electrical energy is turned into chemical energy and stored. Mobile phones, e-bikes and electric cars mostly use lithium-ion batteries. In Switzerland used batteries do not belong in the rubbish, but back in the collection box in the shop.

begriffe.erklaerung: The connection between atoms in a molecule.
A reaction that gives off heat.
A reaction that takes in heat.
Plants turning light, water and carbon dioxide into sugar.
A unit of energy, for example on food packaging.

gewusst: An instant cold pack for sports injuries gets cold because an endothermic reaction takes place inside when you squeeze it.
One gram of fat contains roughly twice as much chemical energy as one gram of sugar.
Your brain alone uses around a fifth of the energy you take in with your food.

teile.einleitung: The Boltzmann constant, abbreviated k, is a constant of nature that links temperature and energy. It shows roughly how much kinetic energy the tiny particles of a substance have at a particular temperature. Since 2019 its value has been fixed exactly and is used to define the unit of temperature, the kelvin.
wichtigste: The Boltzmann constant is exactly 1.380649·10⁻²³ J/K.
Since 2019 its numerical value has been fixed exactly in the SI.
Today the SI base unit kelvin is defined using it.
It equals the gas constant R divided by the Avogadro constant.
The average kinetic energy of a gas particle is 3/2·k·T.
At room temperature of around 300 K, k·T is about 0.026 eV.
The Boltzmann factor gives how likely it is that a state with the energy E is occupied.

abschnitte.text: Everything around us is made of particles that are constantly jiggling and darting about. The warmer a substance is, the faster they move. The **Boltzmann constant** k is the conversion factor between the temperature we measure and the energy of these particles. It has the value 1.380649·10⁻²³ joules per kelvin, an unimaginably small number, because a single particle is so tiny.

In a gas each particle has on average the kinetic energy 3/2 times k times T, where T is the **absolute temperature** in kelvin. At 300 K, that is about 27 °C, this is around 6.2·10⁻²¹ joules. Physicists like to give the quantity k·T in **electronvolts**; at room temperature it is about 0.026 eV. With this you can estimate whether the heat is enough, for example, to break up a molecule.

The Boltzmann constant is closely related to the **gas constant** R, which is around 8.314 J/(mol·K). If you divide R by the **Avogadro constant**, that is around 6.022·10²³ particles per mole, you get k. R applies to a whole mole of a substance, k to a single particle. With k you can also calculate that 1 cm³ of air at 100 kPa and 300 K contains about 2.4·10¹⁹ particles.

The expression e to the power of minus E divided by k·T is called the **Boltzmann factor**. It tells you how likely it is that a particle is in a state with the energy E. States with high energy are very rare at low temperatures and more common at high temperatures. This principle explains, for example, why chemical reactions run faster when it is warm.

The constant is named after the Austrian physicist **Ludwig Boltzmann**, who lived from 1844 to 1906. He explained heat and entropy through the movement of countless particles at a time when many researchers did not yet believe in atoms. The name k and the first precise value, however, were introduced by Max Planck around 1900. Boltzmann’s gravestone in Vienna bears his famous formula S equals k times log W.

In the past the kelvin was defined using the **triple point** of water, at which ice, water and vapour exist at the same time. In the great reform of the **SI system of units** on 20 May 2019, the value of k was fixed exactly instead. Since then the kelvin has been defined using this constant of nature. This has the advantage that the unit could be reproduced in the same way anywhere in the universe.

begriffe.erklaerung: A quantity in physics that has the same value everywhere and always.
The unit of absolute temperature; 0 K is the coldest possible value.
A very small unit of energy, practical for atoms and particles.
A measure of how many ways there are of arranging the particles of a system.

gewusst: Ludwig Boltzmann’s most important formula is carved on his tomb in Vienna’s Central Cemetery.
A thimbleful of air is said to contain more particles than there are grains of sand on all the beaches of the Earth.
The Boltzmann constant is one of the seven constants of nature on which all SI units have been based since 2019.

teile.einleitung: Bertrand Piccard is a Swiss adventurer, doctor and explorer who has made aviation history twice. In 1999 he became the first to fly round the world non-stop in a balloon. In 2016 he completed a journey round the world in a solar aeroplane that flew on solar energy alone.
wichtigste: Bertrand Piccard was born in Lausanne in 1958.
He comes from a famous family of explorers: his grandfather was Auguste Piccard and his father Jacques Piccard.
In 1999, with Brian Jones, he made the first non-stop flight round the world in a balloon.
Later he flew round the world in the solar aeroplane Solar Impulse 2.
The aeroplane got its energy only from the sun.
He took turns flying with André Borschberg; the journey round the world ended in 2016.
Today Piccard campaigns for clean technology and climate protection.

abschnitte.text: Bertrand Piccard was born on 1 March 1958 in **Lausanne**. He studied medicine and became a **psychiatrist**, a doctor for mental health. Even as a young man he was a pioneer of hang-gliding and microlight flying. But he became famous above all for his great journeys round the world.

His grandfather **Auguste Piccard** was one of the first people to rise into the stratosphere in a balloon in 1931, more than 15 kilometres up. His father **Jacques Piccard** dived in the submersible Trieste in 1960 into the Mariana Trench, the deepest place in the world’s oceans. Bertrand Piccard then conquered the Earth all the way round through the air. So over three generations the family has explored height, depth and distance.

In March 1999 Piccard and the Briton **Brian Jones** set off in the balloon **Breitling Orbiter 3** from Château-d'Oex in the canton of Vaud. After almost 20 days and more than 40,000 kilometres they landed in Egypt. It was the first non-stop flight round the world in a balloon. The balloon’s capsule is now on display in the Smithsonian museum in Washington.

With the engineer **André Borschberg**, Piccard developed the solar aeroplane **Solar Impulse**. On the wings lay more than 17,000 solar cells, which drove the motors during the day and charged batteries for the night. The wings of Solar Impulse 2, at around 72 metres, were wider than those of a jumbo jet, but the aeroplane only weighed about as much as a car. The journey round the world began in Abu Dhabi in 2015 and ended there in July 2016. The cockpit only had room for one pilot, so the two took turns from stage to stage.

Piccard wanted to show that **renewable energy** and efficient technology make incredible things possible. With his Solar Impulse Foundation he then collected more than 1000 solutions that protect the environment and are still economical. He gives talks all over the world and advises governments and companies. In Switzerland he is regarded as one of the best-known adventurers.

begriffe.erklaerung: A doctor who helps people with mental health problems.
A component that turns sunlight into electricity.
A layer of the atmosphere that lies about 10 to 50 kilometres above the ground.
A store for electrical energy that can be charged again.

gewusst: Solar Impulse 2 flew round the world without any fuel at all, on solar energy alone.
On the longest flight, across the Pacific, André Borschberg was in the air for almost five days and nights without a break.
The comic character Professor Calculus in “The Adventures of Tintin” was inspired by Bertrand’s grandfather Auguste Piccard.

teile.einleitung: The band gap is a term from solid-state physics that explains why some substances conduct electricity and others do not. It is an energy gap that electrons have to jump over in order to move freely in the material. Without knowledge of band gaps there would be no computer chips, solar cells or light-emitting diodes.
wichtigste: The band gap is the energy difference between the valence band and the conduction band.
Metals have no band gap and therefore conduct electricity very well.
Semiconductors such as silicon have a small band gap, around 1.1 electronvolts for silicon.
Insulators such as diamond have a large band gap, about 5.5 electronvolts for diamond.
The band gap determines which light a material can take in or give out.
Silicon is poorly suited to light-emitting diodes because it has an indirect band gap.
Band gaps are usually given in electronvolts; one electronvolt is around 1.6 times 10 to the power of minus 19 joules.

abschnitte.text: In a solid, billions of atoms lie close together. Their electrons can therefore only have energies in certain ranges, the **energy bands**. The lower band, filled with electrons, is called the valence band; the upper one, in which electrons can move freely, is called the conduction band. The forbidden region between them is the **band gap**.

In **metals** the bands overlap, there is no band gap, and electrons can move easily. In insulators such as diamond or glass the gap is so large that hardly any electron jumps over it. **Semiconductors** such as silicon or germanium lie in between. If you warm a semiconductor, more electrons jump across the gap and it conducts better; with metals it is the other way round.

A particle of light, a **photon**, can lift an electron across the gap if it has enough energy. Red light has little energy, blue light more. From the band gap you can therefore calculate up to which wavelength a material swallows light: germanium, with around 0.67 electronvolts, absorbs light up to about 1850 nanometres. Diamond, with its large band gap, lets visible light through and is therefore transparent.

In a **light-emitting diode** electrons fall back across the band gap and give off light as they do so. The size of the gap determines the colour of the light. Silicon has an indirect band gap, so mainly heat is produced instead of light, which is why other substances such as gallium nitride are used for LEDs. Solar cells do it the other way round: light lifts electrons across the gap, and current flows.

Materials with a large band gap can cope with high voltages and temperatures. **Silicon carbide**, with a band gap of around 3.3 electronvolts, is therefore increasingly used in the power electronics of electric cars. Gallium nitride is found in small, powerful chargers for mobile phones and laptops. In Switzerland, for example, ETH Zurich, EPFL and CSEM in Neuchâtel are researching new semiconductors and solar cells.

begriffe.erklaerung: A very small unit of energy used for electrons and atoms.
A substance that conducts electricity poorly or well depending on conditions, for example silicon.
The energy range in which the electrons are tightly bound to the atoms.
The energy range in which electrons can move freely and conduct electricity.

gewusst: Three Japanese researchers received the Nobel Prize in Physics in 2014 for inventing the bright blue light-emitting diode.
The colour of many gemstones and pigments is linked to the size of their band gap.

teile.einleitung: In electrical engineering, a battery is a store that turns chemical energy into electrical energy. It supplies direct current and makes devices independent of the mains socket. Strictly speaking, a battery is several galvanic cells connected together.
wichtigste: A battery turns chemical energy into electrical energy.
In everyday life people say that a battery stores electricity.
A torch needs a battery to light up.
Every cell has a positive and a negative terminal, the electrodes.
Between the electrodes lies an electrolyte, through which ions travel.
Batteries that can be recharged are called accumulators or rechargeable batteries.
Alessandro Volta built the first battery around 1800.

abschnitte.text: A **battery** supplies electric **direct current**, which always flows in the same direction. In everyday life people say it is a device that stores electricity. Really, though, it stores chemical energy, which it only turns into electrical energy when it is used. A torch, for example, needs a battery to light up.

Every **galvanic cell** consists of two different electrodes with an **electrolyte** between them. At the negative electrode atoms give up electrons, and at the positive electrode other substances take in electrons. The electrons flow through the outer circuit, that is through the device. Inside, travelling ions even out the charges.

Around 1800 the Italian Alessandro Volta stacked discs of zinc and copper with cardboard soaked in salt water between them. This **voltaic pile** was the world’s first battery. The unit of voltage, the volt, is named after Volta. In 1859 Gaston Planté invented the lead-acid battery, which is still found in cars today.

Single-use batteries are technically called **primary cells**, for example alkaline manganese batteries with 1.5 volts. Rechargeable cells are called secondary cells or **accumulators**. The most widespread today are lithium-ion batteries in mobile phones, laptops and electric cars. John Goodenough, Stanley Whittingham and Akira Yoshino received the Nobel Prize in Chemistry in 2019 for developing them.

Batteries contain metals such as lithium, cobalt, nickel or zinc. These raw materials are mined at great effort, so **recycling** is important. In Switzerland there is an obligation to return batteries, and recycling is paid for by an advance fee when you buy them. Today, large battery storage systems help to keep electricity from sun and wind for later.

begriffe.erklaerung: A connection inside the cell where the chemical reaction takes place.
A conducting substance between the electrodes through which ions travel.
Current that always flows in the same direction.
A battery that cannot be recharged.

gewusst: The voltaic pile was so important that in 1801 Napoleon had Volta show him in person how it worked.
A car battery is a lead-acid battery whose basic principle is more than 160 years old.

teile.einleitung: Density tells you how much mass there is in a certain volume. A cube of iron is much heavier than a cube of wood of the same size, because iron has a higher density. Density explains why some things float and others sink.
wichtigste: Density describes how much mass there is in a certain volume.
It is calculated as mass divided by volume.
Water has a density of about 1 gram per cubic centimetre.
Wood floats because it is lighter than the same amount of water.
Things with a greater density than water sink.
Density also depends on temperature.
Gold and platinum are among the densest substances on Earth.

abschnitte.text: **Density** tells you how tightly the mass in a substance is packed. You calculate mass divided by **volume**. The unit is kilograms per cubic metre or grams per cubic centimetre. A litre of water weighs about a kilogram, while a litre of air weighs only just over a gram.

A piece of wood floats because it is lighter than the same amount of water. Its density is less than that of water. A stone or an iron nail has a greater density and therefore sinks. So whether something floats does not depend on weight alone, but on the comparison with the **buoyancy** of the water.

Cork has a density of about 0.2 grams per cubic centimetre, ice about 0.92. Aluminium has 2.7, iron about 7.9 and **gold** 19.3. This means a gold bar is almost twenty times as heavy as the same amount of water. The densest of the natural elements are osmium and iridium, at around 22.6.

Most substances expand when heated and so become less dense. That is why warm air rises and cold air sinks. Water is an exception; it is densest at about 4 degrees Celsius. This **anomaly of water** means that lakes freeze from the top and fish can survive the winter at the bottom.

Carefully pour honey, water and oil into a glass. The liquids form layers, because they have different densities: honey at the bottom, oil at the top. A fresh egg sinks in tap water but floats in very salty water, because salt water is denser. A **hydrometer** is used in this way to measure the density of liquids.

begriffe.erklaerung: Mass divided by volume, that is how heavy a substance is for its size.
How much matter a body has, measured in kilograms.
How much space a body takes up, measured for example in litres.
The special feature that water is densest at 4 degrees.

gewusst: Balsa wood is so light that model aeroplanes and even rafts are made from it.
Saturn has a lower average density than water and would float in a giant bath.

teile.einleitung: A beam balance is one of the oldest kinds of scales in the world. It consists of a beam that can turn about a point in the middle and two pans at the ends. It does not show a weight directly, but compares which side is heavier.
wichtigste: A simple beam balance has two pans.
The beam turns about a pivot in the middle.
The heavier side goes down.
If both sides are equally heavy, the beam is level.
The beam balance was invented several thousand years ago.
A seesaw in the playground works in a similar way to a beam balance.
You can make a simple beam balance yourself with a coat hanger.

abschnitte.text: If you put something on both pans, the Earth pulls both sides down. The heavier side wins and sinks, and the lighter one rises. If both are equally heavy, the beam stays level, and the balance is in **equilibrium**. A small pointer in the middle, the tongue, shows exactly when this is the case.

The beam balance is a **lever**, more precisely a lever with the pivot between the two loads. It is not only the weight that matters, but also how far it is from the **pivot**. A weight twice as far out has twice the effect. On a beam balance both arms are the same length, so it is in equilibrium exactly when both sides are equally heavy.

In ancient Egypt and Mesopotamia, traders were already using beam balances several thousand years ago. Old Egyptian pictures show goods or gold being weighed. To weigh something, you put the goods on one side and **weights** of known mass on the other. Until the 20th century beam balances stood in shops, chemists’ and at markets.

A beam balance compares two weights with each other. Because the same gravity acts on both sides, it actually measures **mass**. On the Moon a beam balance would therefore show the same result as on Earth. A spring balance, on the other hand, would show much less on the Moon.

Hang a coat hanger on a hook and tie a cup to each end with string. Now put marbles, buttons or toy figures in them and find out which is heavier. On the **seesaw**, too, you are playing beam balance: a heavy child has to move closer to the middle to balance a light child. By the way, the balance is also a symbol of justice, which is why the figure of Justice holds scales in her hand.

begriffe.erklaerung: The dish on the balance in which you put what you want to weigh.
The point about which the beam can turn.
A state in which both sides pull equally hard and nothing moves.
A bar that turns about a point and can be used to transmit forces.

gewusst: In the past, very fine beam balances in laboratories could detect differences of a fraction of a milligram.
The star sign and constellation Libra, the scales, are also named after this measuring instrument.

teile.einleitung: A barometer is a measuring instrument for air pressure. The air is constantly pressing on us from all sides without our noticing, and the barometer makes this pressure visible. Because air pressure changes with the weather, it also helps with weather forecasting.
wichtigste: A barometer measures air pressure.
It was invented by the Italian Evangelista Torricelli in 1643 with a column of mercury.
In the weather forecast, air pressure is given in hectopascals.
At sea level normal air pressure is about 1013 hectopascals.
A falling barometer often means worse weather, a rising one better weather.
On high mountains the air pressure is lower than in the valley.
Many smartphones have a built-in air pressure sensor.

abschnitte.text: Above us lies a thick layer of air, the atmosphere. Its weight presses on everything underneath it, and this pressure is called **air pressure**. We do not feel it, because it acts equally strongly from all sides and our body pushes back against it. A **barometer** measures how strong this pressure is at the moment. The name comes from the Greek “baros” for weight and “metron” for measure.

In 1643 the Italian physicist **Evangelista Torricelli** filled a long glass tube with **mercury** and stood it upside down in a dish. The mercury only sank a little way and stopped at a height of about 76 centimetres. The air pressure on the dish held the column up. An almost airless space formed above the mercury. A little later the Frenchman Blaise Pascal showed that the column is lower on a mountain than in the valley.

Because mercury is poisonous, today an **aneroid barometer** is usually used. Inside it is an almost airless metal capsule. If the air pressure rises, it is squeezed more; if it falls, the capsule expands again. Levers turn this movement into the movement of a pointer. A **barograph** draws the air pressure continuously as a curve on a paper strip. Smartphones contain tiny electronic pressure sensors that can even tell which floor you are on.

Many indoor barometers say “Stormy” or “Rain” on the left, “Change” in the middle and “Fair” on the right. With high air pressure, an **area of high pressure**, the weather is often fine and dry. With low air pressure, an **area of low pressure**, there are more often clouds, rain and wind. More important than the exact value is whether the barometer is rising or falling. If it falls quickly, bad weather may come soon.

The higher you climb, the less air lies above you and the lower the air pressure. At sea level it is on average about 1013 **hectopascals**. On the Jungfraujoch at around 3450 metres it is only about two thirds as much. That is why a barometer can also serve as an **altimeter**, for example when hiking or in an aeroplane. In Switzerland, air pressure is measured at many MeteoSwiss weather stations.

begriffe.erklaerung: The pressure that the weight of the air exerts on everything below it.
The unit in which air pressure is given in the weather forecast, hPa for short.
A poisonous metal that is liquid at room temperature.
A barometer that continuously records the air pressure on paper.
An area with high air pressure, often with fine weather.

gewusst: A barometer using water instead of mercury would need a tube more than 10 metres long.
A barometer also works in a closed room, because the pressure inside and outside evens out.
Air pressure presses on every square centimetre of our skin about as hard as a weight of one kilogram.

teile.einleitung: A bimetallic strip is a strip of two different metals that are firmly joined together. When it gets warm, it bends, because the two metals expand by different amounts. This simple trick is found in irons, thermometers, fire alarms and many other devices.
wichtigste: A bimetallic strip consists of two metals firmly joined together.
When heated, the two metals expand by different amounts, so the strip bends.
The strip bends towards the metal that expands less.
When it cools down again, it becomes straight again.
Often an iron-nickel alloy is combined with brass.
Bimetallic strips switch off the heating in irons and other devices when it is hot enough.
Dial thermometers show the temperature with a coiled bimetallic spiral.

abschnitte.text: A bimetallic strip consists of two thin metal strips that are firmly rolled or welded together along their whole length. Often **brass**, which expands a lot, is used with an iron-nickel alloy such as **Invar**, which hardly expands at all. The name comes from the Latin “bi” for two. Bimetallic elements come as straight strips, as discs or as coiled spirals.

Almost all substances expand when heated; this is called **thermal expansion**. For brass it is much greater than for Invar. Because the two strips are firmly joined, one side becomes longer than the other, and the strip has to curve. The metal that expands less is then on the inside of the curve, rather like the inside lane of a running track being shorter.

In an **iron** there is a bimetallic strip that opens an electrical contact as soon as the set temperature is reached. When the iron cools down, the strip bends back and switches the heating on again. Toasters, kettles, fan heaters and older fridges work in a similar way. Such a temperature switch is called a **thermostat**.

In simple fire alarms a bimetallic strip closes a circuit when it gets very hot, and a bell or siren sounds. In circuit breakers a bimetallic strip protects cables from overheating if too much current flows for too long. Many dial thermometers, for example in the oven or on the wall of a house, contain a coiled **bimetallic spiral**. It unwinds when warm and directly moves the pointer as it does so.

In the 18th century the English clockmaker **John Harrison** used bimetallic strips in his very accurate marine clocks. They made up for the fact that metal parts of the clock changed in heat and cold. In this way the clock could keep accurate time on the high seas even when temperatures changed. This helped sailors to work out their position at sea.

begriffe.erklaerung: A strip of two different metals firmly joined together.
Substances get slightly bigger when heated and smaller when cooled.
A switch that turns a device on or off at a certain temperature.
A mixture of metals, for example brass made of copper and zinc.

gewusst: The typical click of an iron or a kettle is often the bimetallic strip switching the current on or off.
The alloy Invar expands so little that its name comes from the French word for “unchanging”.
The Swiss physicist Charles-Édouard Guillaume received the Nobel Prize in Physics in 1920, partly for discovering Invar.

teile.einleitung: The bar is a unit of pressure. One bar corresponds roughly to the air pressure at sea level. You come across it in the weather forecast, with bike tyres, in diving and even with coffee machines.
wichtigste: One bar is exactly 100,000 pascals.
One bar corresponds to 1000 hectopascals or 1000 millibars.
One millibar is exactly the same as one hectopascal.
The bar is not an SI unit, but it is an approved unit in Switzerland and the EU.
The name comes from the Greek word baros, meaning weight.
Normal air pressure at sea level is about 1.013 bar.
Full compressed-air cylinders for scuba divers have about 200 bar.

abschnitte.text: The **bar** is a unit of pressure, that is of force per area. One bar is exactly 100,000 **pascals**, which is the name of the official SI unit of pressure. The name comes from the Greek word **baros**, meaning weight. The bar is practical because one bar is roughly as big as the air pressure we feel every day. With pascals, on the other hand, you would have very large numbers.

One bar is 1000 millibars or 1000 hectopascals. So a **millibar** is exactly one **hectopascal**. 2.5 bar corresponds to 250,000 Pa. A bike tyre with 4 bar of gauge pressure contains 400 kPa more pressure than its surroundings. Important: a tyre pressure gauge usually shows the gauge pressure, that is the pressure on top of the air pressure.

At sea level normal air pressure is about 1013 hPa, that is about 1.013 bar. Weather forecasts used to give the pressure in millibars and today give it in hectopascals; the numbers are the same. An **area of high pressure** often brings fine weather, an area of low pressure more often clouds and rain. In the mountains the air pressure is lower: on the Jungfraujoch at around 3500 m it is only about two thirds of the pressure at the sea. Air pressure is measured with a **barometer**.

Under water the pressure rises quickly. For every 10 metres of water depth, about 1 bar is added. So at a depth of 10 m there are around 2 bar, and at 30 m about 4 bar. That is why scuba divers take compressed-air cylinders filled to about 200 bar. At the deepest point of the ocean, in the Mariana Trench, the pressure is over 1000 bar.

Many devices give their pressure in bar. Car tyres usually have about 2 to 3 bar of gauge pressure, racing bike tyres much more. Good espresso machines force the water through the coffee at around 9 bar. Pressure washers work at over 100 bar. The water in the tap at home is also under a pressure of a few bar.

begriffe.erklaerung: A force acting on an area.
The official unit of pressure, one newton per square metre.
A hundred pascals, the unit for air pressure in the weather forecast.
How much greater the pressure is than the surrounding air pressure.
A measuring instrument for air pressure.

gewusst: The air presses on every square centimetre of your skin about as hard as a weight of one kilogram.
On the summit of Mount Everest the air pressure is only about a third of the pressure at sea level.
High-pressure water-jet cutters work at several thousand bar and can even cut steel.

teile.einleitung: A battery storage system is a large rechargeable battery that keeps electrical energy until it is needed. In this way, for example, solar electricity from midday can be used in the evening. Battery storage exists in houses, in electric cars and as huge installations for the power grid.
wichtigste: A battery storage system stores electricity as chemical energy.
Today mostly lithium-ion batteries are used.
The amount of energy stored is given in kilowatt hours.
A 10 kWh store can supply a 500-watt device for 20 hours.
After many charge cycles the storage capacity slowly decreases.
The Nobel Prize in Chemistry was awarded for the lithium-ion battery in 2019.
The Nant de Drance pumped storage power station in Valais is often called a giant water battery.

abschnitte.titel: How a rechargeable battery stores electricity
abschnitte.text: When charging, a rechargeable battery turns electrical energy into **chemical energy**. When discharging, the chemical reaction runs backwards and current flows again. In a lithium-ion battery, lithium ions travel back and forth between two terminals, rather like commuters between home and work. Unlike an ordinary battery, a rechargeable battery can be charged many hundreds or thousands of times.

How much energy a store holds is given in **kilowatt hours**. A 10 kWh store can run a 500-watt device for 20 hours, because 0.5 kilowatts times 20 hours makes 10 kilowatt hours. The **power** in kilowatts, on the other hand, tells you how fast the energy can be taken out. A home battery often has about 5 to 15 kWh, an electric car much more.

abschnitte.titel: Storage at home and in the grid
abschnitte.text: Many homeowners combine a solar installation on the roof with a **home battery**. At midday the installation often produces more electricity than is needed, and the surplus goes into the battery. In the evening, when the sun is no longer shining, it is used again. Large battery storage systems also help to keep the power grid stable, because they can step in very quickly.

Electricity can also be stored without batteries. At the **pumped storage power station** Nant de Drance near Finhaut in Valais, when there is surplus electricity, water is pumped from Lac d'Emosson into the higher reservoir of Vieux Emosson. When electricity is needed, the water flows back and drives turbines. The plant went fully into operation in 2022 and has an output of 900 megawatts, which is why it is called a giant water battery.

Rechargeable batteries need raw materials such as lithium, nickel and **cobalt**. A large part of the cobalt comes from the Democratic Republic of the Congo, where it is often mined under difficult and dangerous conditions. That is why batteries without cobalt are also being developed, for example with lithium iron phosphate. Old batteries lose capacity over time and should never go in the rubbish, but back to the shop, so that the raw materials can be recycled.

The lithium-ion battery was developed in the 1970s and 1980s. John Goodenough, Stanley Whittingham and Akira Yoshino received the **Nobel Prize** in Chemistry for it in 2019. Goodenough was 97 years old at the time, making him the oldest Nobel Prize winner of all time. Today this technology is found in mobile phones, laptops, e-bikes and electric cars.

begriffe.erklaerung: Also called an accumulator, a battery that can be charged again.
A unit of energy, for example for the amount of electricity a store holds.
Charging fully once and discharging again.
A power station that stores electricity by pumping water into a higher lake.

gewusst: The machine hall of Nant de Drance lies in a huge cavern deep inside the mountain.
Rechargeable batteries like neither great heat nor strong cold, which is why electric cars often have a shorter range in winter.

teile.einleitung: Motion means that a body changes its position over time. A rolling ball, a moving bus and a swing are in motion. Physics explains why things start rolling, get faster, brake or swing back and forth.
wichtigste: A ball at rest needs a push, that is a force, to start rolling.
A ball soon stops rolling on the grass, because friction slows it down.
You slip most easily on ice, because the friction there is very small.
If the bus brakes suddenly, passengers fall forwards, because their bodies want to keep going.
This property is called inertia.
A bike tyre has a tread with grooves so that it grips better.
A swing that you push once swings back and forth.

abschnitte.text: A body is in **motion** when it changes its position. Motion is described with distance, time and **speed**. Whether something is moving depends on where you are looking from: in the train you are sitting still, but for someone on the platform you are going past. There are straight-line motions, circular motions and oscillations.

A ball at rest stays where it is until someone pushes it. To start, brake or steer a motion, you need a **force**. Isaac Newton described this in 1687 in his laws of motion. The harder the push, the faster the ball starts rolling.

Every body wants to keep its state of motion; this is called **inertia**. If a bus brakes suddenly, the passengers’ bodies want to keep going, so they tip forwards. If the bus starts with a jolt, they are pushed backwards. That is why seat belts in cars are so important.

A ball on the grass gets slower because **friction** slows it down. Friction arises when two surfaces rub against each other. On ice it is very small, which is why you slip easily there and skaters glide a long way. A bike tyre has a **tread** with grooves so that it has more grip and holds even on wet roads.

A swing that you push once swings back and forth. This kind of motion is called an **oscillation**. For a pendulum, the time of one swing depends on its length, not on its weight. Because of friction, however, the swing slowly gets smaller until it stops. Pendulum clocks use this regular motion to measure time.

begriffe.erklaerung: Something that can push, brake or deform a body.
The tendency of a body to carry on as before.
A braking force between two surfaces.
A motion that goes regularly back and forth.

gewusst: In space there is almost no friction, so space probes keep flying for decades without a motor.
Even when you are sitting still, you are moving round the sun with the Earth at around 30 kilometres per second.

teile.einleitung: An excavator is a large construction machine that digs out and loads earth, stones and rubble. With its strong arm and bucket it manages in minutes what people with shovels would need days for. Its enormous strength comes from hydraulics, that is from oil being pressed into cylinders.
wichtigste: An excavator digs with a bucket at the end of its arm.
The power for the arm comes from oil being pressed into cylinders at high pressure.
Large excavators often run on caterpillar tracks so that they do not sink into mud.
On many excavators the upper part with the cab can turn right round in a circle.
The excavator driver sits in the cab.
Instead of the bucket, you can fit a hydraulic breaker, for example.
The walking excavator with legs was invented in Switzerland for steep slopes.

abschnitte.text: An excavator consists of an **undercarriage** with wheels or caterpillar tracks and an upper part. On the upper part sit the engine, the cab and the arm, the boom. On many excavators the upper part can turn right round in a circle, so the excavator can dig out earth and load it straight onto a lorry. Caterpillar tracks spread the weight over a large area so that the machine does not sink into soft ground.

abschnitte.titel: Hydraulics as a source of power
abschnitte.text: A diesel engine or an electric motor drives a pump. This presses **hydraulic oil** at very high pressure into cylinders on the arm. In the cylinder, the oil pushes out a piston, and so the boom, the dipper arm and the bucket move. Because oil can hardly be compressed, you can control huge forces with small movements of a lever.

The **bucket** is the most important tool. But it can be swapped for other tools, such as a grab, shears or a **hydraulic breaker**, which smashes concrete. When houses are demolished you often see excavators with long arms and demolition shears. With a grab an excavator can even lift tree trunks or scrap metal.

On the steep slopes of the Swiss mountains, ordinary excavators can hardly make progress. That is why in the 1960s the businessman Ernst Menzi from Widnau in the St Gallen Rhine valley developed the **walking excavator**. It has legs with wheels and can use them to move like an insect over obstacles and through stream beds. Under the name Menzi Muck it is known today on building sites in many countries.

There are tiny mini excavators that even fit into a garden. In open-cast mines where coal is dug out, on the other hand, gigantic **bucket-wheel excavators** are at work. The German Bagger 288 is over 200 metres long and weighs more than 13,000 tonnes. It is one of the largest vehicles in the world that can move.

begriffe.erklaerung: Technology in which liquids such as oil transmit forces.
The long arm of the excavator.
A moving band of links instead of wheels, which travels well on soft ground.
A heavy chisel on an excavator that smashes concrete and rock.

gewusst: With its legs a walking excavator can support itself safely even on very steep ground and in stream beds.
Electric excavators are quieter and produce no exhaust fumes on the building site, so they are being used more and more in towns.

teile.einleitung: A frame of reference is the point of view from which a motion is described. Whether something is at rest or moving depends on what you compare it with. Someone sitting in a train is at rest for the other passengers, but moving fast for the cows in the field.
wichtigste: A frame of reference is the point of view from which a motion is observed and described.
Rest and motion are always relative, that is they depend on the frame of reference.
In everyday life we usually measure speeds relative to the Earth’s surface, for example the road.
The sun seems to move across the sky because the Earth turns on its own axis.
A geostationary satellite seems to stand still because it orbits the Earth exactly as fast as the Earth turns.
In a train travelling steadily in a straight line, a ball falls straight down for the passengers.

abschnitte.text: Mia is sitting in a moving train reading a book. For the person sitting next to her she is not moving at all, so she is at **rest**. For a farmer beside the railway line, however, she is whizzing past at perhaps 120 km/h. Both are right, because they are using different **frames of reference**.

abschnitte.titel: Frames of reference in everyday life
abschnitte.text: When we say a car is doing 50 km/h, we almost always mean: 50 km/h relative to the **road**. The road and the ground are our usual frame of reference. If a car is driving at 50 km/h beside another car also doing 50 km/h, the speed between the two is zero. That is why at the same speed you can wave from car to car as if you were standing still.

Many people know this: you are sitting in a stationary train, the train next to you starts moving, and you think your own train is rolling. This happens because you unconsciously take the other train as your frame of reference. Only a glance at the **platform** or a building shows who is really moving. So our brain needs a fixed point of comparison to recognise motion correctly.

Seen from the Earth, the sun rises in the east and sets in the west. In reality the Earth turns once a day on its **axis**. A point on the equator travels around 40,075 km in 24 hours, which is around 1670 km/h. We feel nothing of this, because we move along with the whole Earth, the air and everything around us.

Television satellites circle at a height of around 36,000 km above the equator. They take exactly as long for one lap as the Earth takes to turn once. That is why, seen from Earth, they always seem to be in the same place in the sky; they are called **geostationary**. That is why a satellite dish on a balcony can point firmly in one direction.

abschnitte.titel: Inertial frames and the history of physics
abschnitte.text: A frame of reference that moves steadily in a straight line is called an **inertial frame**. In such a frame the laws of physics apply exactly as in one at rest. That is why in a smoothly moving train a ball falls straight down below your hand, whereas for someone outside it flies in a curve. Galileo Galilei already recognised this idea, and Albert Einstein built his theory of relativity on it in Bern.

begriffe.erklaerung: The point of view or object with which a motion is compared.
Depending on where you look at something from.
A frame of reference that is at rest or moves steadily in a straight line.
Always in the same place in the sky as seen from the Earth.

gewusst: Even when you are sitting completely still on the sofa, you are racing round the sun with the Earth at around 30 km per second.
Albert Einstein published his special theory of relativity in 1905, when he was working at the patent office in Bern.
For an astronaut on the Moon the Earth does not rise and set; it stays almost always in the same place in the sky.

teile.einleitung: Bernoulli’s equation describes how pressure and speed are connected in flowing liquids and gases. Its main message is surprising: where the flow is faster, the pressure is lower. With it, water pipes, sprayers and partly also flying can be explained.
wichtigste: Bernoulli’s equation applies to flowing liquids and gases.
In a faster-flowing liquid or gas, the pressure is lower.
It is named after the Basel scholar Daniel Bernoulli.
Bernoulli published it in 1738 in his book “Hydrodynamica”.
The equation is based on the conservation of energy.
Among other things, it helps to explain how aeroplane wings produce lift.
Engineers need it for pipes, nozzles and measuring instruments.

abschnitte.text: Daniel Bernoulli lived from 1700 to 1782 and came from a famous **family of scholars in Basel**. He was a doctor, mathematician and physicist and taught at the University of Basel. In 1738 his work **Hydrodynamica** appeared, in which he described the behaviour of flowing liquids. His father Johann and his uncle Jakob were also important mathematicians.

A flowing liquid has energy in two forms: kinetic energy and pressure energy. If no energy is lost, the total stays the same. If the flow gets faster, the kinetic energy rises, so the **pressure** must fall. This rule is also called **Bernoulli’s principle**.

When water flows through a pipe that gets narrower, it must flow faster at the narrow point. That is exactly where the pressure falls. This effect is called the **Venturi effect**, after the Italian Giovanni Battista Venturi. It is used in water-jet pumps, perfume sprayers and, in the past, in the carburettors of car engines.

Over a curved aeroplane wing the air flows faster than underneath, so the pressure at the top is lower. This difference in pressure contributes to **lift**. Physicists stress, however, that deflecting the air downwards is also important. You also know the effect from the shower curtain, which bulges inwards when the water is running.

Hold two sheets of paper close together and blow between them. Instead of flying apart, they move towards each other, because the air pressure between them falls. A table tennis ball stays floating in the stream of air from a hairdryer. A **pitot tube** is used in a similar way to measure the speed of aeroplanes.

begriffe.erklaerung: How strongly a force presses on an area.
The movement of a liquid or a gas.
The drop in pressure at a narrow point of a pipe, where the flow is faster.
Energy is not lost; it only changes its form.

gewusst: The Bernoulli family produced eight important mathematicians over three generations.
When two ships sail close side by side, they can be drawn together because of the drop in pressure between them.

teile.einleitung: Lighting means making rooms, streets or objects bright with artificial light. Since the invention of the electric lamp we can read, work and travel safely at night too. Modern LED lamps need much less electricity for this than the old light bulbs.
wichtigste: LED lamps need the least electricity for the same amount of light.
Old light bulbs get hot because they give off most of their energy as heat.
For some years, most classic light bulbs have no longer been allowed to be sold in Switzerland.
During the day it is best to use daylight instead of a lamp.
The last person to leave a room should switch off the light; this is always worth it, even with LEDs.
A motion detector switches the light on when someone moves.
Too much light at night disturbs animals and hides the starry sky.

abschnitte.text: For thousands of years people lit their homes with fire, candles and oil lamps. In the 19th century gas lamps came to the streets of towns. Around 1879 Thomas Edison and Joseph Swan developed usable **light bulbs**. Today **LED lamps** are the most widespread; they consist of small semiconductor chips that light up when current flows through them.

In a light bulb a thin wire of tungsten gets so hot that it glows. Only a small part of the energy becomes light; the rest becomes heat. An LED needs only a fraction of the electricity for the same brightness and lasts much longer. That is why most classic light bulbs have been banned in Switzerland and the EU for some years.

How brightly a lamp shines is given in **lumens**, and its electricity use in watts. Good LED lamps produce a lot of lumens per watt. The colour of the light is given in kelvin: warm white light feels cosy, cool white light looks more like daylight. For desks and classrooms bright, even light is important so that the eyes do not get tired.

The simplest tip: switch the light off when you leave the room; this always saves electricity, even with LEDs. During the day **daylight** through the window is often enough. In stairwells and garages, motion detectors or timers only switch the light on when it is needed. Light-coloured walls also help, because they reflect the light.

Too much artificial light at night is called **light pollution**. Many insects fly round lamps until they are exhausted, and migrating birds can lose their way. In towns you can hardly see any stars, and the Milky Way cannot be made out at all. In Switzerland, for example, the Gantrisch nature park and many municipalities are working for darker nights, for instance by making street lamps shine downwards or dimming them at night.

begriffe.erklaerung: Light-emitting diode, an energy-saving lamp made of a small semiconductor chip.
The unit for how much light a lamp gives off.
A sensor that detects movement and switches the light on.
Too much artificial light at night, which disturbs nature and the starry sky.

gewusst: A light bulb turns only about five per cent of its energy into light; the rest is heat.
In a fire station in California a light bulb has been burning almost without a break for over 100 years.
Good LED lamps often last 15,000 hours and more, an old light bulb usually only about 1000 hours.

teile.einleitung: Didier Queloz is a Swiss astronomer who in 1995, together with Michel Mayor, discovered the first planet orbiting a sun-like star outside our solar system. This planet is called 51 Pegasi b. For this discovery Queloz received a share of the Nobel Prize in Physics in 2019.
wichtigste: Didier Queloz was born in Switzerland in 1966 and studied at the University of Geneva.
In 1995, with Michel Mayor, he discovered the exoplanet 51 Pegasi b.
51 Pegasi b is a hot Jupiter, a gas giant very close to its star.
Queloz and Mayor each received a quarter of the 2019 Nobel Prize in Physics.
The other half went to the cosmologist James Peebles.
The discovery was made with the radial velocity method.
Today several thousand exoplanets are known.

abschnitte.text: Didier Queloz is an astronomer from French-speaking Switzerland. He studied physics at the **University of Geneva** and wrote his doctoral thesis there under Michel Mayor. Later he also did research at the University of Cambridge in England. For some years he has also been working at ETH Zurich, where he studies how life can arise in the universe. He is regarded as one of the pioneers of exoplanet research.

In 1995 Queloz and Mayor observed the star 51 Pegasi in the constellation of Pegasus. To do so they used a very precise measuring instrument, a **spectrograph**, at the Haute-Provence Observatory in France. They found that the star wobbles slightly back and forth regularly, about every four days. From this they concluded that a large planet was orbiting it. It was the first confirmed planet orbiting a sun-like star outside the solar system.

A star and its planet both circle round their common centre of mass. That is why the star also moves in a small orbit. The **radial velocity** is the part of its velocity along our line of sight. If the star moves away from us, its spectral lines are shifted towards red; if it comes towards us, towards blue. From this change the mass of the planet can be estimated.

A second method is the **transit**: when a planet passes in front of its star, the star gets a little darker. If the planet has a radius of a tenth of the star’s radius, the brightness falls by around one per cent. In this way the radius of the planet is found. If you know the mass and the radius, you can calculate its average density. This tells you whether a planet is made mainly of gas or of rock.

51 Pegasi b is about half as heavy as Jupiter, but orbits its star much more closely than Mercury orbits the sun. Such planets are called **hot Jupiters**. Because of the strong tidal forces, it probably always shows its star the same side. It is thought that such gas giants formed further out and later moved inwards. This discovery showed that other planetary systems can look completely different from ours.

begriffe.erklaerung: A planet that orbits a star other than the sun.
An instrument that splits light into its colours and measures it precisely.
Light looks redder when its source is moving away from us.
A planet passes in front of its star as seen from us.

gewusst: A year on 51 Pegasi b lasts only about four Earth days.
The planet 51 Pegasi b was later also given the name Dimidium.
Before 1995 researchers did not know for sure whether there were any planets at all orbiting other sun-like stars.

teile.einleitung: In archery you shoot arrows at a target with a bow. In the past the bow was used for hunting and in war; today archery is an Olympic sport. There is a lot of physics behind it: elastic energy, flight paths and gravity.
wichtigste: The cord on the bow is called the string.
When drawn, the bent bow stores the force as elastic energy.
The further you pull back the string, the faster the arrow flies.
The feathers at the end of the arrow make it fly straight.
Because the arrow drops on the way, you aim a little higher for distant targets.
In Olympic archery the target is 70 metres away, and its centre is yellow.
In the legend, William Tell shot with a crossbow, not with a bow.

abschnitte.text: A bow consists of an elastic stave, the limbs, and the **string**, which joins its ends. In the past bows were made of wood such as yew; today they are mostly made of wood, fibreglass and carbon fibre. Arrows today are often made of aluminium or carbon and have a point at the front and the **fletching** at the back. In sport the main kinds are the recurve bow, with ends curving forwards, and the compound bow, with pulleys.

When you pull back the string, the bow bends and stores **elastic energy**, rather like a stretched spring. When you let go, the bow springs back and passes the energy on to the arrow. It becomes the **kinetic energy** of the arrow. The further you draw the string, the more energy is stored in the bow and the faster the arrow flies.

As soon as the arrow has left the string, **gravity** pulls it downwards. That is why it does not fly dead straight, but in a slight curve, a parabola. For a distant target you therefore have to aim a little higher. The feathers at the end of the arrow act like the fins of a rocket and keep the arrow steady in the direction of flight.

Archery was already an Olympic sport in 1900 and has been a permanent part of the programme since 1972. In the Olympic recurve competition the target is 70 metres away. It has a diameter of 122 cm and ten rings in the colours white, black, blue, red and **yellow** in the middle. A hit right in the centre scores 10 points, which is about like hitting a CD from 70 metres away.

The best-known Swiss shooting story is the legend of **William Tell**. In Altdorf he had to shoot an apple off his son’s head, and he did it with a **crossbow**. On a crossbow the bow is fixed crosswise on a stock, and the drawn string is held by a trigger. Today archery is practised in many clubs in Switzerland, including field archery in the woods.

begriffe.erklaerung: The cord that joins the two ends of the bow.
The feathers or plastic vanes at the back end of the arrow.
Energy stored in an object that has been bent or stretched.
An Olympic bow whose ends curve forwards, away from the archer.
A weapon with a bow lying crosswise on a stock and a trigger.

gewusst: Ötzi, the roughly 5300-year-old glacier mummy from the Alps, was carrying an unfinished yew bow and a quiver of arrows.
An arrow from a competition bow is so fast that it covers the 70 metres in well under a second.
The Tell monument in Altdorf shows William Tell with the crossbow over his shoulder and his son Walter.

teile.einleitung: Thunder is the loud crash and rumble you hear in a thunderstorm. It happens because lightning heats the air extremely strongly in an instant. Because sound is much slower than light, you can even use thunder to work out how far away a thunderstorm is.
wichtigste: Thunder happens because lightning heats the air very quickly.
First you see the lightning, and only afterwards do you hear the thunder.
Light is much faster than sound.
The seconds between lightning and thunder divided by 3 give roughly the distance in kilometres.
If lightning and thunder come almost at the same time, the storm is very close.
It is not the thunder that is dangerous, but the lightning.
After the last thunder you should stay indoors for about another 30 minutes.

abschnitte.text: **Lightning** is a huge electric spark between a cloud and the ground or between clouds. In the lightning channel the air is heated in fractions of a second to about 30,000 degrees, which is hotter than the surface of the sun. The hot air expands explosively and creates a **pressure wave**. We hear this wave as thunder.

A lightning flash is often several kilometres long. The sound from nearby parts of the flash reaches us earlier than the sound from distant parts. That is why you do not hear just one bang, but a long roll and rumble. Mountains, houses and clouds also throw the sound back as an **echo**.

Light reaches us almost instantly, while sound takes about 3 seconds for a kilometre. The **speed of sound** in air is around 340 metres per second and depends mainly on the air temperature. If you count 3 seconds between lightning and thunder, the storm is about 1 kilometre away; at 9 seconds about 3 kilometres; at 12 seconds about 4 kilometres. Rule of thumb: seconds divided by 3 gives kilometres.

You seek shelter from the lightning, not from the thunder. If there are fewer than 30 seconds between lightning and thunder, the storm is at most about 10 kilometres away, and you should go into a **house** or a car. Outdoors you should avoid single trees, summits, ridges and water. After the last thunder you wait about another 30 minutes before going out again.

In Switzerland thunderstorms happen mainly in summer, when warm, moist air rises and forms tall **thunderclouds**. Lightning and thunder are especially frequent in Ticino and along the edge of the Alps. MeteoSwiss warns of strong thunderstorms with hail and squalls. In the mountains thunder echoes for a particularly long time between the valley walls.

In the past people explained thunder with gods. The Germanic peoples believed that the god Donar, or Thor, was striking with his hammer. **Thursday** is named after him, as is the German word for it, “Donnerstag”. In Greek legend the father of the gods, Zeus, hurled the lightning bolts.

begriffe.erklaerung: Vibrations of the air that we hear with our ears.
A spreading wave of squeezed-together air.
How fast sound travels, about 340 metres per second in air.
A very tall cloud, also called cumulonimbus, in which lightning forms.

gewusst: Thunder can usually only be heard up to about 20 kilometres away; more distant lightning is often seen only as silent heat lightning.
Light is almost a million times faster than the sound of thunder.
The day Thursday is named after the Germanic thunder god Thor, called Donar in German.

teile.einleitung: A lift, which is also called a lift in Switzerland, carries people and goods comfortably from one floor to another. A car travels up and down a vertical shaft. Without lifts there would be no tower blocks, because nobody wants to walk up 50 floors.
wichtigste: In Switzerland a lift is usually called a “Lift” rather than an “Aufzug”.
The car of a traction lift hangs on steel cables.
At the other end of the cables hangs a counterweight that takes work off the motor.
Elisha Otis invented a safety brake that stops the lift if the cable breaks.
If there is a fire in the building, you must not use the lift.
The highest outdoor lift in Europe stands on the Bürgenstock on Lake Lucerne.
The Swiss company Schindler is one of the biggest lift makers in the world.

abschnitte.text: The car hangs on several **steel cables** that run over a grooved wheel, the traction sheave. An electric motor turns this wheel and so pulls the car up or lets it down. At the other end of the cables hangs a heavy **counterweight**. Because the car and the counterweight almost balance each other, the motor needs much less force, rather like on a seesaw.

Modern lifts have many safety devices. Light barriers make the door open again if something is in the way. A sign shows how many people or how many kilograms may travel, and if it is overloaded the lift does not move. In a fire you should never take the lift but use the **stairs**, because the power can fail and smoke can spread in the shaft.

abschnitte.titel: Elisha Otis and the safety brake
abschnitte.text: In the past people were afraid that a cable might break and the car would crash down. The American **Elisha Otis** therefore invented a safety catch. At a famous demonstration in New York in the 1850s, he stood on a platform and had the rope cut through, and the brake held him. After that passenger lifts became more and more popular, and tower blocks became possible.

In 1874 Robert Schindler founded the company in Lucerne that became today’s **Schindler** group, based in Ebikon. Schindler builds lifts and escalators for buildings all over the world. A special one is the **Hammetschwand Lift** on the Bürgenstock, which has been travelling around 150 metres up a rock face since 1905. It is regarded as the highest outdoor lift in Europe and offers a wonderful view over Lake Lucerne.

As well as traction lifts there are **hydraulic lifts**, in which a piston with oil pushes the car up. They are often used for just a few floors or for heavy loads. There are passenger lifts, goods lifts, bed lifts in hospitals and car lifts. For people in wheelchairs or with pushchairs lifts are especially important, so that buildings are accessible to everyone.

begriffe.erklaerung: The space in which you travel in a lift.
A heavy weight that balances the car and takes the strain off the motor.
An emergency brake that clamps the car to the rails if it goes too fast.
The vertical tunnel in the building in which the lift travels.

gewusst: In very tall skyscrapers the fastest lifts travel at over 60 kilometres per hour.
In many tower blocks you have to change lifts, because a single lift does not go all the way to the top.
When a lift starts going up, you briefly feel as if you are getting heavier.

teile.einleitung: The work done in accelerating is the work you have to do to make a body faster. Whether it is a bike, a car or a sprinter: anyone who wants to set off or start running has to put energy in. Afterwards this energy is stored in the body as kinetic energy.
wichtigste: Work done in accelerating is the work that makes a body faster.
Starting from rest: work equals one half times mass times speed squared.
With a constant force the work is force times distance; 500 newtons over 20 metres gives 10,000 joules.
The work done in accelerating is then stored in the body as kinetic energy.
Going from 50 to 100 km/h takes a car three times as much work as going from 0 to 50 km/h.
Without losses, a car of 1000 kg needs about 386 kilojoules to reach 100 km/h.
Electric cars can recover some of their kinetic energy when braking through regenerative braking.

abschnitte.titel: What is work done in accelerating?
abschnitte.text: In physics you do **work** when a force moves a body along a path. If the body gets faster in the process, it is called **work done in accelerating**. Like all energy, it is measured in joules. One joule is roughly the work needed to lift a 100-gram bar of chocolate by one metre.

If a constant force F acts over the distance s, the work W equals F times s. If a body of 2 kilograms is accelerated at 3 metres per second squared over 4 metres, the force is 6 newtons and the work 24 joules. Starting from rest, it is also true that W equals one half times m times v squared. So a sprinter of 70 kilograms who accelerates to 10 metres per second does 3500 joules of work.

Because the speed appears squared, it gets more and more expensive at higher speeds. Going from 0 to 50 km/h takes a car a certain amount of work, but from 50 to 100 km/h three times as much. From a starting speed to a final speed, you calculate with the **difference of the squares**. That is why a bike and rider of 100 kilograms need 3750 joules to go from 5 to 10 metres per second.

Without losses, a train of 400 tonnes needs 80 megajoules to go from standing to 20 metres per second, that is 72 km/h. A car of 1000 kilograms needs about 386 kilojoules for 100 km/h. In reality it needs even more energy, because **air resistance** and rolling friction slow it down. That is why frequent starting and braking in town traffic uses a lot of fuel.

The work done in accelerating is not lost; it is stored as **kinetic energy** in the moving vehicle. With normal braking this energy becomes heat in the brakes. Electric cars, e-bikes and many trains, on the other hand, can use the motor as a generator when braking. This **regenerative braking** charges the battery again, and in this way SBB feeds electricity back into the railway grid when trains brake.

begriffe.erklaerung: In physics: force times distance, that is energy that is transferred.
The unit of work and energy.
The unit of force.
Recovering kinetic energy when braking.

gewusst: A cheetah needs so much energy for its sprint that it is exhausted after a short chase and has to rest.
The work done in accelerating a car to 100 km/h corresponds roughly to the energy needed to lift it around 39 metres.

teile.einleitung: Conservation of angular momentum is a basic law of physics for everything that turns. It says that the momentum of a rotation is kept as long as nothing from outside changes it. That is why a figure skater spins faster when she pulls in her arms.
wichtigste: Angular momentum is conserved if no outside torque acts.
Angular momentum depends on the moment of inertia and the speed of rotation.
If a figure skater pulls in her arms, her moment of inertia falls and she spins faster.
Kepler’s second law, the law of equal areas, follows directly from the conservation of angular momentum.
Neutron stars spin extremely fast because their radius shrinks greatly when they collapse.
The tail rotor of a helicopter stops the body from turning against the main rotor.
According to Noether’s theorem, conservation of angular momentum follows from all directions in space being equivalent.

abschnitte.text: **Angular momentum** describes how much momentum a turning body has. It is the product of the **moment of inertia** and the angular velocity. The moment of inertia is large when the mass is far from the axis of rotation. Conservation of angular momentum says that this product stays the same as long as no outside torque acts.

A figure skater spins at 2 revolutions per second and has a moment of inertia of 4 kg·m². If she pulls in her arms, it falls to 1.6 kg·m². Because the angular momentum stays the same, she now spins at 5 revolutions per second. The extra **rotational energy** comes from the work of her muscles pulling her arms inwards. Divers also spin faster in a somersault when they curl up.

A planet moves faster close to the sun than far away from it. This is described by Johannes Kepler’s second law, the **law of equal areas**, and it follows from the conservation of angular momentum. When a huge star collapses into a **neutron star**, it shrinks to about 20 kilometres across. Like the figure skater, it then spins enormously faster, some of them hundreds of times a second.

When a helicopter’s engine turns the main rotor, the body would turn the other way without something to counter it. The **tail rotor** pushes sideways against this and keeps the body straight. Helicopters with two main rotors turning in opposite directions do not need a tail rotor. Satellites also point themselves with fast-spinning flywheels without using any fuel.

Sit on a swivel chair and hold a fast-spinning bicycle wheel with its axle upright. If you turn the wheel over, the chair starts to turn with you. The total angular momentum of you and the wheel has to stay the same. In 1918 the mathematician Emmy Noether showed with **Noether’s theorem** that this law follows from the fact that no direction in space is preferred.

begriffe.erklaerung: A measure of the momentum of a turning motion.
Tells you how hard it is to set a body turning, depending on how its mass is spread out.
The turning effect of a force, for example with a spanner.
A law of nature according to which a certain quantity always stays the same.

gewusst: A falling cat can turn in the air and land on its paws without changing its total angular momentum.
A rolling bike also stays balanced more easily thanks to its spinning wheels.
The Earth has been turning for billions of years, because hardly anything slows down its angular momentum.

teile.einleitung: A balloon rocket is a simple experiment in which a blown-up balloon whizzes along a string. The air rushing out backwards drives the balloon forwards. Real rockets fly into space on exactly the same principle.
wichtigste: A balloon rocket is driven by the air rushing out.
If the air flows backwards, the balloon moves forwards.
You thread a drinking straw onto a tight string.
The string gives the balloon its direction.
A balloon blown up more usually flies further.
When there is no more air in the balloon, the rocket stops.
The experiment shows the principle of recoil, which Isaac Newton already described.

abschnitte.text: The balloon rocket is a popular physics **experiment** that you can do at home or at school. A balloon is stuck to a drinking straw that can slide along a tight string. When you let go of the balloon, it shoots along the string. The experiment shows clearly how **recoil** works.

You need a balloon, a drinking straw, a long piece of string and sticky tape. Thread the **straw** onto the string and stretch the string between two chairs or across the room. Blow up the balloon, hold the opening closed and stick it to the straw with two strips of tape. When you let go, the rocket shoots off.

In the blown-up balloon the air is squeezed together, and the stretched rubber skin pushes it out. The air rushes out backwards through the opening. At the same time an equal force acts on the balloon in the opposite direction and pushes it forwards. This law is called the **principle of interaction**, or action equals reaction.

The more air there is in the balloon, the longer the thrust lasts and the further it usually flies. The string gives the direction; otherwise the balloon would flap wildly through the air. A smooth, tightly stretched string reduces **friction**. You can also test whether long or round balloons are faster, or whether the rocket can get up a sloping string.

Real **rockets** work on the same principle. Instead of air, they push out hot gases produced by burning fuel. Because they carry the oxygen for burning with them, they can even fly in airless space. The English scientist **Isaac Newton** described the principle of force and counter-force as early as 1687.

You can also see recoil in other places. If you jump from a small boat onto the bank, the boat slides backwards away from you. A garden hose that suddenly sprays water jerks back. Octopuses and jellyfish also move by pushing water out behind them.

begriffe.erklaerung: The movement of a body in the opposite direction when it pushes something out backwards.
A law of physics: every force produces an equal counter-force.
A force that slows down movement when things rub against each other.
The driving force of a rocket or an engine.

gewusst: The balloon often squeals as it flies, because the rubber opening vibrates rapidly as the air rushes out.
With two balloons stuck one behind the other you can build a two-stage rocket, as with real rockets.
Jet aeroplanes are also driven by recoil, by pushing air and exhaust gases out backwards at high speed.
