teile.einleitung: A fuel cell is a device that produces electricity directly from hydrogen and oxygen. Unlike an engine, it does not burn the fuel with a flame. The only exhaust it produces is water.
wichtigste: A fuel cell turns the chemical energy of hydrogen and oxygen directly into electricity.
The waste product is almost only water and some heat.
It works rather like a battery, but does not need to be recharged.
As long as fuel is supplied, it produces electricity.
The principle was discovered by Christian Friedrich Schönbein in Basel in 1838.
Fuel cells drive cars, lorries, buses and spacecraft.
It is important that the hydrogen is produced in a climate-friendly way.

abschnitte.text: A **fuel cell** is an energy converter. It is continuously supplied with fuel, usually **hydrogen**, and with oxygen from the air. From these it makes electricity directly, without fire and without moving parts. Unlike a battery, the fuel is topped up from outside, so it is never flat as long as supplies keep coming.

A cell consists of two **electrodes** with a thin membrane between them. On one side hydrogen atoms are split into protons and electrons. The protons travel through the membrane, while the electrons have to flow round the outside, and that is the electric current. On the other side they all join up again with oxygen to form **water**.

The chemist Christian Friedrich Schönbein, a professor at the University of Basel, described the principle in 1838. Shortly afterwards the Briton William Grove built the first working cell. For a long time the technology was expensive and hardly used. The breakthrough only came with **space travel**: NASA’s Apollo spacecraft produced their electricity with fuel cells, and the astronauts drank the water produced.

Today **fuel cell cars**, buses and lorries run on hydrogen. In Switzerland, from 2020, a few dozen Hyundai hydrogen lorries were on the roads for retailers such as Coop and Migros. Submarines, forklift trucks and emergency power systems also use fuel cells. Some houses have small fuel cell heating systems that supply electricity and heat at the same time.

Fuel cells are quiet and give off no CO₂ while driving. They are only climate-friendly, however, if the hydrogen is produced with electricity from water, sun or wind; then it is called **green hydrogen**. Producing, storing and transporting hydrogen is complicated and expensive. In addition, there are still only a few hydrogen filling stations.

begriffe.erklaerung: The lightest chemical element, a gas that is used as an energy carrier.
A connection at which a chemical reaction produces electricity.
A very thin layer that only lets certain particles through.
Hydrogen produced with renewable electricity.

gewusst: Schönbein from Basel also discovered the gas ozone and invented guncotton.
The exhaust of a fuel cell car is so clean that it consists only of water vapour.

teile.einleitung: Beta decay is one of the ways in which unstable atomic nuclei change. A neutron in the nucleus turns into a proton or the other way round, and one chemical element becomes another. It is caused by the weak interaction, one of the four fundamental forces of nature.
wichtigste: In beta-minus decay a neutron becomes a proton, and an electron and an electron antineutrino leave the nucleus.
In beta-plus decay a proton becomes a neutron.
In electron capture the nucleus takes in an electron from the innermost shell.
Beta decay is caused by the weak interaction.
The electrons have a continuous energy spectrum up to a maximum energy.
Tritium decays to helium-3, strontium-90 to yttrium-90.
A free neutron has a half-life of around 10 minutes.

abschnitte.text: In **beta-minus decay** a neutron becomes a proton, and the atomic number rises by one. In **beta-plus decay** a proton becomes a neutron, and a positron and a neutrino are given off. In **electron capture** the nucleus grabs an electron from the innermost shell and uses it to turn a proton into a neutron. The mass number, that is the number of all the particles in the nucleus, stays the same in all three cases.

Strontium-90 has the atomic number 38 and becomes yttrium-90, with the atomic number 39, through beta-minus decay. Tritium, a heavy hydrogen with one proton and two neutrons, becomes helium-3. Carbon-14 decays to nitrogen-14, which is used in dating. A free neutron outside a nucleus also decays; its **half-life** is around 10 minutes.

abschnitte.titel: The puzzle of the missing energy
abschnitte.text: In many decays all the particles always have the same energy. In beta decay, however, measurements showed a **continuous spectrum**: the electrons had every possible energy up to a maximum value. It looked as if energy was being lost. In 1930 Wolfgang Pauli, who taught at ETH Zurich, suggested an invisible neutral particle that carries away the missing energy.

In 1934 the Italian **Enrico Fermi** developed a theory of beta decay and gave the particle the name neutrino, meaning “little neutral one”. Neutrinos are so shy that they pass through almost any material unhindered. Only in 1956 did Clyde Cowan and Frederick Reines manage to detect neutrinos at a nuclear reactor. Strictly speaking, beta-minus decay produces an electron antineutrino.

Nature has four fundamental forces: gravity, the electromagnetic force, and the strong and the **weak interaction**. The weak interaction is responsible for beta decay. Inside a neutron one quark turns into another, and for a moment a so-called W boson is created. Without the weak interaction the sun would not shine either, because it takes part in the nuclear fusion inside the sun.

begriffe.erklaerung: The number of protons in the nucleus; it determines the chemical element.
The time after which half of the nuclei have decayed.
One of the four fundamental forces; among other things it causes beta decay.
A tiny building block of which protons and neutrons are made.

gewusst: Pauli first presented his idea of the neutrino in a letter that he sent to a meeting of physicists in Tübingen instead of going there himself.
Wolfgang Pauli received the Nobel Prize in Physics in 1945, but for a different discovery, the exclusion principle.

teile.einleitung: Coulomb’s law describes the force between two electrically charged particles. This force is called the Coulomb force and can attract or repel. It holds atoms together and makes rubbed balloons stick to the wall.
wichtigste: The force between two electrically charged particles is called the Coulomb force.
Like charges repel each other, unlike charges attract.
The bigger the charges, the stronger the force.
At twice the distance the force is only a quarter as big.
Charles-Augustin de Coulomb found the law in 1785.
The unit of charge, the coulomb, is named after him.

abschnitte.text: Electric **charges** come in two kinds, positive and negative. Between them acts a force, the **Coulomb force**. Like charges repel each other, unlike charges attract. If you rub a balloon on your hair, it becomes charged and then attracts the hair.

**Coulomb’s law** says how big the force is. It grows with the product of the two charges. At the same time it decreases with the square of the distance: at twice the distance only a quarter of the force acts, at three times the distance only a ninth. This form is similar to Isaac Newton’s law of gravitation.

The French physicist and engineer lived from 1736 to 1806. In 1785 he measured the force between charged little balls with a very fine **torsion balance**. The force twisted a thin wire, and from the twist he could read off the strength. The unit of charge, the **coulomb**, is named after him.

The Coulomb force keeps the negatively charged electrons close to the positively charged **atomic nucleus**. It also makes atoms join together into molecules. Compared with gravity it is enormously strong: between two electrons it is around 10 to the power of 42 times stronger than their attraction to each other through gravity. The reason we notice little of it in everyday life is that positive and negative charges usually balance each other out.

Electrostatic effects show the Coulomb force well. **Lightning** happens when large charges separate in thunderclouds and suddenly even out. Photocopiers and laser printers hold toner powder on the paper with electric charges. The little shock you get when you touch a door handle after walking over a carpet also comes from separated charges.

begriffe.erklaerung: A property of particles that can be positive or negative.
The unit of electric charge.
A sensitive measuring instrument that measures small forces through a twisted wire.
The study of electric charges at rest.

gewusst: Without the Coulomb force all objects would fall apart, because it holds the atoms together in tables, stones and our bodies.
In the atomic nucleus the protons repel each other, but the even stronger nuclear force still holds them together.

teile.einleitung: Atoms are the tiny building blocks that all substances are made of, from water and air to our own bodies. An atom has a small, heavy nucleus and a shell of electrons. Today 118 different kinds of atom are known: the chemical elements.
wichtigste: The word atom comes from the Greek “átomos” and means indivisible.
The Greek philosopher Democritus already taught that everything is made of atoms.
An atom is about one ten-millionth of a millimetre across.
The nucleus consists of protons and neutrons, the shell of electrons.
An atom consists almost entirely of empty space.
An atom is electrically neutral because it has as many protons as electrons.
Hydrogen has the simplest atom, with just one proton.
Today 118 chemical elements are known (as of 2025).

abschnitte.text: As early as the 5th century BC the Greek philosopher **Democritus** taught that everything is made of tiny, indivisible particles. He called them átomos, which means indivisible. He could not prove it. Only around 1808 did the Englishman **John Dalton** develop a scientific atomic theory that could explain chemical reactions.

In the centre lies the **atomic nucleus**, made of positively charged **protons** and uncharged **neutrons**. Round the nucleus is the shell with the negatively charged electrons. Because an atom has as many protons as electrons, it is electrically neutral from outside. The number of protons decides which element it is. Hydrogen has one proton, carbon six and gold 79.

An atom is about one ten-millionth of a millimetre across. If you enlarged an atom to the size of a football stadium, the nucleus would only be as big as a pea in the middle. Even so, almost all the mass is in the nucleus. The rest is almost entirely **empty space**, in which the tiny electrons move about.

In 1897 Joseph John Thomson discovered the **electron**. In 1911 Ernest Rutherford found out that an atom has a tiny, heavy nucleus. In 1913 the Dane Niels Bohr presented his **Bohr model of the atom**, in which the electrons circle the nucleus on fixed orbits, rather like planets round the sun. Today the electrons are described with quantum physics as clouds in which they are likely to be found. In 1932 James Chadwick discovered the neutron.

Atoms with the same number of protons form a **chemical element**. Today 118 elements are known, arranged in the periodic table. Atoms can join together to form **molecules**, for example two hydrogen atoms and one oxygen atom to make a water molecule. The whole variety of substances in the world is built up from these compounds.

At **CERN** in Geneva scientists from all over the world study the smallest building blocks of matter. At the Paul Scherrer Institute in Aargau atoms and particles are studied with large facilities. In 1905 in Bern, Albert Einstein wrote a paper that helped prove that atoms exist. With modern scanning tunnelling microscopes, developed at IBM in Rüschlikon, individual atoms can even be made visible.

begriffe.erklaerung: The tiny, heavy centre of the atom, made of protons and neutrons.
A positively charged particle in the atomic nucleus.
An uncharged particle in the atomic nucleus.
A tiny, negatively charged particle in the shell of the atom.
A substance that consists only of atoms with the same number of protons.

gewusst: A single drop of water contains more atoms than there are stars in the Milky Way.
The scanning tunnelling microscope, with which you can see atoms, was invented at IBM in Rüschlikon and won the Nobel Prize in 1986.
Most of the hydrogen atoms in our body date from the time shortly after the Big Bang.

teile.einleitung: The focal length is the distance between the centre of a lens and its focal point. It tells you how strongly a lens refracts light: the shorter the focal length, the stronger the lens. The focal length is important for glasses, magnifying glasses, cameras and our own eyes.
wichtigste: The focal length is the distance between the centre of the lens and the focal point.
A lens with a short focal length refracts light more strongly.
The more strongly curved a converging lens is, the shorter its focal length.
The lens of the eye curves more strongly when looking at something close, and its focal length gets shorter.
A telephoto lens with a long focal length brings distant things up close and large.
The focal length of a magnifying glass is measured as the distance to the smallest bright spot of sunlight.
The focal length is usually given in millimetres or centimetres.

abschnitte.text: When parallel light falls on a converging lens, the rays meet at the **focal point**. The distance from the centre of the lens to this point is called the **focal length** and is abbreviated with the letter f. For camera lenses it is given in millimetres, at school often in centimetres. If a lens has a focal length of 20 cm, twice the focal length lies 40 cm away from it.

A strongly curved, thick lens refracts light strongly, and its focal length is short. A flat lens refracts it only a little, and its focal length is long. Opticians give the strength of a lens as its **refractive power** in dioptres. The number of dioptres is 1 divided by the focal length in metres, so a lens with a focal length of 0.5 m has 2 dioptres.

You can work out the focal length of a **magnifying glass** very easily. Hold it in the sun and move it above a sheet of paper until the spot of light is smallest and brightest. Then measure the distance between the magnifying glass and the paper; that is roughly the focal length. Careful: do not point the spot at the paper for too long, and never look at the sun through the magnifying glass.

abschnitte.titel: The focal length in the eye
abschnitte.text: The eye contains an elastic **lens** that can change its shape. When you look into the distance, it is flatter and has a longer focal length. When you look at something close, small muscles contract, the lens curves more strongly and the focal length becomes shorter. This adjustment is called **accommodation** and becomes weaker with age, which is why many older people need reading glasses.

With cameras the focal length determines how large an object appears in the picture. A **wide-angle lens** with a short focal length shows a lot of the surroundings, for example a whole mountain landscape. A **telephoto lens** with a long focal length brings distant things up close and large, for example an ibex on a mountainside. A **zoom lens** can change its focal length, as with many mobile phone cameras, which combine several lenses.

begriffe.erklaerung: The distance between the centre of the lens and the focal point, abbreviated f.
The unit for the strength of a lens, 1 divided by the focal length in metres.
The focusing of the eye by changing the shape of the lens.
A camera lens with a long focal length for distant subjects.

gewusst: The lenses in a mobile phone camera often have a focal length of just a few millimetres.
Wildlife photographers use telephoto lenses with a focal length of 600 mm and more, which can be as long as a forearm.
The focal length of a diverging lens is given with a minus sign, which is why glasses for short-sighted people have negative dioptres.

teile.einleitung: An atomic clock is the most accurate clock there is. Instead of a pendulum or a quartz crystal, it counts the tiny, extremely regular vibrations of atoms. Good atomic clocks do not go wrong by even one second in many millions of years.
wichtigste: An atomic clock measures time with the help of the vibrations of atoms.
Since 1967 the second has been defined by the caesium-133 atom and no longer by the movement of the Earth.
A second lasts exactly 9,192,631,770 periods of the radiation of caesium-133.
The first working caesium atomic clock ran in Great Britain in 1955.
The long-wave transmitter DCF77 broadcasts the time for radio-controlled clocks in central Europe.
Without atomic clocks, satellite navigation with GPS would not work.
Optical atomic clocks are even more accurate, because they use a much higher frequency of vibration.

abschnitte.text: Every clock needs something that repeats itself very regularly, for example a pendulum. In an atomic clock it is the electrons in the atoms, which can only take in very particular amounts of energy. If microwaves with exactly the right **frequency** are shone on caesium atoms, they react especially strongly. A control loop keeps the microwaves exactly at this frequency, and electronics count the vibrations.

In the past the second was determined by the rotation of the Earth or its path round the sun. The Earth, however, does not turn completely evenly; it is slowed down slightly by the tides, for example. That is why in 1967 it was decided to define the **second** using caesium-133. Since then a second has been exactly 9,192,631,770 vibrations of this radiation.

The first working caesium atomic clock went into operation in 1955 at the National Physical Laboratory in Great Britain. It was built by Louis Essen and Jack Parry. Today there are so-called **caesium fountains**, in which atoms are gently tossed upwards and fall back down. The newest optical atomic clocks work with laser light and atoms such as strontium or ytterbium.

abschnitte.titel: World time and the leap second
abschnitte.text: Many atomic clocks in institutes all over the world are compared with each other and averaged. This produces **International Atomic Time, TAI**. Because the Earth turns irregularly, civil time has been adjusted to the Earth’s rotation now and then since 1972 with a **leap second**. Experts have decided to abolish leap seconds by 2035 at the latest.

Every GPS satellite contains atomic clocks. A navigation device calculates its position from the travel time of the radio signals, which move at the speed of light. If a clock is wrong by just one microsecond, the position is already around 300 metres out. **Radio-controlled clocks** in homes receive the time signal from the DCF77 transmitter near Frankfurt am Main and set themselves in this way.

In Switzerland the Federal Institute of Metrology, **METAS**, in Bern-Wabern is responsible for official time. Several atomic clocks run there and are compared with clocks abroad. In this way Swiss time feeds into worldwide atomic time. Station clocks, computers and mobile phones also ultimately get their exact time from such atomic clocks.

begriffe.erklaerung: A soft metal whose atoms are used to define the second.
Tells you how often something vibrates per second.
An extra second used to adjust the time to the rotation of the Earth.
A clock that sets itself to the correct time using a radio signal.

gewusst: The most accurate optical atomic clocks would not have gone wrong by even one second since the Big Bang.
Atomic clocks are so accurate that they show that time passes a tiny bit faster on a high mountain than in the valley.
A radio signal that travels for one microsecond covers around 300 metres.

teile.einleitung: Refraction is the change in direction of a wave when it passes at an angle from one material into another. The best known is the refraction of light: that is why a straw in a glass of water looks bent. Without refraction there would be no glasses, magnifying glasses or rainbows.
wichtigste: Light changes direction when it hits water from the air at an angle.
The reason is that light travels at different speeds in different materials.
In water light is slower than in air, and in glass slower still.
The law of refraction is also called Snell’s law.
Lenses in glasses, cameras and microscopes use refraction.
Because of refraction, a swimming pool looks shallower than it is.

abschnitte.text: When a ray of light hits water from the air at an angle, it is **refracted** and changes direction. That is why a straw in a glass looks bent at the surface of the water. If the ray comes in exactly at right angles, on the other hand, it carries on without bending. Refraction happens not only with light but with all **waves**, including sound and water waves.

In a vacuum light travels at about 300,000 kilometres per second, in water only about three quarters of that. When a ray hits water at an angle, one side is slowed down earlier than the other. It is like a toy car rolling at an angle from a smooth floor onto a carpet and turning as it does so. How strongly a material slows light down is given by its **refractive index**.

Around 1621 the Dutchman Willebrord Snellius found out how strongly light is refracted. The **law of refraction** links the angles before and after the boundary with the refractive indices. If light goes from water into air and the angle is very shallow, it is even reflected back completely. This **total internal reflection** is used in fibre-optic cables for the internet.

Curved pieces of glass, **lenses**, refract light so that it is brought together or spread out. A magnifying glass enlarges, and glasses correct short- or long-sightedness. Cameras, binoculars, microscopes and telescopes also contain lenses. Even our eye has a lens that focuses the light onto the retina.

A **rainbow** forms when sunlight is refracted and reflected in raindrops. On hot days the air shimmers above roads because warm air refracts light differently from cool air. This is also how mirages that look like puddles of water appear. From an angler’s point of view, fish appear in a different place from where they really are.

begriffe.erklaerung: The change in direction of a wave when it passes into a different material.
A number that tells you how strongly a material slows light down.
A curved, transparent piece of glass or plastic that focuses or spreads out light.
When light is completely reflected back at a boundary.

gewusst: Diamonds sparkle so strongly because they have a very high refractive index of about 2.4.
Because of refraction in the atmosphere, you can still see the sun in the evening when it is actually already below the horizon.

teile.einleitung: A battery is a small store of energy that supplies electricity when you need it. Batteries are found in torches, remote controls, watches and many toys. Inside them, chemical energy is turned into electrical energy.
wichtigste: A battery stores energy for electricity.
Its two terminals are called plus and minus.
A torch often works with batteries.
When the battery is flat, the device stops working.
A battery that can be recharged is called a rechargeable battery.
Used batteries belong at the collection point and never in the rubbish.
In Switzerland you can return batteries wherever they are sold.

abschnitte.text: A **battery** is a container with chemical substances inside it. These substances react with each other as soon as a device is switched on. Electrons then flow from one terminal through the device to the other terminal. This produces electric **current**, which, for example, makes a lamp light up.

Every battery has two terminals, the **positive terminal** and the **negative terminal**. On a round battery the positive terminal is usually the little button at the top. You must put the battery into the device the right way round, otherwise it does not work. Little symbols on the battery compartment show how the battery should go in.

Batteries come in many sizes, for example AA, AAA or flat button cells in watches. A normal AA battery has a voltage of 1.5 volts. Batteries are found in torches, remote controls, smoke alarms, hearing aids and toy cars. When the energy has been used up, the battery is **flat** and the device stops working.

A battery that can be recharged is called a **rechargeable battery**, or accumulator. Mobile phones, tablets, e-bikes and electric cars have rechargeable batteries, usually lithium-ion batteries. A rechargeable battery can be charged hundreds of times. This is kinder to the environment and saves money in the long run.

Batteries contain metals that are valuable but can also harm the environment. That is why used batteries belong at the **collection point**, never in household rubbish. In Switzerland you can take them back to any shop that sells batteries, for example the supermarket. When you buy them, you already pay a small fee for **recycling**, which recovers metals such as zinc and manganese.

begriffe.erklaerung: A store of energy that produces electricity with chemical substances.
A battery that can be charged up again.
One of the two connections of a battery, plus or minus.
Reusing waste so that raw materials can be used again.

gewusst: In 1800 the Italian Alessandro Volta built the first battery from metal discs stacked on top of each other.
With a lemon, a piece of copper and a galvanised nail you can make a small battery yourself.

teile.einleitung: Atomic physics is the branch of physics that studies the structure of atoms. Above all it investigates the electrons in the shell of the atom and how atoms give out or take in light. Without atomic physics there would be no lasers, no atomic clocks and no LED lamps.
wichtigste: Everything around us is made of tiny atoms.
An atom has a positively charged nucleus and a shell of negatively charged electrons.
Rutherford’s scattering experiment with a gold foil showed that atoms have a tiny, positively charged nucleus.
In diameter an atom is about ten thousand to a hundred thousand times bigger than its nucleus.
Isotopes of an element differ in the number of neutrons in the nucleus.
Electrons can only take on certain energy levels.
Every element gives out light with very particular colours, its spectral lines.

abschnitte.text: Atoms are the smallest building blocks of the chemical elements. An atom is about one ten-millionth of a millimetre across. In the centre sits the **atomic nucleus** of protons and neutrons, and round it move the **electrons**. The number of protons decides which element it is; for example, hydrogen has one and carbon six.

Around 1909, researchers in Ernest Rutherford’s laboratory fired alpha particles at an extremely thin **gold foil**. Most simply flew through, but a few were strongly deflected or even bounced back. In 1911 Rutherford concluded from this that almost all the mass sits in a tiny, positively charged **nucleus**. So the atom is mostly empty space: if the nucleus were the size of a pinhead, the atom would be as big as a football stadium.

abschnitte.titel: The Bohr model of the atom
abschnitte.text: In 1913 the Danish physicist Niels Bohr developed a new model. In it the electrons only circle on certain orbits with fixed energies, the **energy levels**. In the hydrogen atom the electron in its ground state has an energy of minus 13.6 electronvolts. If an electron jumps from a higher to a lower orbit, it gives out a particle of light, a **photon**. In the jump from n = 2 to n = 1 this photon has an energy of 10.2 eV.

If you send the light of a glowing gas through a prism, you see individual coloured lines instead of a rainbow. These **spectral lines** are like a fingerprint of the element. For hydrogen, the series of lines in the visible range is called the **Balmer series**, named after the Basel teacher Johann Jakob Balmer, who found a formula for it in 1885. With spectral lines astronomers can find out what distant stars are made of.

Atoms of the same element always have the same number of protons, but not always the same number of neutrons. Such variants are called **isotopes**. Carbon-12 and carbon-14, for example, are two isotopes of carbon. Carbon-14 is radioactive and is used to work out the age of bones or wood.

Atomic physics is found in many everyday devices. **Lasers** in barcode readers and **LED** lamps work because electrons jump between energy levels. Atomic clocks use the vibrations of atoms and are extremely accurate; they also control satellite navigation. In Switzerland the Federal Institute of Metrology, METAS, runs atomic clocks for official Swiss time.

begriffe.erklaerung: The tiny, heavy centre of an atom, made of protons and neutrons.
A very light, negatively charged particle in the shell of the atom.
A particle of light, that is a small packet of light energy.
A tiny unit of energy used in atomic physics.
A kind of atom of an element with a particular number of neutrons.

gewusst: Johann Jakob Balmer from Basel was actually a maths teacher at a girls’ school when he found his famous formula.
If you removed all the empty space from the atoms of the whole of humanity, the remaining matter would fit into a cube about the size of a sugar cube.

teile.einleitung: A crowbar is a long steel bar with which you can lift heavy things or prise something open. It is an example of a lever, one of the oldest machines of humankind. With it a single person can move loads they could never manage with bare hands.
wichtigste: A crowbar is used to lift heavy things or prise something open.
It is usually made of steel and is also called a pry bar.
The crowbar works as a lever with a pivot.
Because it is long, you need less force.
If you press the long end down, the load moves up.
A block of wood under the bar can serve as a fixed pivot.
The slot at the curved end is used for pulling out nails.

abschnitte.text: A crowbar is a strong bar of hardened **steel**, often 60 cm to over a metre long. One end is usually flat and wedge-shaped, the other curved like a hook. At the curved end there is often a **slot** with which you can pull out nails. In German the tool is also nicknamed “cow’s foot” or “nail iron”.

The crowbar is a **lever**: a bar that turns about a fixed point. This point is called the **pivot**; often it is an edge or a block of wood placed underneath. On one side is the load, and on the other you press with your hand. The law of the lever says: effort times effort arm equals load times load arm.

If the effort arm is ten times as long as the load arm, you need only a tenth of the force. That is why a crowbar is fairly long. If you press the long end down, the short end with the load rises. To do this, however, you have to move the handle a much longer way, so the **work** stays the same.

Building workers use crowbars to lift heavy stones or loosen planks and floor slabs. In emergencies the **fire brigade** often opens jammed doors with a crowbar or a similar tool. Joiners and tradespeople also need it when breaking up old wooden parts. Smaller levers work in exactly the same way, for example a bottle opener, scissors or a seesaw.

In the Stone Age people already moved heavy boulders with wooden poles used as levers. When pyramids and temples were built, levers helped to shift large stones. The Greek scholar **Archimedes** described the law of the lever precisely more than 2200 years ago. The famous saying that if you gave him a fixed point he could move the Earth comes from him.

begriffe.erklaerung: A bar that turns about a fixed point and can multiply force.
The point about which a lever turns.
The distance between the pivot and the place where you press.
The distance between the pivot and the load.

gewusst: In German the crowbar is called “cow’s foot” because its split end looks a little like a cow’s hoof.
With a long enough crowbar a child could in theory lift a car.
Your forearm is also a lever, with the elbow as the pivot.

teile.einleitung: An arch bridge is a bridge whose load-bearing part has the shape of an arch. Many old stone bridges are arch bridges, because this shape carries weight especially well. The Romans already built arch bridges that are still standing today, after almost 2000 years.
wichtigste: In an arch bridge an arch carries the load.
The arch leads the weight diagonally down to the sides.
In the arch the stones are pressed together, not pulled apart.
That is why stone and concrete are well suited to arch bridges.
The Romans built famous arch bridges and aqueducts such as the Pont du Gard.
In Switzerland the Landwasser Viaduct and the Salginatobel Bridge are well-known arch bridges.

abschnitte.text: An **arch bridge** rests on one or more arches spanning a valley or a river. The arch is the most important load-bearing part. The road or the railway lies either on top of the arch or hangs below it. At both ends the arch rests on solid foundations called **abutments**. Without these strong supports the arch would slide apart.

When a car drives over an arch bridge, its weight presses downwards. The arch leads this force along its curve to the sides and into the ground. The stones of the arch are pressed firmly together; this is called **compression**. Stone withstands compression very well, but cracks easily if you pull on it. That is why the arch shape suits stone perfectly.

A masonry arch is made of wedge-shaped stones. The top stone in the middle is called the **keystone**. Only when it has been put in do all the stones hold each other firmly in place. During building the arch is therefore supported by a wooden frame called centring. Once the keystone is in, the frame can be removed and the arch supports itself.

The Romans were masters at building arches. Their bridges and **aqueducts**, that is water channels, are still standing in many places today. The Pont du Gard in southern France was built in the 1st century AD and has three rows of arches one above the other. The Romans used large stone blocks for it, some of which hold together without any mortar at all. This shows how strong the arch shape is.

In Switzerland there are many impressive arch bridges in the mountains. The **Landwasser Viaduct** near Filisur in the Grisons was built in 1902 for the Rhaetian Railway and is around 65 metres high. The trains run straight into a tunnel in the rock face. The Salginatobel Bridge near Schiers was built of concrete by the engineer Robert Maillart in 1930. Because of its slim, elegant shape it is regarded as a masterpiece of bridge building.

begriffe.erklaerung: A solid foundation at the end of an arch on which it rests.
The top stone in the middle of a masonry arch.
A force that presses something together.
A bridge on which water was carried in a channel in the past.

gewusst: Even a raw egg is surprisingly strong if you press on its curved ends, because the shape acts like an arch.
The Landwasser Viaduct is part of the UNESCO World Heritage Site Rhaetian Railway in the Albula and Bernina landscapes.

teile.einleitung: Kinetic energy is the energy a body has because it is moving. A rolling ball, a moving car and a flying tennis ball all have kinetic energy. The heavier and above all the faster something is, the more energy it contains.
wichtigste: Every body that moves has kinetic energy.
It is calculated with the formula E equals one half times mass times speed squared.
With twice the mass and the same speed, the kinetic energy doubles.
With twice the speed, the kinetic energy becomes four times as great.
That is why the braking distance becomes about four times as long at twice the speed.
If the speed rises by 10 per cent, the kinetic energy grows by 21 per cent.
Kinetic energy is measured in joules.

abschnitte.text: Energy is the ability to make something happen, for example to move, deform or heat something. A rolling ball can knock into another ball, and a moving car can bend metal in an accident. This ability lies in the movement, which is why it is called **energy of motion** or **kinetic energy**. Like all energy, it is measured in joules.

Kinetic energy is calculated with E equals one half times m times v squared, where m is the mass in kilograms and v the speed in metres per second. So a cyclist of 90 kilograms at 10 metres per second has 4500 joules. A car of 1200 kilograms at 72 km/h, which is 20 metres per second, has 240 kilojoules. A lorry of 40 tonnes at 90 km/h even has 12.5 megajoules.

Because the speed appears **squared**, it has a much stronger effect than the mass. If you double the mass, the energy doubles; but if you double the speed, it quadruples. Just 10 per cent more speed means 21 per cent more energy, because 1.1 times 1.1 makes 1.21. A small tennis ball of 58 grams at 50 metres per second still has 72.5 joules.

When braking, all the kinetic energy has to be turned into **heat** in the brakes. At twice the speed there is four times as much energy, so the **braking distance** becomes about four times as long. That is why in Switzerland there are often 30 km/h limits or shared zones with 20 km/h in front of schools and in residential areas. In a collision at high speed much more energy is also released, which makes accidents far more dangerous.

Energy is never lost; it only changes form. On a **roller coaster**, potential energy is turned into kinetic energy on the way down and back again on the way up. Wind turbines use the kinetic energy of the air, and hydroelectric power stations that of flowing water. Knowing about this change of form is the core of the **law of conservation of energy**.

In the 17th century Gottfried Wilhelm Leibniz already recognised that mass times speed squared is an important quantity; he called it “living force”. The factor of one half was only added later, among others by the Frenchman Gaspard-Gustave de Coriolis in the 19th century. The term kinetic comes from the Greek word for movement. Today the formula is one of the most important in physics.

begriffe.erklaerung: The ability to do work, that is to move, heat or change something.
Means connected with movement.
Energy that a body has because it is high up.
The distance a vehicle needs from starting to brake until it stops.

gewusst: A car at 50 km/h has about as much kinetic energy as if it fell from a height of around 10 metres, roughly from the third floor.
A meteorite can be so fast that even a small lump makes a large crater when it hits the ground.

teile.einleitung: The decibel, abbreviated dB, is a unit used above all to say how loud a sound is. The decibel scale is special: it does not simply count up evenly, but in ratios. Just 10 dB more means ten times as much sound intensity.
wichtigste: The decibel is a unit for levels, especially sound level.
The prefix “deci” means a tenth, so a decibel is a tenth of a bel.
The bel is named after Alexander Graham Bell.
If the level rises by 10 dB, the sound intensity is ten times as great.
To our ears 10 dB more sounds about twice as loud.
Two equally loud lawnmowers together are only about 3 dB louder than one.
Sound level is measured with a sound level meter.

abschnitte.text: The decibel is not really an ordinary unit like the metre or the kilogram. It describes a **ratio** between two quantities, for example between a sound and the quietest sound intensity a person can hear. The basic unit is called the bel, after Alexander Graham Bell, the inventor of the telephone. Because a bel is too big a step, the decibel, a tenth of a bel, is usually used. As well as for sound, decibels are also used in radio technology and electronics.

The human ear handles a huge range of sound intensities. A jet aircraft is trillions of times more intense than the quietest audible rustle. So that you do not have to calculate with huge numbers, a **logarithmic scale** is used. On it every step of 10 dB means ten times the intensity, and 20 dB more already means a hundred times. If you double the sound source, the level only rises by about 3 dB.

The threshold of hearing is at 0 dB; this is not complete silence, but the quietest sound a young, healthy ear can hear. Whispering is about 30 dB, a normal conversation around 60 dB. Heavy road traffic reaches about 80 dB, a pneumatic drill nearby over 100 dB. From about 120 to 130 dB the **threshold of pain** begins. There is often an “A” after the figure, dB(A), because the value has been adjusted to how we hear.

Loud noise can permanently damage the fine hair cells in the inner ear. Even long-lasting levels of about 85 dB and above can harm your hearing. Loud music through headphones and concerts close to the loudspeakers are especially dangerous. That is why workers on building sites wear **ear protection**, and earplugs are handed out at concerts. In Switzerland a regulation controls how loud music may be at events.

How loud we perceive a note also depends on its pitch. We hear very low and very high notes as quieter than middle notes at the same level. That is why there is a unit for perceived loudness, the **phon**. For a note of 1000 hertz, phons and decibels are the same. A sound level meter contains a microphone and electronics that show the level directly in decibels.

begriffe.erklaerung: A measure of how strong a sound is, given in decibels.
A scale on which each equal step means multiplying by the same factor.
The quietest sound a person can just hear.
A unit of loudness as the ear perceives it.

gewusst: Ten equally loud lawnmowers together are only 10 dB louder than a single one.
Values in decibels can also be negative, if a sound is quieter than the reference value.
A rocket launch from close by is one of the loudest sounds that humans produce.

teile.einleitung: The Bohr model of the atom is an idea of how an atom is built. The Danish physicist Niels Bohr presented it in 1913. In it, electrons circle the atomic nucleus only on very particular orbits, rather like planets round the sun.
wichtigste: According to Bohr, electrons move on allowed orbits without giving off energy.
When an electron jumps to a lower orbit, the atom gives out light.
In hydrogen the electron at level n = 2 has an energy of minus 3.4 eV.
The smallest orbit radius, the Bohr radius, is around 0.053 nanometres.
The orbit radius grows with the square of n; for n = 3 it is 9 times bigger than for n = 1.
The model explains hydrogen well, but reaches its limits with atoms that have several electrons.
Niels Bohr received the Nobel Prize in Physics in 1922.

abschnitte.text: Niels Bohr lived from 1885 to 1962 and did most of his research in Copenhagen. He built on the model of Ernest **Rutherford**, who had shown in 1911 that an atom has a tiny, heavy nucleus. Bohr combined this idea with Max Planck’s new quantum theory. He received the Nobel Prize in 1922 for his work on the structure of atoms.

According to the old physics, a circling electron would constantly give off light and crash into the nucleus. Bohr boldly claimed that there are **allowed orbits** on which this does not happen. On these orbits the angular momentum of the electron is a whole-number multiple of h divided by 2π; this is the **quantum condition**. The orbits are numbered n = 1, 2, 3 and so on.

Each orbit has a fixed energy; in hydrogen it is minus 13.6 eV divided by n squared. If an electron jumps from a higher orbit to a lower one, the difference in energy is given out as a **photon**. In the jump from n = 3 to n = 2 this is around 1.89 eV, and you see red light. That is why every gas glows only in very particular colours, its **spectral lines**.

The visible lines of hydrogen belong to the Balmer series, whose jumps end at n = 2. The **Lyman series** ends at the ground state n = 1 and lies in the invisible ultraviolet. With his model Bohr was able to calculate the wavelengths of these lines precisely. This was a huge success and convinced many researchers.

Even for helium, with two electrons, the model gives wrong results. From 1925 researchers such as Werner Heisenberg and Erwin Schrödinger developed **quantum mechanics**, in which electrons do not have fixed orbits but are spread out in regions called orbitals. Even so, the Bohr model is still taught at school, because it is easy to picture. The shell model used in chemistry is based on it.

begriffe.erklaerung: The tiny, heavy centre of an atom, made of protons and neutrons.
A very small unit of energy used for atoms and particles.
A particle of light, that is a small packet of light energy.
The lowest orbit with the least energy; for hydrogen n = 1.

gewusst: If the atomic nucleus were the size of a pinhead, the whole atom would be as big as a football stadium.
The chemical element bohrium is named after Niels Bohr.
The picture of an atom with electrons on circular orbits is still a popular symbol of science today.

teile.einleitung: Lead shielding is a protective wall or cover made of lead that keeps out dangerous radiation. You find it at the dentist’s, in hospitals, in laboratories and in nuclear power stations. Lead is so popular for this because it is very heavy and dense.
wichtigste: Lead shields gamma and X-rays especially well, because it has a high density and a high atomic number.
The half-value thickness is the thickness after which only half the radiation gets through.
Each further half-value thickness halves the radiation once more.
The protective effect of an X-ray apron is given as a lead equivalent in millimetres.
Lead hardly helps against slow neutrons; boron is used for that.
The three basic rules of radiation protection are distance, shielding and time.

abschnitte.text: Lead has the atomic number 82, so its nucleus contains 82 protons and is surrounded by many electrons. A cube of lead with sides of 1 cm weighs about 11.3 grams, much more than iron. In such a dense material **gamma rays** and X-rays very often hit electrons and are swallowed or deflected. Lead is also soft, easy to shape and fairly cheap.

In lead, radiation is not stopped suddenly but gets weaker layer by layer. The **half-value thickness** tells you after how many centimetres only half gets through. If it is 1 cm, then 2 cm still let through a quarter and 4 cm only 6.25 per cent. With a half-value thickness of 1.2 cm, you need 3.6 cm so that only an eighth is left. The radiation never drops completely to zero, but it becomes very small.

**Alpha radiation** is already stopped by a sheet of paper or the skin. High-energy beta radiation is first shielded with plastic such as Perspex, because in lead a lot of new X-ray radiation, called **bremsstrahlung**, would be produced. Only behind the plastic comes a layer of lead. For neutrons you need substances rich in hydrogen, such as water or paraffin, and additives such as boron, which captures slow neutrons.

abschnitte.titel: In hospital and at the dentist’s
abschnitte.text: When you have an X-ray, a heavy **X-ray apron** is often put on you to protect parts of the body that are not meant to appear in the image. Its protective effect is given as a lead equivalent, for example 0.25 or 0.5 millimetres of lead. The walls of X-ray rooms also often contain lead sheets. Through special windows of lead glass, the staff can look in without being exposed to radiation.

In the laboratory heavy lead bricks are stacked into a **lead castle** round a radiation source. As well as shielding, two other rules apply: keep a good **distance** and stay nearby for as short a time as possible. In German these are known together as the three A’s of radiation protection. In Switzerland the Federal Office of Public Health monitors radiation protection in medicine.

Lead is poisonous, so it must be worked with carefully and disposed of correctly. That is why today there are also aprons made of other heavy substances such as bismuth or antimony. For very large shields, for example round a reactor, thick **concrete** is often used, because it is cheaper. Tungsten shields even better than lead, but is much more expensive.

begriffe.erklaerung: The thickness of a material after which only half as much radiation gets through.
Very high-energy, invisible radiation produced when atomic nuclei decay.
Tells you how many millimetres of lead a protective layer replaces in its effect.
X-ray radiation produced when fast electrons are slowed down in a material.

gewusst: An X-ray apron can weigh several kilograms.
Through 10 half-value thicknesses, only about a thousandth of the radiation gets through.
In ancient Rome water pipes were made of lead, which is where the English word “plumber” comes from.

teile.einleitung: The contact area is the surface with which an object rests on what is underneath it. Its size determines how strongly the object presses on the ground. That is why you sink in less with snowshoes than with hiking boots.
wichtigste: The contact area is the surface where a body touches what it rests on.
Pressure is force divided by area.
The bigger the contact area, the smaller the pressure for the same weight.
A small contact area produces a high pressure.
The unit of pressure is the pascal; 1 Pa is 1 newton per square metre.
Many wheels, wide caterpillar tracks and snowshoes spread the weight over a large area.
Knives and nails use a tiny area to produce a high pressure.

abschnitte.text: Every object that stands or lies on something touches the surface underneath with a certain area. This area is called the **contact area**. A brick has three sides of different sizes that you can lay it on. Its weight always stays the same, but the contact area changes. This also changes how strongly it presses on the ground.

**Pressure** is the force divided by the area: p = F : A. Its unit is the **pascal**, named after the Frenchman Blaise Pascal. A brick weighing 30 N on 0.02 m² produces a pressure of 1500 Pa. If you stand it on its smallest side, the pressure is greatest. If you lay it on its largest side, the pressure is smallest.

A **piste basher** has wide caterpillar tracks instead of wheels so that it does not sink into the snow. For the same reason walkers wear snowshoes in winter and skiers wear skis. Heavy lorries have many wheels so that the weight is spread over a larger area. A house stands on a wide **foundation** so that it does not sink into the ground. Good rucksacks also have wide shoulder straps that spread the load and press less.

Narrow stiletto heels can damage a wooden floor, because the small area produces a high pressure. A person weighing 60 kg on a thin heel presses harder on the floor than an elephant on its wide foot. Sometimes, though, high pressure is wanted. The tip of a **nail** or the edge of a knife is tiny. That way they go into wood or bread with little force.

If someone has fallen through thin ice, they should move lying flat. That way the weight is spread over a large area and the ice breaks less easily. Helpers also crawl towards them flat on their stomachs or push a ladder or a board over the ice. It is safest, however, only to walk on frozen lakes when they have been officially declared safe. In Switzerland many municipalities announce when natural ice is safe.

begriffe.erklaerung: The surface with which a body rests on what is underneath it.
Force per area, measured in pascals.
The unit of pressure, one newton per square metre.
The wide, solid base of a building in the ground.

gewusst: Thanks to its wide, soft soles, a camel hardly sinks into the desert sand.
A fakir can lie on a bed of nails because his weight is spread over hundreds of nails.
The mountain hare in the Alps has wide, thickly furred hind paws, with which it sinks less deeply into the snow.

teile.einleitung: Torque describes how strongly a force makes something turn. It does not only depend on how hard you push, but also on how far away from the axis of rotation. That is why screws are much easier to undo with a long spanner.
wichtigste: Torque is force times lever arm.
It is measured in newton metres, abbreviated Nm.
A longer lever arm gives a greater torque with the same force.
Pulling at right angles to the lever is most effective.
If you push directly on the axis of rotation, the lever arm is zero and nothing turns.
If two torques act against each other, the bigger one wins.
Torque is a vector that is at right angles to the lever arm and the force.

abschnitte.text: **Torque** is the turning effect of a force. It is calculated with the formula force times **lever arm**. The lever arm is the distance between the axis of rotation and the point where the force acts. The unit is the **newton metre** (Nm); one newton is roughly the weight of a small 100-gram bar of chocolate.

If you push with 50 N at the end of a spanner 30 cm long, that gives 50 N times 0.3 m, which is 15 Nm. If a wheel nut needs 120 Nm and the wheel brace is 40 cm long, you have to apply 300 N at the end of the handle. A child weighing 500 N sitting 1.5 m from the pivot of a seesaw produces 750 Nm. So you can rearrange the formula: force equals torque divided by lever arm.

Torque is greatest when the force acts at **right angles** to the lever. If you pull at a slant, only part of the force has a turning effect. If, for example, 100 N act at 30 degrees on a lever 0.5 m long, the torque is only 25 Nm instead of 50 Nm. If you push exactly in the direction of the axis of rotation, there is no torque at all.

The door handle is as far as possible from the hinges, because a long lever arm needs less force. If you push right next to the hinges, the door hardly moves. On a **seesaw** a light child can balance a heavy child if it sits further out. Bike pedals, screwdrivers and steering wheels also use torque.

If an anticlockwise torque of 30 Nm and a clockwise torque of 20 Nm act on a lever, it turns anticlockwise. If both torques are equal, the lever stays in **balance**. This **law of the lever** was already described by the Greek scholar Archimedes more than 2200 years ago. Beam balances and building cranes also work on this principle.

With a **torque wrench**, screws such as the wheel nuts on a car are tightened to exactly the prescribed value. For engines, torque tells you how powerfully the shaft turns. Electric cars have a large torque right from the start and therefore accelerate quickly. In physics torque is treated as a vector that points at right angles to the lever arm and the force.

begriffe.erklaerung: The distance between the axis of rotation and the point where the force acts.
The unit of torque, force in newtons times length in metres.
The line or point about which something turns.
A lever is in balance when the torques on both sides are equal.

gewusst: Archimedes is said to have said that with a long enough lever he could move the whole Earth.
Although torque and energy are both measured in newtons times metres, torque is written as Nm and energy is preferably given in joules.

teile.einleitung: Glasses are a frame with two lenses that is worn in front of the eyes. Usually they help people to see sharply again; sometimes they protect the eyes from sun, wind or snow. Behind them lies the physics of lenses, which bend light rays.
wichtigste: Many people wear glasses to see better.
The first glasses were invented in Italy in the 13th century.
Short-sighted people see distant things blurred, long-sighted people tend to see close things blurred.
Spectacle lenses are lenses that guide the light so that a sharp image forms on the retina.
Many older people need reading glasses for small print.
Sunglasses and ski goggles protect against glaring light, snow and wind.
Instead of glasses you can also put contact lenses directly on the eye.

abschnitte.text: A pair of glasses consists of two **lenses** held in a frame. The bridge rests on the nose and the **arms** lie over the ears. Today the lenses are usually made of light plastic, in the past of glass. Glasses are usually fitted and sold at the optician’s, and the eyes are often examined by an eye doctor or an optometrist.

In the eye the light rays should meet exactly on the **retina**. In short-sighted people they meet before it, which is why they see distant things blurred. They need a **diverging lens**, which is thinner in the middle. For long-sightedness a converging lens, which is thicker in the middle, helps. The strength of glasses is given in dioptres, with minus for short-sighted and plus for long-sighted.

In children the lens in the eye is very elastic and can adjust well to close things. From about the age of 45 it becomes stiffer; this is called **presbyopia**. Then you need reading glasses for reading. Varifocal glasses have an area for distance at the top and one for close up at the bottom.

**Sunglasses** dim glaring light and should protect against UV radiation. In the mountains this is especially important, because snow strongly reflects sunlight. Ski goggles also protect against wind, snow and cold. In workshops and laboratories people wear safety glasses against splinters and splashes.

As early as the Middle Ages monks used polished **reading stones**, which they placed on the writing. Towards the end of the 13th century the first glasses were made in northern Italy; they were held in front of the eyes. Arms that hold behind the ears only became common in the 18th century. Benjamin Franklin invented glasses with two viewing areas, bifocals.

begriffe.erklaerung: You see close things clearly but distant things blurred.
The unit for the strength of a spectacle lens.
A transparent, curved body that focuses or spreads out light rays.
A specialist who fits, makes and sells glasses.

gewusst: Without sunglasses you can become snow-blind in the mountains; the eyes then become painfully inflamed.
With a lens for long-sighted people you can focus sunlight like a magnifying glass.
Old paintings from the 14th century already show scholars wearing glasses.

teile.einleitung: A diffraction grating is a plate with a great many very fine parallel lines or slits. When light falls on it, it is diffracted and fanned out into its colours. That is why the underside of a CD shimmers in all the colours of the rainbow.
wichtigste: An optical grating consists of many evenly spaced slits or lines.
The distance between two lines is called the grating spacing g.
The position of the maxima is given by g · sin α = k · λ.
The more lines per millimetre, the more strongly the light is deflected.
The maxima are much sharper than with a double slit, because a great many slits interfere at once.
With white light the zero-order maximum stays white.
Gratings are used in spectrometers to split light into its wavelengths.

abschnitte.text: A **diffraction grating**, or optical grating, has hundreds to thousands of fine lines per millimetre. Light that passes through the gaps or is reflected by the lines spreads out like a wave behind each slit. These many waves overlap; this is called **interference**. In certain directions they strengthen each other into bright stripes, the **maxima**. In between they almost completely cancel each other out.

The distance between two lines is called the **grating spacing** g. A grating with 500 lines per millimetre has g = 1 mm : 500 = 2 µm. The direction of the maxima is calculated with g · sin α = k · λ, where k is the order and λ the wavelength. With g = 2 µm and red light of 600 nm there are maxima up to the 3rd order at most, because sin α cannot be greater than 1. If a laser of 633 nm produces the first maximum at 30 degrees, the grating spacing is about 1.27 µm.

Each colour has a different wavelength and is therefore deflected by a different amount. Red light is deflected more strongly than blue. When white light falls on a grating, a small rainbow, a **spectrum**, appears in each order. Only the zero-order maximum in the middle stays white, because all the colours coincide there. A grating with 1200 lines per mm deflects the light more strongly than one with 300.

The data tracks of a CD or DVD lie very close together. They act as a **reflection grating** and split the light into rainbow colours. Some security features on banknotes and credit cards also work with fine grating structures. At school a laser pointer is often shone through a grating onto a wall, showing a row of bright dots.

Around 1821 the German optician **Joseph von Fraunhofer** built the first precise diffraction gratings from fine wires. With them he was able to measure the wavelengths of light. Today gratings are found in **spectrometers** in laboratories and telescopes. Astronomers use them to find out what stars are made of and how fast they are moving. A grating with many lines separates wavelengths that are very close together: with 2000 illuminated lines it reaches a resolving power of 4000 in the 2nd order.

begriffe.erklaerung: The bending of light or other waves away from a straight line at edges and slits.
The overlapping of waves, which strengthen or cancel each other out.
The distance between two neighbouring lines of a grating.
Light split into its colours.
The distance between two wave crests; for light it determines the colour.

gewusst: With a grating, red light is deflected more strongly than blue; with a glass prism it is exactly the other way round.
Good gratings for astronomy have over a thousand lines on a single millimetre.
The shimmering colours of some beetles also come from tiny regular structures rather than from pigments.

teile.einleitung: Diffuse reflection means that light is thrown back in many different directions by a rough or matt surface. Thanks to it, we can see most things around us from every direction. A sheet of paper, a white wall or the full moon are good examples.
wichtigste: In diffuse reflection light is thrown back in many directions.
This happens mainly at rough and matt surfaces such as paper.
That is why you can see a book from all directions in a room.
The opposite is specular reflection, as in a mirror.
A wet road dazzles more at night, because the water reflects the light more directionally.
The full moon shines because its surface reflects sunlight diffusely.
Snow reflects a great deal of sunlight, which is why you need sunglasses in the mountains.

abschnitte.text: When light hits an object, part of it is thrown back; this is called **reflection**. If the surface is smooth like a mirror, the light carries on in a single direction. If it is rough, the light is scattered in many directions. This scattering is called **diffuse reflection**. The word diffuse comes from Latin and means roughly scattered.

Even a surface that looks smooth can be full of tiny bumps under the microscope. Paper, for example, consists of many fine fibres lying every which way. Each ray of light hits a slightly different sloping spot and is deflected differently. Together this gives a glow in all directions. Some of the light also goes a little way into the material and comes out again at a different point.

For a mirror the **law of reflection** applies: the angle of incidence equals the angle of reflection. That is why you see a clear image in a mirror, but only from certain directions. A sheet of paper, on the other hand, shows no reflection, but looks equally bright from everywhere. Most things lie somewhere in between; they shine a little and scatter at the same time. A wet road, for example, becomes more mirror-like and dazzles at night in the headlights.

A cinema screen is made of matt white fabric so that all the audience can see the picture, wherever they sit. Blackboards and screens are often made matt so that they reflect less. The colours we see also usually come from diffuse reflection. A red tomato reflects mainly red light and swallows the other colours. Without diffuse reflection we would only see light sources and reflections.

Fresh snow reflects a very large share of the sunlight diffusely. That is why it is very bright in the mountains in winter, and without sunglasses there is a risk of **snow blindness**. The share of the light reflected is called **albedo**. The Moon, on the other hand, has a fairly dark, grey surface and reflects only a small part of the light. Even so, the full moon looks bright, because it is strongly lit by the sun and scatters its light diffusely towards us.

begriffe.erklaerung: The throwing back of light at a surface.
Light is thrown back in a single direction, as in a mirror.
How much light a surface reflects, as a share of the light falling on it.
Not shiny, with a rough surface that scatters light.

gewusst: Moon rock is actually about as dark as old tarmac.
White paint contains tiny grains that scatter light especially strongly in all directions.
Because snow reflects so much light, you can get sunburnt in the mountains even in the shade.

teile.einleitung: Planets, moons and comets do not move on exact circles, but on ellipses, that is on slightly or strongly stretched circles. Such an orbit is called an elliptical orbit. If you understand it, you can work out when a planet is closest to the sun or when a comet will return.
wichtigste: An elliptical orbit is the oval path of one celestial body round another.
How stretched an ellipse is, is given by the eccentricity e.
A circular orbit has an eccentricity of 0.
The Earth’s orbit has an eccentricity of only about 0.017 and is almost a circle.
Mercury has the greatest orbital eccentricity of all the planets in the solar system.
The closest distance to the sun is calculated as a·(1−e), where a is the semi-major axis.
The orbital period depends only on the semi-major axis.

abschnitte.text: An ellipse looks like a stretched circle or a flat egg with two equal sides. It has two special points inside it, the **foci**. In a planet’s orbit the sun is at one of these foci, not in the middle. Half the length of the ellipse is called the **semi-major axis** a, and half its width the semi-minor axis.

The **eccentricity** e describes how much an ellipse differs from a circle. A circle has e = 0, a strongly stretched ellipse has a value just under 1. The Earth’s orbit has e of about 0.017, Mercury’s about 0.21. If e is exactly 1, the path is no longer a closed ellipse but a parabola. A body moving at exactly escape velocity flies off along such a parabola and never comes back.

The point of an orbit closest to the sun is called the **perihelion**, the furthest the **aphelion**. The distance at perihelion is a·(1−e), the distance at aphelion a·(1+e). The Earth is closest to the sun at the beginning of January, at about 147 million kilometres. At the beginning of July it is furthest away, at about 152 million kilometres. The seasons, however, are not caused by this difference but by the tilt of the Earth’s axis.

At the beginning of the 17th century the astronomer **Johannes Kepler** discovered that planets move on ellipses. His second law says that a planet is faster near the sun than far from it. The third law links the orbital period and the semi-major axis: the square of the orbital period is proportional to the cube of the semi-major axis. That is why the semi-major axis alone determines the orbital period, no matter how stretched the orbit is.

**Halley’s Comet** has an orbital period of about 76 years. If you calculate with Kepler’s third law, you get a semi-major axis of about 18 **astronomical units**. An astronomical unit is the average distance from the Earth to the sun, around 150 million kilometres. Its orbit is very strongly stretched, so it comes close to the sun and then flies far out beyond the orbit of Neptune.

begriffe.erklaerung: One of two special points in an ellipse; for planets, the sun is there.
Half the length of the ellipse; it determines the orbital period.
A number that tells you how stretched an ellipse is; 0 is a circle.
The point of the orbit at which a body is closest to the sun.
The average distance from the Earth to the sun, about 150 million kilometres.

gewusst: The Earth is closest to the sun in January, in the middle of the Swiss winter.
You can draw an ellipse yourself with two nails, a loop of string and a pencil.
Satellites orbiting the Earth also move on elliptical orbits.

teile.einleitung: Buoyancy is the force with which water or air pushes a body upwards. That is why you feel lighter in the swimming pool, and why even huge ships made of steel float. The principle was discovered by the Greek scientist Archimedes more than 2000 years ago.
wichtigste: Buoyancy is a force that acts upwards in liquids and gases.
It arises because the pressure at the bottom of a body is greater than at the top.
Buoyancy is as great as the weight of the displaced liquid.
The buoyant force is measured in newtons.
For a fully submerged body, buoyancy does not depend on its mass but on its volume.
A ship made of steel floats because it is hollow inside and full of air.
There is also buoyancy in air, which is why hot-air balloons rise.

abschnitte.text: When you get into the bath, **the water rises**, because your body needs space. The water presses on you from all sides, but more strongly from below than from above. This results in an upward force, **buoyancy**. That is why a heavy stone is easier to lift in water than on land, and why air bubbles rise.

The Greek scientist **Archimedes** lived in the 3rd century BC in Syracuse on Sicily. According to legend he recognised the principle in the bath and shouted “Eureka”, which means “I have found it”. **Archimedes’ principle** says: a body experiences a buoyancy as great as the weight of the liquid it displaces. It applies in all liquids and gases.

Buoyancy is calculated from the **density** of the liquid, the submerged volume and the gravitational factor g. A body with a volume of 0.5 dm³ displaces exactly 0.6 kg of water in salt water of 1.2 kg per dm³. With g equal to 10 N/kg, this gives a buoyancy of about **6 newtons**. How heavy the body itself is does not matter for buoyancy, only its volume.

If the buoyancy is greater than the weight, a body floats; if it is smaller, it sinks. A steel ship floats because its **hollow hull** displaces a great deal of water. A **submarine** fills tanks with water to dive and blows them empty with air to rise. Divers wear a lead belt so that they can dive more easily.

Air also produces buoyancy, but much less than water, because it is lighter. A **hot-air balloon** rises because the warm air in the balloon is lighter than the cool air outside. In 1783 the Montgolfier brothers launched the first manned hot-air balloon in France. Every winter a big international balloon festival takes place in Château-d'Oex in Vaud.

abschnitte.titel: Examples from nature and everyday life
abschnitte.text: Many fish have a **swim bladder**, with which they control their buoyancy. In the Dead Sea you can lie on the water almost without moving, because the very salty water has a high density. Life jackets contain foam or air and so increase buoyancy. The passenger boats on Swiss lakes also use Archimedes’ principle.

begriffe.erklaerung: The force with which a liquid or a gas pushes a body upwards.
The water that a body pushes aside when it goes in.
How much mass there is in a certain volume.
A gas-filled organ with which fish hover in the water.

gewusst: An egg sinks in tap water, but floats in very salty water.
Only about a tenth of a large iceberg sticks out of the water.
People float better after breathing in, because the air in the lungs increases buoyancy.

teile.einleitung: Orbital speed tells you how fast a body is moving along its path, for example a point on a turning wheel or a satellite round the Earth. In circular motion it depends on how big the circle is and how fast it is travelled round. Even when you are sitting still, you have a high orbital speed because of the Earth’s rotation.
wichtigste: Orbital speed is the distance travelled along the path per unit of time.
For a circular path: v = 2·π·r divided by the period T.
With the angular velocity ω, simply v = ω·r.
A point twice as far from the axis is twice as fast.
A place in Switzerland moves at around 1140 km/h because of the Earth’s rotation.
The ISS orbits the Earth at around 28,000 km/h.

abschnitte.text: The **orbital speed** v gives how many metres a body travels along its path per second. In circular motion the path is a circle with the circumference 2·π·r. If the body takes the time T for one lap, then v = 2·π·r / T. The direction of the velocity always points along the path, that is tangentially to the circle.

A point on a circle with a radius of 0.3 m that goes round once in 0.5 s has an orbital speed of around 3.8 m/s. A **big wheel** 50 m in diameter that turns once in 10 minutes moves its gondolas at only around 0.26 m/s. A disc turning at 500 revolutions per minute moves a point 6 cm from the axis at around 3.1 m/s. A bike wheel with a radius of 0.35 m turning at 20 rad/s moves a point on the tyre at 7 m/s.

The **angular velocity** ω tells you how fast something is turning, measured in radians per second. All points on a rigid disc have the same angular velocity. Their orbital speeds, however, are different, because v = ω·r. If a point is twice as far from the axis, it is twice as fast, because it travels twice as far in the same time.

The Earth turns once on its axis in about 24 hours. At the **equator** the ground therefore moves at over 1600 km/h. In Switzerland, at about 47 degrees north, the circle is smaller, and you move at around 1140 km/h. On top of that, the Earth flies round the sun at about 30 kilometres per second, which is over 100,000 km/h.

The International Space Station, **ISS**, orbits the Earth at a height of about 400 kilometres at around 28,000 km/h. It takes only about 90 minutes to go round the Earth once. This high orbital speed is necessary so that it does not fall to Earth. The further a satellite is from the Earth, the more slowly it must fly to stay in its orbit.

begriffe.erklaerung: How fast a body moves along its path, for example in m/s.
How fast something turns, measured as angle per unit of time.
A unit of angle; a whole circle has about 6.28 radians.
The time for one whole lap of the path.

gewusst: On a roundabout you go faster on the outside than on the inside, even though everything turns at the same rate.
The astronauts on the ISS see about 16 sunrises a day.
At the North Pole you turn with the Earth, but you hardly move from the spot.

teile.einleitung: Diffraction is the property of waves to spread out round obstacles and behind openings. As a result a wave also gets into the shadow region, where it really should not reach. Diffraction can be seen with water waves, sound and light, and it is clear proof that light behaves like a wave.
wichtigste: In diffraction a wave enters the shadow region behind an obstacle.
Diffraction is strongest when the opening is about the same size as the wavelength.
Sound is diffracted more strongly than light, because sound waves are much longer.
That is why you can hear a person round the corner of a house, but not see them.
Behind a single slit there is a broad central maximum with weaker side maxima.
Refraction, on the other hand, is caused by a change in speed at a boundary.
With an optical grating, light can be split into its colours.

abschnitte.text: When waves hit an obstacle or an opening, they do not simply carry on straight ahead. They also spread out sideways behind the edge, into the so-called **shadow region**. You can see this nicely at a harbour: even behind a narrow harbour entrance there are still waves in the whole harbour basin. In the 17th century the Dutch physicist Christiaan Huygens explained this by saying that every point of a wave is itself the starting point of new small waves; this is **Huygens’ principle**.

abschnitte.titel: Size of the opening and wavelength
abschnitte.text: How strongly a wave is diffracted depends on the ratio between the opening and the **wavelength**. If the slit is much bigger than the wavelength, there is hardly any diffraction. If it is about as big as the wavelength, the wave spreads out behind it in almost all directions. If water waves with a wavelength of 0.1 metres hit a slit 0.2 metres wide, the first minimum lies at an angle of 30 degrees.

In everyday life sound waves are a few centimetres to several metres long. Light waves, on the other hand, are tiny, only about 400 to 700 nanometres, that is less than a thousandth of a millimetre. That is why sound is strongly diffracted at the corner of a house, but light hardly at all. So you hear a person calling round the corner, but you do not see them.

If light passes through a very narrow **single slit**, you see a broad bright central maximum on a screen with weaker stripes beside it. An **optical grating** has a great many fine slits side by side. With 500 lines per millimetre, red light of 600 nanometres appears in the first maximum at about 17.5 degrees. Because each colour is deflected at a different angle, a grating splits light into a rainbow.

abschnitte.titel: Diffraction in everyday life and research
abschnitte.text: The shimmering rainbow colours on a CD or DVD appear because its fine grooves act like a grating. With **X-rays** diffracted by crystals, scientists find out how atoms are arranged in a substance. This is also how the structure of the genetic material DNA was worked out in 1953. Diffraction, however, also limits how sharply microscopes and telescopes can see.

Diffraction and refraction are often confused. **Refraction** happens when a wave changes its speed at a boundary, for example when passing from air into water, and changes direction as a result. Diffraction, on the other hand, happens at edges and openings, even when the wave stays in the same material. The name diffraction was coined in the 17th century by the Italian scholar Francesco Maria Grimaldi.

begriffe.erklaerung: A vibration that spreads out through space and carries energy as it goes.
The distance between two wave crests.
The overlapping of waves, which can strengthen or cancel each other out.
A plate with a great many fine, parallel slits or grooves.

gewusst: Because low notes have longer waves than high ones, from a party in the house next door you mainly hear the bass.
The colours on some butterfly wings and beetle shells also come from fine structures that diffract light.

teile.einleitung: The Doppler effect describes how the frequency of a wave that you perceive changes when the source or the observer moves. You hear it when an ambulance with its siren goes past: first the note sounds higher, then lower. It is named after the Austrian physicist Christian Doppler.
wichtigste: In the Doppler effect the perceived frequency changes because the source or the observer moves.
If a sound source comes closer, the note sounds higher.
If it moves away, the note sounds lower.
Christian Doppler described the effect in 1842.
The effect applies to sound, light and all other waves.
Police speed traps measure speeds with the Doppler effect.
Astronomers use it to recognise that distant galaxies are moving away from us.

abschnitte.text: When an ambulance with its **siren** drives past you, the note suddenly changes. As it comes closer it sounds higher, and as it drives away it sounds lower. The driver in the ambulance, on the other hand, always hears the same note. This change in the perceived **frequency** is called the **Doppler effect**.

Sound spreads out in waves, rather like circles in water. If the source moves towards you, the waves in front of it are squeezed together, and more waves per second reach your ear. That sounds higher. Behind the source the waves are stretched out, and the note seems lower.
