Christian Doppler was born in Salzburg in 1803 and died in Venice in 1853. In 1842 he presented his idea in Prague, at first for the light of stars. In 1845 the Dutchman Buys Ballot tested the effect with trumpeters on a moving train. Musicians played a note, and observers with good hearing beside the track confirmed the **change in pitch**.

The police use **radar** to measure the speed of cars, because the radio waves bounced back change their frequency. Doctors use Doppler ultrasound to examine how fast blood flows in the blood vessels. Weather radars use it to recognise how rain and wind are moving in thunderstorms. Bats also use the effect to locate prey in flight.

With light the effect shows up as a shift in colour. If a star or a galaxy is moving away, its light is shifted towards the red end of the spectrum; this is called **redshift**. In 1929 Edwin Hubble found that almost all distant galaxies are redshifted. This was an important sign that the universe is expanding. In 1995 the Geneva astronomers Michel Mayor and Didier Queloz used a similar measuring method to discover the first planet orbiting a sun-like star.

begriffe.erklaerung: How many vibrations take place per second; it determines the pitch.
A wave of changes in pressure in the air, which we hear as a sound.
The shift of light towards red when a light source is moving away.
A device that uses radio waves to locate objects and measure their speed.

gewusst: Michel Mayor and Didier Queloz of the University of Geneva received the Nobel Prize in Physics in 2019 for their discovery.
At Formula One races you can hear the Doppler effect especially clearly when the cars race past the grandstand.

teile.einleitung: Binding energy is the energy you would have to put in to break an atomic nucleus down into its individual building blocks. The other way round, exactly this energy is released when protons and neutrons join together to form a nucleus. It explains why the sun shines and why nuclear power stations can produce electricity.
wichtigste: Binding energy is the energy that holds an atomic nucleus together.
Protons and neutrons, the nucleons, are held together by the strong interaction.
The nuclear force only acts over very short distances of around 10⁻¹⁵ m.
The binding energy per nucleon is greatest for iron and nickel, around 8.8 MeV.
Heavy nuclei release energy when they split, light nuclei when they fuse.
A nucleus is lighter than the sum of its building blocks; this difference is called the mass defect.
The Bethe-Weizsäcker formula describes binding energy using the liquid drop model.

abschnitte.text: An atomic nucleus consists of **protons** and **neutrons**, together called nucleons. The positively charged protons should really repel each other. Even so, the nucleus holds together, because the **strong interaction** is much stronger. The energy you would need to separate all the particles from each other again is called binding energy.

The force between the nucleons acts only over a tiny distance of around 10⁻¹⁵ m, which is about the diameter of a proton. That is why each nucleon only feels its immediate neighbours. In large nuclei the electrical repulsion of the many protons therefore becomes more and more important. That is one reason why very heavy nuclei are unstable and can decay.

To compare nuclei, the total binding energy is divided by the number of nucleons. For the deuteron, made of one proton and one neutron, the total is only around 2.2 **MeV**. Helium-4 has around 28.3 MeV, that is about 7.1 MeV per nucleon. The value is highest for **iron** and nickel, at around 8.8 MeV; these nuclei are especially stable.

Because iron is the most strongly bound, energy can be obtained in two ways. Very heavy nuclei such as uranium are split; the fragments are more strongly bound, and the difference is released; this is used in **nuclear fission** in power stations. Light nuclei such as hydrogen fuse into helium; this is **nuclear fusion**, which takes place in the sun. In both cases you move along the curve towards iron.

An atomic nucleus weighs slightly less than its individual building blocks put together. This missing part is called the **mass defect**. According to Albert Einstein’s formula E equals m times c², it corresponds exactly to the binding energy. Because c, the speed of light, is so huge, even a tiny mass contains an enormous amount of energy.

Physicists imagine an atomic nucleus, in simplified form, like a drop of water; this is the **liquid drop model**. From it Carl Friedrich von Weizsäcker and Hans Bethe developed a formula in the 1930s that estimates binding energy well. It is called the Bethe-Weizsäcker formula. With it you can predict which nuclei are stable and which decay.

begriffe.erklaerung: The collective name for the building blocks of the nucleus, the proton and the neutron.
The very strong but short-range force that holds the atomic nucleus together.
Megaelectronvolt, a unit of energy for tiny particles.
The missing mass of a nucleus compared with its individual building blocks.
The joining of light atomic nuclei to form heavier ones.

gewusst: Every second the sun turns millions of tonnes of mass into energy, because it fuses hydrogen into helium.
The iron in your blood comes from inside old stars, because that is where it was made by nuclear fusion.
Chemical bonds also have a binding energy, but it is around a million times smaller than for atomic nuclei.

teile.einleitung: Archimedes of Syracuse was a Greek mathematician, physicist and inventor who lived in the 3rd century BC. Among other things, he discovered why things float or sink in water and explained the law of the lever. He is regarded as one of the greatest scientists of ancient times.
wichtigste: Archimedes lived from about 287 to 212 BC in Syracuse on Sicily.
He explained why things float or sink in water.
According to a story, he had his famous idea in the bath.
Afterwards he is said to have shouted “Eureka”, which means “I have found it”.
King Hiero II had him check whether a crown was made of pure gold.
Archimedes described how heavy things can be lifted with a lever.
The Archimedean screw carries water upwards.

abschnitte.text: Archimedes was born around 287 BC in **Syracuse**, a Greek city on the island of Sicily. He was probably acquainted with King Hiero II and worked for him. Archimedes studied mathematics, physics, astronomy and technology. Many of his writings have survived to this day.

The Roman writer **Vitruvius** passed down a famous story. King Hiero II feared that his goldsmith had mixed silver into the gold of his crown. While bathing, Archimedes noticed that his body pushed water aside, and he shouted out excitedly: **Eureka**. A crown containing silver pushes aside more water than a lump of gold of the same weight, because silver has a lower density and needs more room. Galileo Galilei later suspected that Archimedes was more likely to have tested the crown with a balance under water.

Archimedes recognised that a body in water experiences **buoyancy**. This is exactly as great as the weight of the water that the body pushes aside. If a body displaces 2 litres of water, the buoyancy is about 20 newtons. If the buoyancy is greater than the weight of the body, it floats; otherwise it sinks.

Archimedes described the **law of the lever**: with a long lever you can lift heavy loads with little force. The famous saying that he could move the Earth if he were given a fixed point comes from him. The **Archimedean screw**, a spiral inside a tube, carries water upwards. When Syracuse was being defended, he is said to have built war machines such as giant grabbing arms.

Archimedes calculated the number pi astonishingly accurately by drawing polygons inside and around a circle. He found that pi lies between 3 10/71 and 3 1/7. He also calculated the areas and volumes of spheres and cylinders. He was especially proud of the discovery that a sphere has two thirds of the volume of the cylinder that fits round it.

In 212 BC the Romans captured the city of Syracuse during the Second Punic War. Archimedes was killed by a Roman soldier, even though the general wanted to spare him. According to legend, he said beforehand: “Do not disturb my circles.” His grave is said to have shown a sphere inside a cylinder.

begriffe.erklaerung: The force with which water pushes a body upwards.
Tells you how heavy a substance is for the same volume.
A bar with which you can move a lot with little force.
Greek for: I have found it.
The water that a body pushes aside when it is put in.

gewusst: A crown of pure gold with a mass of 965 grams has a volume of only 50 cubic centimetres, because gold is very dense.
According to the story, after his discovery Archimedes ran through the streets of Syracuse without any clothes on.
A crater on the Moon is named after Archimedes.

teile.einleitung: In bungee jumping you hurl yourself down from a bridge, a crane or a dam, tied to an elastic rope. The rope stretches, slows the fall and flings the jumper back up again. In the process energy changes several times from one form into another.
wichtigste: When falling, potential energy is turned into kinetic energy.
The stretched rope stores elastic energy and slows the jumper down.
The speed is greatest shortly after the rope starts to stretch.
At the lowest point the speed is zero.
The jumper bounces up less and less, because energy is turned into heat.
The idea comes from the tower jumpers of Vanuatu.
The Verzasca dam in Ticino, about 220 m high, became famous through a James Bond film.

abschnitte.text: In bungee jumping the jumper is attached by the feet or with a harness to a **rubber rope**. The rope consists of many thin rubber strands surrounded by a cover. It is calculated so that the jumper is slowed down well above the ground or the water. Before every jump, body weight, rope length and equipment are carefully checked.

At the top the jumper has a lot of **potential energy**. In free fall it turns into **kinetic energy**, and they get faster and faster. As soon as the rope starts to stretch, some of the energy is stored in the rope as **elastic energy**. Shortly after that the jumper is at their fastest, because only from then on does the rope slow them down more than gravity speeds them up.

abschnitte.titel: Right at the bottom and back up
abschnitte.text: At the lowest point the rope is stretched to its maximum and the speed is exactly zero. Now the rope pulls the jumper back up, and the elastic energy turns into kinetic and potential energy again. Because the rope and the air turn some of the energy into **heat**, they never reach the jumping-off height again. So they swing less and less until they hang still on the rope.

The idea comes from Pentecost Island in the island nation of **Vanuatu** in the South Pacific. There young men have long jumped from tall wooden towers with only vines tied to their feet. In 1979 members of the Dangerous Sports Club in England jumped for the first time with rubber ropes from the Clifton Suspension Bridge in Bristol. In the 1980s the New Zealander A. J. Hackett then made bungee jumping known worldwide as a leisure sport.

The best-known bungee jump in Switzerland is from the **Verzasca dam** in Ticino. The dam, also called the Contra Dam, is about 220 m high. In the 1995 James Bond film “GoldenEye” the hero jumps down from it; the scene was filmed with a real stuntman. Today brave people can jump there themselves; it is regarded as one of the highest bungee jumps in the world.

begriffe.erklaerung: An elastic rope made of many rubber strands that can stretch a long way.
Energy stored in an object that has been stretched or tensioned.
A fall in which only gravity acts.
A high wall that holds back the water of a reservoir.

gewusst: The tower jumpers on Vanuatu do not use rubber ropes, but vines measured to exactly the right length.
A bungee rope can stretch to several times its original length.
The jump from the Verzasca dam in the film GoldenEye was later voted one of the best film stunts in polls.

teile.einleitung: Why is the sky blue on a fine day and not white or black? The reason is the scattering of sunlight by the tiny particles of the air. Blue light is spread out in all directions much more strongly than red light.
wichtigste: Sunlight contains all the colours of the rainbow.
The molecules of the air scatter blue light much more strongly than red; this is called Rayleigh scattering.
The scattered blue light reaches us from all directions, which is why the whole sky glows blue.
There is no air on the Moon, so the sky there is black.
High up in the mountains the blue of the sky gets darker.
Clouds are white because their water droplets scatter all colours equally.
At sunset the path through the air is long, and mainly red light arrives.

abschnitte.text: The light of the sun looks white, but it contains all the colours from red to violet. On its way through the **atmosphere** it meets countless tiny nitrogen and oxygen molecules. These deflect part of the light in other directions; this is called **scattering**. Blue light, with its short wavelength, is scattered about five times more strongly than red. This blue reaches us from all directions, and the sky glows blue.

The British physicist **Lord Rayleigh** explained this phenomenon mathematically in 1871, which is why it is called **Rayleigh scattering**. Violet light is scattered even more strongly than blue. The sky still looks blue, though, because the sun gives out less violet and our eyes are more sensitive to blue. Air in a glass does not look blue, because there is far too little air in it. Only a thick layer of air many kilometres deep makes the blue visible.

At sunrise and sunset the sun is low, and its light travels a very long way through the air. On the way most of the blue is scattered out. What reaches us is mainly yellow, orange and red, which we see as a **sunset glow**. Distant mountains, on the other hand, often look bluish because of all the air in between. Painters call this aerial perspective.

The droplets in clouds are much bigger than air molecules. They scatter all colours equally strongly, which is why clouds are white. Thunderclouds are so thick that little light gets through, and they look dark grey. Deep water in lakes and the sea looks blue because the water itself swallows red light. That is a different reason from the sky.

On the **Moon** there is no atmosphere, so the sky there is black even during the day. The higher you climb on Earth, the less air there is above you and the darker the blue becomes. On **Mars** the sky is yellowish to reddish brown during the day, because fine dust floats in the thin air. At sunset, however, the Martian sky turns bluish around the sun.

With the **foehn** the air in Switzerland is often very clear, with views far into the distance, and the sky glows deep blue. In the 18th century the Geneva naturalist Horace-Bénédict de Saussure invented the cyanometer. With this ring of different shades of blue he measured how blue the sky was, including high up in the Alps. He found that the sky is a darker blue at great heights.

begriffe.erklaerung: The layer of air that surrounds the Earth.
The deflection of light in many directions by small particles.
Scattering by very small particles, which affects blue light much more strongly than red.
The distance between two wave crests; for light it determines the colour.

gewusst: Photos of the Earth taken from the Moon show our planet as a bright blue ball against a black sky.
After big volcanic eruptions there are often especially bright sunset colours, because dust floats high in the air.
The sky is not equally blue everywhere: directly above you it is usually darker than near the horizon.

teile.einleitung: The becquerel is the unit used to measure radioactivity. It counts how many atomic nuclei decay in one second. Becquerels are used, for example, to state how radioactive food, soil or the air in cellars is.
wichtigste: One becquerel (Bq) means: one atomic nucleus decays in one second.
The unit is named after the French physicist Henri Becquerel.
Maximum levels of radioactivity in food are given in becquerels per kilogram.
The concentration of radon in indoor air is measured in becquerels per cubic metre.
The older unit of 1 curie corresponds to 3.7·10^10 becquerels.
The body of an adult has a natural activity of a few thousand becquerels.
Most of this comes from the nuclide potassium-40.

abschnitte.text: Some atomic nuclei are unstable and at some point break down by themselves, giving off **radiation** as they do. This process is called **radioactive decay**. The becquerel gives the **activity**, that is the number of decays per second. A sample of 2 kBq, that is 2000 becquerels, has 120,000 decays in one minute. A becquerel is a very small unit, so large numbers often appear.

In 1896 the Frenchman **Henri Becquerel** discovered that uranium salts give off an invisible radiation that blackens photographic plates. In doing so he had discovered radioactivity. In 1903 he received the Nobel Prize in Physics for this together with Marie and Pierre Curie. In the past the unit **curie** was used, which was originally based on the activity of one gram of radium-226. Today the becquerel is the official unit in the International System of Units.

For food there are maximum levels in **becquerels per kilogram**. After the Chernobyl reactor accident in 1986, mushrooms and game, for example, were closely checked in Europe. In Switzerland, too, radioactive caesium-137 is still measured today in wild boar meat from some regions. The authorities test samples and make sure that the limits are kept to.

**Radon** is a natural radioactive gas that comes out of the ground. It can collect in cellars and badly aired rooms. The radon concentration is measured in **becquerels per cubic metre** of air. In Switzerland there is a reference value of 300 becquerels per cubic metre for this, and the values are often higher, especially in Alpine and Jura areas. Airing rooms regularly and sealing buildings well help against radon.

Our own body is also slightly radioactive. An adult has a natural activity of a few thousand becquerels. Most of it comes from **potassium-40**, which gets into the body with food, for example with bananas or potatoes. Potassium is vital, and a very small part of it just happens to be radioactive. This natural radiation is normal and not dangerous.

begriffe.erklaerung: The number of atomic nuclei that decay per second.
An unstable atomic nucleus changes by itself and gives off radiation in the process.
A particular kind of atom, for example potassium-40.
An invisible radioactive gas that rises out of the ground.

gewusst: Because of its potassium, a banana has a tiny natural radioactivity of about 15 becquerels.
Henri Becquerel discovered radioactivity rather by chance, because he kept uranium salts and photographic plates together in a drawer.
One curie is 37 billion times as big as one becquerel.

teile.einleitung: A pressure cooker is a cooking pot with a lid that closes completely tightly. Inside, the pressure rises, and so the water gets hotter than 100 degrees. In this way potatoes, beans or meat are cooked much faster.
wichtigste: The lid of a pressure cooker closes completely tightly.
The pressure in the pot rises, and the water gets hotter than 100 degrees.
That is why food cooks faster in a pressure cooker.
A valve rises and shows that there is pressure in the pot.
A pressure cooker saves time and energy.
Without some water there is no steam, so the pot always needs liquid.
It may only be opened when there is no more pressure inside.

abschnitte.text: A pressure cooker is a particularly sturdy stainless steel pot with a **sealing ring** in the lid. The lid is pressed firmly onto the pot with a catch. When the water boils, the steam cannot simply escape. It collects in the pot, and the pressure rises. In German it is also called a quick cooker, and in Switzerland often just a “steam cooker”.

Normally water boils at about 100 degrees when the air pressure is as high as at sea level. If the pressure rises, the water needs more energy to evaporate, and the **boiling point** rises. In a pressure cooker the water therefore reaches about 115 to 120 degrees. At this higher temperature food becomes soft much faster. Potatoes often need only about a third of the usual cooking time.

A pressure cooker has a **valve** that rises as soon as there is pressure in the pot. Rings on the valve pin often show whether you are cooking on the gentle or the fast setting. If the pressure gets too high, the valve lets out steam with a hiss. In addition there is a safety device that releases steam if the pressure is too high. The lid cannot be opened while there is pressure in the pot, which protects against dangerous scalds.

As early as 1679 the French physicist **Denis Papin** built a pressure pot, known as Papin’s digester. He even wanted to use it to cook bones until they were soft. Pressure cookers only became popular in home kitchens in the 20th century. In Switzerland the company Kuhn Rikon from the Töss valley is well known; it has been making pressure cookers since the middle of the 20th century.

In the mountains the air pressure is lower than in the lowlands. That is why at about 3000 metres water already boils at around 90 degrees. Pasta and potatoes take longer to cook there in a normal pot. A pressure cooker makes up for this, because it creates the necessary pressure itself. That is why it is also useful in mountain huts.

begriffe.erklaerung: A pressure that is higher than the air pressure outside.
The temperature at which a liquid starts to boil.
A part that lets steam or gas out in a controlled way.
A rubber ring that makes sure no steam escapes at the lid.

gewusst: A pressure cooker can greatly reduce the energy used to cook potatoes or pulses.
Hospitals and laboratories also use the same principle in large devices, autoclaves, to sterilise instruments.
On high mountains an egg in a normal pot without a pressure cooker would only become hard after a longer time.

teile.einleitung: Resolving power tells you how well an eye, a microscope or a telescope can still see two points that are close together as separate. If it is too small, the points blur into a single spot. The better the resolving power, the finer the details you can see.
wichtigste: Resolving power gives the smallest distance or angle that can still be seen as separate.
Because of the diffraction of light, every optical instrument has a limit of resolution.
In 1873 Ernst Abbe worked out the resolution limit of the light microscope.
Light with a shorter wavelength allows better resolution.
Telescopes with a larger aperture can tell apart finer details in the sky.
A healthy human eye resolves about one minute of arc.
In 2014 Stefan Hell received the Nobel Prize for STED microscopy, which gets round the Abbe limit.

abschnitte.text: Imagine two little lamps shining side by side in the distance. Close up you see two lights; from far away only one. The smallest distance or **angle** at which you can still see two separate points describes the resolving power. It applies to eyes, cameras, microscopes and telescopes.

Light is a wave, and waves are diffracted at openings. That is why a point of light is never shown as a perfect point, but as a small disc with rings. If two such discs lie too close together, they overlap. According to the **Rayleigh criterion**, for a round opening with diameter D the smallest angle is about 1.22 times the wavelength divided by D.

The bigger the mirror or lens of a telescope, the finer its resolution. The Hubble Space Telescope has a mirror 2.4 metres in diameter. For green light of 550 nanometres, this gives about 0.058 seconds of arc. On Earth, however, the shimmering **turbulence of the air** gets in the way, which is why telescopes are built on high mountains or sent into space.

In 1873 the German physicist **Ernst Abbe** showed that a light microscope can only separate structures down to about half the wavelength of light. More precisely, the limit depends on the wavelength and the **numerical aperture** of the objective lens. With light of 500 nanometres and a numerical aperture of 1.4, it is about 179 nanometres. A drop of immersion oil between the objective and the specimen increases the numerical aperture and so improves the resolution.

With light of shorter wavelength, such as blue or ultraviolet light, you can see finer details. Electron microscopes use electrons, whose wavelength is much smaller than that of light, and so can even make out the arrangement of individual atoms. Stefan Hell developed **STED microscopy**, in which fluorescent dyes are cleverly switched on and off. He received the Nobel Prize in Chemistry for this in 2014.

A healthy eye can resolve about one minute of arc, which is a sixtieth of a degree. With this, from about 3.5 metres away you can still make out two points one millimetre apart. In an eye test at the eye doctor’s, it is exactly this **visual acuity** that is measured. With screens, people also talk about resolution, meaning the number of pixels.

begriffe.erklaerung: Waves spread out sideways too behind an opening or an edge.
A sixtieth of a degree, that is a very small angle.
A number that tells you how much light an objective lens can collect.
The distance from one wave crest to the next.

gewusst: An eagle can resolve much more finely than a human and spots a mouse from a great height.
Several radio telescopes round the Earth were linked together and in 2019 produced the first image of a black hole.

teile.einleitung: The barometric formula describes how air pressure decreases as you go higher. The higher you get, the less air lies above you, and the thinner the air becomes. With the formula you can calculate the height from the air pressure and the other way round.
wichtigste: The barometric formula describes how air pressure decreases with height.
In an atmosphere with the same temperature everywhere, air pressure falls exponentially.
The simple form is p = p₀·e^(−h/H) with a scale height H of around 8 kilometres.
At sea level the air pressure falls by around 1 hectopascal when you climb 8 metres higher.
On Mount Everest the air pressure is only about a third of the value at sea level.
Barometric altimeters use the formula to calculate height from air pressure.
Changes in the weather can fool an altimeter.

abschnitte.text: Air has weight and presses downwards. At the bottom there is the most air above us, so that is where the air pressure is greatest. If you climb up, there is less air above you, and the pressure falls. Because air can be compressed, it is denser at the bottom than at the top. The **barometric formula** describes exactly how this pressure gets smaller with height.

If you assume that the temperature of the air is the same everywhere, the simple form is p = p₀·e^(−h/H). Here p₀ is the pressure at the ground, about 1013 hectopascals, and h is the height. The **scale height** H is around 8 kilometres. So the pressure does not fall evenly but **exponentially**: with each further step in height, it gets smaller by the same proportion. For the Dufourspitze, at 4634 metres, the formula gives around 568 hectopascals.

At sea level the air pressure falls by around 1 hectopascal when you climb 8 metres higher. At a height of around 3500 metres, for example on the **Jungfraujoch**, only around 660 hectopascals are measured. On the summit of **Mount Everest** the pressure is only about a third of the value at sea level. That is why breathing is very difficult there, and many climbers use oxygen bottles. Because the air pressure is lower, water in the mountains also boils below 100 degrees.

A **barometric altimeter** measures air pressure and converts it into a height using the formula. Such instruments are found in aeroplanes, sports watches and smartphones. Air pressure, however, also changes with the weather. If it falls because of a low, the altimeter shows a greater height even though you are standing still. That is why altimeters have to be reset regularly at known points.

A half-empty plastic bottle that you close on a summit gets squashed in the valley. A **weather balloon** expands more and more as it rises, because the outside pressure falls, until it bursts. In a fast cable car your ears feel pressure, and swallowing or yawning evens it out. In airliners the cabin pressure during the flight corresponds at most to the pressure at about 2400 metres above sea level. Endurance athletes often train at altitude, for example in St Moritz, because in thin air the body makes more **red blood cells**.

In reality the air is not equally warm everywhere. In the lowest 11 kilometres or so, it gets colder on average as height increases. More precise formulas, such as those used in aviation with the **standard atmosphere**, take this drop in temperature into account. For school problems and rough estimates, however, the simple formula is good enough. It shows the most important thing: around half of the mass of the air lies below a height of about 5.5 kilometres.

begriffe.erklaerung: The pressure exerted by the weight of the air.
When a quantity gets smaller or larger by the same proportion in equal steps.
The height after which the air pressure has fallen to about 37 per cent; for the Earth around 8 kilometres.
An instrument that calculates height from air pressure.
A fixed average pattern of pressure and temperature used in aviation.

gewusst: On the Jungfraujoch water boils at just under 90 degrees, which is why pasta takes longer to cook there.
A bag of crisps sealed in the valley puffs up noticeably on a high mountain pass.
Even a lift ride up a few floors can be measured with a sensitive pressure sensor.

teile.einleitung: In the double-slit experiment, light or tiny particles are sent through two very narrow slits close together. On a screen behind them there is not a simple picture of the two slits, but a pattern of bright and dark stripes. This experiment is one of the most famous in the whole of physics.
wichtigste: Behind a double slit a pattern of bright and dark stripes appears.
The pattern proves that light behaves like a wave.
Bright stripes appear where the path difference is a whole number of wavelengths.
Red light produces stripes that are further apart than blue light does.
If you double the distance between the slits, the distance between the stripes halves.
Even electrons sent one at a time gradually build up an interference pattern.
If you measure which slit a particle goes through, the pattern disappears.

abschnitte.text: You need a light source, a plate with two narrow **slits** and a screen. The light passes through both slits and hits the screen. You would expect two bright lines, but you see many bright and dark stripes side by side. The experiment works best with a laser, because its light has only one colour. The British scientist Thomas Young carried out such an experiment as early as around 1802.

The explanation is **interference**: light behaves like a wave. Behind each slit a new wave spreads out, and the two waves overlap. Where crest meets crest, they strengthen each other and a bright stripe appears. Where a crest meets a trough, they cancel each other out and it becomes dark. As with water waves crossing in a pool, a regular pattern forms.

Whether a stripe is bright depends on the **path difference**, that is how much further one wave has to travel. If the difference is a whole number of wavelengths, it is bright. The distance between neighbouring bright stripes is calculated from the wavelength times the distance to the screen divided by the distance between the slits. With 600 nanometres, 2 metres to the screen and 0.3 millimetres between the slits, this is 4 millimetres. The other way round, the wavelength of the light can be worked out from the pattern.

In the 20th century the experiment was also done with **electrons**, that is tiny particles. If you send them off one at a time, each lands at a single point on the screen. But after many electrons, the points again form a pattern of stripes. So particles also behave like waves; this is called **wave-particle duality**. This insight is a cornerstone of quantum physics.

What is especially astonishing is what happens when you check which slit a particle goes through. Then the interference pattern disappears, and only two stripes appear. So the measurement itself changes the result. The physicist Richard Feynman therefore called the double-slit experiment the central mystery of **quantum mechanics**. The experiment has since even been done with whole molecules.

begriffe.erklaerung: The overlapping of waves, in which they strengthen or cancel each other out.
The distance from one wave crest to the next.
How much further one wave has to travel than the other to reach a point.
The physics of the smallest particles, in which particles also have wave properties.

gewusst: In a survey of physicists, the double-slit experiment was voted the most beautiful experiment in physics.
You can also see an interference pattern at home with a laser pointer and a fine hair, but you must never look into the laser beam.
Even molecules made of 60 carbon atoms produced an interference pattern in the experiment.

teile.einleitung: CERN is the European Organization for Nuclear Research and one of the largest research centres in the world. It lies near Geneva on the border between Switzerland and France. Here thousands of researchers use huge machines to study the smallest building blocks of matter.
wichtigste: CERN was founded in 1954, and Switzerland is one of the founding states.
Its main site is in the Geneva municipality of Meyrin.
The largest particle accelerator is the Large Hadron Collider, with a circumference of 27 kilometres.
In 2012 the Higgs boson was detected at CERN.
The World Wide Web was invented at CERN in 1989.
According to its Convention, CERN does no research for military purposes.
The Globe of Science and Innovation was a gift from Switzerland.

abschnitte.text: The name CERN comes from the French **Conseil Européen pour la Recherche Nucléaire**, that is European Council for Nuclear Research. The organisation was founded in 1954 by twelve European states, including Switzerland. Today it has over 20 member states. At CERN researchers from all over the world work together in **particle physics**.

The main site is in **Meyrin** in the canton of Geneva, right on the border with France. The large accelerators run in tunnels deep underground and cross the national border several times. Part of the facilities therefore lies in France. Next to the main site stands the wooden **Globe of Science and Innovation**, a gift from the Swiss Confederation for CERN’s 50th anniversary.

The **Large Hadron Collider**, LHC for short, is a ring-shaped tunnel with a circumference of 27 kilometres, lying around 100 metres deep. In it tiny particles are accelerated to almost the speed of light and fired at each other. Huge detectors such as **ATLAS** and CMS photograph what is produced in these collisions. The magnets are cooled for this to minus 271 degrees Celsius, colder than outer space.

In 1983 researchers at CERN detected the **W and Z bosons**, for which Carlo Rubbia and Simon van der Meer received the Nobel Prize in Physics in 1984. Georges Charpak received the Nobel Prize in 1992 for the multiwire proportional chamber, a particle detector. On 4 July 2012 the detection of the **Higgs boson** was announced. For predicting this particle, Peter Higgs and François Englert received the Nobel Prize in 2013.

In 1989 the British computer scientist **Tim Berners-Lee** proposed a system at CERN for exchanging information between computers. From this came the **World Wide Web**, the websites that we use every day. The world’s first website went online at CERN in 1991. In 1993 CERN released the technology so that everyone could use it free of charge.

In 2023 the **Science Gateway** visitor centre opened, designed by the Italian architect Renzo Piano. There school classes and families can discover the world of particles through exhibitions and experiments. CERN’s founding document, the Convention, states that CERN does no research for military purposes. The results are published and are open to everyone.

begriffe.erklaerung: A huge machine that makes tiny particles extremely fast.
Research into the smallest building blocks of matter.
A measuring instrument that tracks down particles and records their tracks.
A particle that explains why other particles have mass.

gewusst: In the LHC the particles race round the 27-kilometre ring more than 11,000 times in one second.
The Globe of Science and Innovation first stood at the national exhibition Expo.02 in Neuchâtel.
Antimatter is also made and studied at CERN, but only in tiny amounts.

teile.einleitung: The focal point is the point at which parallel light rays meet after passing through a converging lens or being reflected by a concave mirror. There the light is so strongly concentrated that it can even set paper alight. That is where the focal point gets its German name, which means “burning point”.
wichtigste: At the focal point of a converging lens, rays coming in parallel meet.
With a magnifying glass you can set paper alight in sunlight, because the light is concentrated at the focal point.
A thin lens has two focal points, one on each side.
The focal points lie on the optical axis, which runs at right angles through the centre of the lens.
A ray through the focal point runs parallel to the axis behind the converging lens.
A lamp at the focal point produces a parallel beam of light.
A concave mirror also gathers parallel rays at a focal point.

abschnitte.text: A **converging lens** is thicker in the middle than at the edge. When parallel light, for example sunlight, falls on it, all the rays are refracted so that they meet at one point. This point is called the **focal point** or focus. It lies on the **optical axis**, the imaginary line at right angles through the middle of the lens.

If you hold a magnifying glass in the sun, a tiny, very bright spot of light appears. There all the solar energy falling on the lens is concentrated on a small area. That is why it gets so hot at the focal point that paper or dry leaves can start to burn. For the same reason you must never leave glass bottles or magnifying glasses lying in the sun in a forest.

abschnitte.titel: Two focal points and their paths
abschnitte.text: A thin lens has two **focal points**, one in front of and one behind the lens, both the same distance away. The path of the light can also be reversed: a ray coming through the front focal point runs parallel to the axis behind the lens. If you put a small lamp exactly at the focal point, you therefore get a **parallel beam of light**. This is how spotlights and lighthouses work.

Light from very distant things such as the Moon or the stars reaches us almost parallel. That is why their image forms roughly at the focal point behind a converging lens. In a **telescope** or a camera, that is therefore where the image is that you then look at or record. If you focus a camera on “infinity”, the sensor lies exactly at the focal point.

Not only lenses but also curved mirrors have a focal point. A **concave mirror** curves inwards and reflects parallel rays to a single point. A satellite dish gathers radio waves in this way onto the receiver, which sits exactly at the focal point. And in Olympia in Greece the Olympic flame is lit each time with a concave mirror in sunlight.

begriffe.erklaerung: The point at which parallel rays meet behind a lens or in front of a concave mirror.
A lens that is thicker in the middle and focuses light.
A mirror that curves inwards and gathers light.
The Latin word for hearth, another word for focal point.

gewusst: The word focus comes from the Latin “focus” and means hearth or fireplace.
Solar furnaces gather sunlight with huge concave mirrors and reach thousands of degrees at the focal point.
You can even light a fire with a lens made of clear ice, if it is well shaped.

teile.einleitung: ATLAS is one of the biggest and most complicated particle detectors in the world. It stands at the CERN research centre near Geneva in a huge cavern deep underground. With ATLAS, researchers detected the long-sought Higgs boson in 2012.
wichtigste: ATLAS is a particle detector at CERN’s LHC particle accelerator.
The name originally stood for “A Toroidal LHC ApparatuS”.
The detector is around 46 metres long and 25 metres high.
ATLAS is bigger, but lighter, than the CMS detector.
Like an onion, ATLAS consists of several layers with different tasks.
A trigger system selects the interesting collisions for storage in real time.
In 2012 ATLAS and CMS together detected the Higgs boson.

abschnitte.text: In the **LHC**, CERN’s Large Hadron Collider, protons race round a ring 27 kilometres long at almost the speed of light. They collide at four points, and that is where the big detectors stand. **ATLAS** is the biggest of them and stands near Meyrin in the canton of Geneva. It is around 46 metres long and 25 metres high and weighs about 7000 tonnes. The CMS detector is smaller but about twice as heavy.

ATLAS consists of several layers round the collision point. Inside, the **inner detector** measures the tracks of charged particles. Because a strong magnetic field bends their paths, their momentum can be worked out from the curvature. Around it lie the **calorimeters**, which slow particles down and so measure their energy. Right on the outside sits the **muon spectrometer**, because muons pass through the inner layers almost unhindered.

The name ATLAS refers to the **toroid magnets**, which are arranged in a ring round the detector. They are superconducting and have to be cooled to very low temperatures for this. Their eight big coils give the detector its typical appearance. The magnetic fields bend the particles so that they can be measured.

In the detector, bunches of protons collide up to 40 million times a second. No computer could store that much data. That is why the **trigger system** selects the interesting collisions in real time and throws the rest away. Particles such as neutrinos, which fly through the detector unnoticed, are recognised by ATLAS through **missing momentum** at right angles to the beam.

On 4 July 2012 the ATLAS and CMS teams announced the discovery of a new particle, the **Higgs boson**. It explains why other elementary particles have mass. A year later Peter Higgs and François Englert, who had predicted the particle, received the Nobel Prize in Physics. Several thousand researchers from many countries work together on ATLAS, including from Swiss universities.

begriffe.erklaerung: A measuring instrument that tracks down and measures particles from collisions.
The Large Hadron Collider, the largest particle accelerator in the world, at CERN.
A part of a detector that measures the energy of particles by slowing them down.
An elementary particle similar to the electron but around 200 times heavier.
An elementary particle connected with how mass comes about.

gewusst: ATLAS is about half the size of Notre-Dame Cathedral in Paris.
The ATLAS cavern lies around 100 metres underground.
ATLAS weighs about as much as the Eiffel Tower.

teile.einleitung: A CCD sensor is an electronic image sensor that turns light into electrical signals. For a long time it was the heart of digital cameras, video cameras and telescopes. Its invention even won the Nobel Prize in Physics in 2009.
wichtigste: CCD stands for charge-coupled device.
Willard Boyle and George Smith invented the CCD sensor at Bell Labs in 1969.
In each pixel the internal photoelectric effect turns light into electric charge.
The charges are shifted row by row to a read-out amplifier.
A single sensor gets colours through a colour filter mosaic such as the Bayer filter.
In astronomy CCD cameras are strongly cooled to reduce the dark current.
In most mobile phone cameras the CMOS sensor has replaced the CCD sensor.

abschnitte.text: A CCD sensor is a small chip of **silicon** divided into millions of tiny fields, the **pixels**. Each pixel measures how much light falls on it. Together all the measurements make up a digital image. The name charge-coupled device describes how the charges are passed on from pixel to pixel.

When light hits a pixel, it knocks electrons free in the silicon; this is the **internal photoelectric effect**. The more light, the more electrons collect, like rain in a bucket. After the exposure the packets of charge are shifted row by row to the edge, as in a bucket chain. There an amplifier measures each packet, and a computer turns them into brightness values.

A pixel can only measure brightness, not colour. That is why there is a mosaic of red, green and blue filters over the sensor, the **Bayer filter**, in which half the fields are green. If a pixel is strongly overexposed, the charge overflows into the neighbouring pixels; this is called **blooming**. In photos you then see bright stripes next to very bright light sources.

CCD sensors changed astronomy greatly, because their **quantum efficiency** is much higher than that of photographic film. They catch a large share of the arriving particles of light, while film catches only a few per cent. This makes it possible to photograph much fainter stars and galaxies. So that heat does not produce false signals, the **dark current**, the cameras are strongly cooled. The Hubble Space Telescope also worked with CCD cameras.

Willard Boyle and George Smith developed the idea at Bell Labs in the USA in 1969. In 2009 they received the Nobel Prize in Physics for it, together with Charles Kao. Today mobile phones and most cameras contain **CMOS sensors**, which use less electricity and are cheaper. In science and in some special cameras, however, CCD sensors are still used.

begriffe.erklaerung: The smallest dot of a digital image or sensor.
Light frees electrons from their bonds in a material.
The share of particles of light that a sensor actually turns into a signal.
An interfering signal caused by heat, even when no light falls on the sensor.

gewusst: Originally the CCD was not meant as a camera sensor at all, but as a store for data.
Some astronomical CCD cameras are cooled with liquid nitrogen to far below minus 100 degrees.
Many scanners and photocopiers also worked with CCD sensors.

teile.einleitung: Benjamin Franklin was an American inventor, scientist, writer and politician of the 18th century. With his famous kite experiment he showed that lightning is made of electricity, and he invented the lightning rod. He is also one of the Founding Fathers of the United States of America.
wichtigste: Benjamin Franklin lived in North America from 1706 to 1790.
He was a printer, scientist, inventor and politician.
In 1752 he flew a kite in a thunderstorm.
With it he wanted to show that lightning is made of electricity.
He invented the lightning rod and glasses for both near and far.
He helped the USA to gain its independence.
His kite experiment is extremely dangerous and must never be copied.

abschnitte.text: Benjamin Franklin was born on 17 January 1706 in **Boston** and was one of the many children of a soap boiler. He only went to school for a short time and taught himself most things. As a teenager he learnt the trade of **printer** and later moved to Philadelphia. There he published a newspaper and a popular almanac and became wealthy.

In Franklin’s time people did not yet know what lightning really was. In 1752 Franklin flew a **kite** during a thunderstorm, with a metal key hanging from its wet string. When he moved his hand towards the key, small sparks jumped across. In this way he showed that thunderclouds are electrically charged and that lightning is made of **electricity**.

Franklin was very lucky, because a direct lightning strike could have killed him. The scientist Georg Wilhelm Richmann was killed in Saint Petersburg in 1753 during a similar experiment. That is why such experiments must never be copied. In a thunderstorm you should also not fly kites and should keep away from tall trees standing on their own.

From his experiments Franklin developed the **lightning rod**, a metal rod on the roof that leads lightning safely into the ground. He also invented **bifocal glasses**, whose lenses are ground for distance at the top and for close up at the bottom. He also designed an economical stove and a musical instrument made of glass bowls, the glass harmonica. The terms positive and negative charge in the study of electricity also go back to him.

Franklin worked for the American colonies to break away from Great Britain. In 1776 he signed the **Declaration of Independence** of the United States. As envoy to France he won the French over as allies. Later he also worked on the Constitution of the USA.

Franklin died on 17 April 1790 in Philadelphia. He is regarded as one of the most important **Founding Fathers** of the USA. His portrait can still be seen on the 100-dollar note today. Many schools, towns and even a term in physics remind us of him.

begriffe.erklaerung: A metal rod with a wire that leads lightning safely into the earth.
A form of energy produced by electric charges, for example current and lightning.
Glasses with two areas in the lens, one for distance and one for close up.
Men who played an important role in founding the USA.

gewusst: On his sea voyages Franklin also studied the Gulf Stream, a warm ocean current in the Atlantic, and drew a map of it.
Franklin only went to school for about two years and still became one of the most famous scientists of his time.
For his work on electricity Franklin received a high award from the British Royal Society.

teile.einleitung: The Carnot cycle is an imagined, ideal cycle for turning heat into work. It shows how good a heat engine can possibly be in the very best case. This makes it one of the foundations of thermodynamics, the science of heat and energy.
wichtigste: The Frenchman Sadi Carnot described the cycle in 1824 in his work on the motive power of fire.
It consists of two isotherms and two adiabats.
Heat is taken in at high temperature during isothermal expansion.
The work gained per cycle equals the enclosed area in the p-V diagram.
In the T-S diagram the Carnot cycle has the shape of a rectangle.
No cycle between two temperatures can have a higher efficiency.
Run backwards, it becomes an ideal refrigerator or heat pump.

abschnitte.text: Nicolas Léonard **Sadi Carnot** was a young French engineer who lived from 1796 to 1832. At that time steam engines were spreading, but nobody knew how good they could possibly become. In 1824 Carnot published his “Reflections on the Motive Power of Fire”. He recognised that an engine can only do work if heat flows from a hot place to a cold one.

First a gas expands at a high, constant temperature and takes in heat; this is **isothermal expansion**. Then it expands further without any exchange of heat and cools down; this is an **adiabatic** expansion. In the third step the gas is compressed at low temperature and gives off heat. Finally it is compressed further without any exchange of heat until it is hot again and the cycle starts again.

The **Carnot efficiency** is 1 minus the low temperature divided by the high temperature, both measured in kelvin. If a cycle works between 600 K and 300 K, it is 50 per cent. If it takes in 1000 J of heat at 600 K, it gives off 500 J at 300 K, and 500 J become work. The greater the temperature difference, the better the efficiency.

In the pressure-volume diagram the cycle encloses an area that corresponds exactly to the work gained. In the temperature-entropy diagram it becomes a simple rectangle. After a complete cycle the **entropy** of the working gas is the same as at the start. Because nothing is lost, the cycle is called **reversible**.

The Carnot cycle cannot be built exactly, because it would have to run infinitely slowly and without any friction at all. Real engines and power stations therefore always reach less than the Carnot efficiency. It does, however, serve as a yardstick for engineers. Run backwards, the cycle pumps heat from cold to warm, like a fridge or a **heat pump**, which heats many houses in Switzerland.

begriffe.erklaerung: A process in which a gas passes through several states and ends up back where it started.
A change of state in which the temperature stays the same.
A change of state without exchange of heat with the surroundings.
The share of the energy put in that comes out as useful work.

gewusst: Sadi Carnot died at only 36, and his work only became really famous after his death.
Even a perfect engine can never turn heat completely into work.
The Kelvin temperature scale is closely linked to ideas about the Carnot cycle.

teile.einleitung: A brake block is a block that is pressed against a wheel, or lies in front of it, so that it slows down or stays still. On a bike these are the little rubber blocks of the rim brake; on the railway they are large blocks that press on the wheels. A wedge behind the wheel of a lorry is also often called a brake block in German.
wichtigste: With a rim brake on a bike, the brake block presses against the rim of the wheel.
Bike brake blocks are usually made of rubber.
A brake block brakes by rubbing on the wheel and turning kinetic energy into heat.
In the rain a rim brake works less well, because the wet rim is more slippery.
Brake blocks wear down over time and often squeal when they are worn.
A wedge is placed behind the wheels of a lorry parked on a slope.
Railway wagons also often brake with brake blocks that press directly on the wheels.

abschnitte.text: With a **rim brake** there are two brake blocks, one on the left and one on the right of the wheel. When you pull the brake lever, they press against the **rim**, the metal ring of the wheel, from both sides. The blocks are usually made of a special rubber mixture in a holder of metal or plastic. Many bikes today have disc brakes instead of rim brakes, in which small brake pads press on a disc.

abschnitte.titel: How does a brake block brake?
abschnitte.text: The brake block rubs on the turning wheel, and this **friction** slows the movement down. The kinetic energy does not disappear; it becomes **heat**. On a long descent with a lot of braking, the blocks and rims therefore get hot. In the rain a film of water forms on the rim, and the brake only grips properly after a short moment.

Each time you brake, a little material is rubbed off the brake block. Many blocks have grooves that act as a **wear indicator**: when they have disappeared, the blocks should be replaced. Worn or dirty blocks often squeal and brake less well. A bike mechanic can swap them in a few minutes.

Many goods wagons brake with large brake blocks, also called **brake shoes**, that press directly on the running surface of the wheels. In the past they were made of grey cast iron, a kind of cast iron. These made the wheels rough, so the trains were very noisy when running. Today blocks made of composite material are often used, which keep the wheels smooth so that the wagons run much more quietly.

A **wheel chock** is also often called a brake block in everyday German. It is placed behind the wheels of a lorry, trailer or aeroplane so that it does not roll away. This is especially important on a slope, in case the handbrake gives way. On the railway there is the **skid**, which is placed on the rail and stops wagons safely.

begriffe.erklaerung: A block that slows a wheel down by friction or stops it from rolling away.
The outer ring of a wheel, on which the tyre sits.
The wearing down of a part through use.
A wedge placed in front of or behind a wheel so that it does not roll.
A wedge on the rail that stops railway wagons.

gewusst: There are special brake blocks for bikes with carbon rims, because normal rubber blocks would brake badly on them.
Switzerland has invested a lot of money so that goods wagons run with quieter brake blocks and people living nearby hear less noise.
Aeroplanes on the ground are secured by mechanics with large wedges called “chocks” in English.

teile.einleitung: The Cavendish experiment is a famous experiment in which the English scientist Henry Cavendish measured the tiny attraction between lead balls in the laboratory in 1797 and 1798. With it he was the first to work out the average density, and so the weight, of the whole Earth. That is why the experiment is often called “weighing the Earth”.
wichtigste: Henry Cavendish published the results of his gravity experiment in 1798.
He worked with a torsion balance originally designed by John Michell.
Large and small lead balls attracted each other very weakly.
Cavendish wanted to find the average density of the Earth.
He got about 5.4 times the density of water, very close to today’s value.
He watched the balance through a telescope from outside the room so that nothing disturbed the measurement.
The gravitational constant G can be worked out from the experiment.

abschnitte.text: Isaac Newton had recognised that all bodies with mass attract each other; this is **gravity**. Between everyday objects, however, this force is so weak that you hardly notice it. Henry Cavendish managed to measure it between lead balls in the laboratory. His real aim was to find the **average density** of the Earth.

The heart of it was a **torsion balance**: a wooden rod around 1.8 m long with a small lead ball at each end, hung from a thin wire. Next to the small balls Cavendish placed two large lead balls of about 158 kg. The attraction turned the rod a tiny amount, and the wire twisted. From this twisting he could calculate the force. The torsion balance had been designed by the geologist **John Michell**, who died before the experiment.

Even the smallest disturbances would have spoiled the result, such as air currents or the **body heat** of a person in the room. That is why Cavendish put the torsion balance in a closed room. He moved the large balls from outside and read off the movements through a **telescope** through an opening in the wall. One swing of the rod took several minutes.

Cavendish found an average density for the Earth of about **5.4 times** the density of water. Today’s value is around 5.5, so he was only slightly out. Because the Earth is much denser than the rock on its surface, it must have a heavy core inside. The **gravitational constant** G, which today is about 6.674·10⁻¹¹, can also be calculated from his measurements.

Henry Cavendish lived in England from 1731 to 1810 and came from a very rich aristocratic family. He was regarded as extremely shy and hardly spoke to other people, but he did research tirelessly. As early as 1766 he described **hydrogen** as a substance of its own, and later he showed that water is produced when hydrogen burns. The famous Cavendish Laboratory at the University of Cambridge is named after his family.

begriffe.erklaerung: The force of attraction that all bodies with mass exert on each other.
A measuring instrument in which a tiny force twists a rod hanging from a wire.
How much mass there is in a certain volume.
The constant of nature G, which tells you how strong gravity is.

gewusst: The force Cavendish measured was about as big as the weight of a tiny grain of sand.
His measurement made it possible for the first time to work out that the Earth weighs about six million billion billion kilograms.
The gravitational constant is still one of the least precisely known constants of nature.

teile.einleitung: A down jacket is a particularly warm and light jacket filled with down. Down is the soft, fluffy feathers of ducks or geese. Its secret is the air that it holds between its fine little branches.
wichtigste: Down is the soft feathers of ducks or geese.
On the bird it grows under the large outer feathers.
Down holds a lot of air, and still air insulates very well.
For the warmth it gives, a down jacket is very light.
You can squash it up small, because you press the air out as you do so.
The jacket is quilted so that the down does not slip.
If the down gets completely wet, it keeps you less warm.

abschnitte.text: **Down** is very soft feathers without a hard quill. Many fine little branches grow in all directions from a small centre, so that each piece of down looks like a little ball of fluff. In ducks and geese it grows close to the body under the large outer feathers. In this way it protects the water birds from getting cold even in icy water. For jackets, down from geese or ducks that were bred for meat is usually used.

Air conducts heat very badly when it cannot move. Down holds countless little cushions of air, and these slow down the **loss of heat** from the body. The jacket itself produces no heat; it only keeps the body’s warmth in. The more the down puffs up, the more air it holds and the warmer the jacket. This property is called **loft**.

abschnitte.titel: How a down jacket is made
abschnitte.text: A down jacket consists of a tightly woven outer fabric, a lining and the filling in between. The jacket is divided into many compartments; this is called **quilting**. Without these compartments the down would slip downwards and there would be cold spots at the top. The filling often contains a share of small feathers as well as down. The fabric has to be woven so tightly that the fine down does not poke out.

If down gets completely wet, it sticks together and loses its cushions of air. Then it keeps you much less warm, and it only dries slowly. That is why mountaineers often wear a waterproof jacket over it in the rain. Down jackets can be washed with special down detergent and then dried in a tumble dryer with tennis balls so that they become fluffy again. As an alternative there are jackets with synthetic fibres, which still keep you fairly warm when damp.

In the past, in some countries, feathers were plucked from live geese, which causes the animals great pain. Today many manufacturers make sure that the down comes from animal-friendly sources. There are quality labels for this, such as the **Responsible Down Standard**. Especially valuable is eider down, which people in Iceland collect from the nests of eider ducks after the breeding season. Down from old jackets and duvets can also be recycled.

begriffe.erklaerung: A very soft feather without a hard quill that grows close to the bird’s skin.
Protection that stops heat escaping to the outside.
How much down puffs up and how much air it can hold.
Seams that divide a jacket into many small compartments.

gewusst: A light down jacket can be packed up so small that it fits into a trouser pocket.
Eider ducks line their nests with their own down, which is collected later.
Down duvets on beds work on exactly the same principle as down jackets.

teile.einleitung: The buoyant force is the force with which a liquid or a gas pushes a body upwards. It decides whether something floats, hovers or sinks. Thanks to it, ships carry thousands of tonnes and hot-air balloons rise into the sky.
wichtigste: The buoyant force equals the weight of the displaced liquid or gas.
A body floats if its average density is less than that of water.
A body with a volume of 2 dm³ fully submerged in water experiences around 19.6 N of buoyancy.
In salty sea water the buoyancy is greater than in fresh water.
A submarine dives by flooding its ballast tanks with water.
A hot-air balloon rises because hot air has a lower density than the surrounding air.
Around 90 per cent of an iceberg lies below the surface of the water.

abschnitte.text: In a liquid the pressure rises with depth. So more pressure acts on the underside of a body than on its top. The difference gives an upward force, the **buoyant force**. According to **Archimedes’ principle** it is as great as the weight of the displaced liquid. A body of 2 dm³ displaces 2 kg of water and experiences around 19.6 N of buoyancy.

If the average **density** of a body is less than that of water, it floats on the surface. If it is the same, it hovers in the water. If it is greater, it sinks. A block of wood of 600 kg/m³ is 60 per cent submerged when it floats. If a stone weighs 30 N in air and only 18 N under water, its buoyancy is 12 N, and you can calculate its density as 2500 kg/m³.

A ship made of steel floats because its hollow hull displaces a lot of water. When a cargo ship sails from the sea into a freshwater river, it sinks a little deeper, because fresh water has a lower density. To dive, a **submarine** floods its ballast tanks with water. To surface, it forces the water out again with compressed air. Fish control their buoyancy with an air-filled **swim bladder**.

Air also produces buoyancy, though much less than water. A **hot-air balloon** rises because the hot air in the envelope has a lower density than the cooler surrounding air. Gas balloons are filled with helium, which is much lighter than air. In 1999 the Swiss Bertrand Piccard and the Briton Brian Jones became the first to fly non-stop round the Earth, in the balloon Breitling Orbiter 3. His grandfather Auguste Piccard had already risen into the stratosphere in a balloon in 1931.

In the **Dead Sea** you hardly go under, because the very salty water has a high density. You can lie on your back there and read a newspaper. Ice has a density of about 917 kg/m³, sea water of about 1025 kg/m³. That is why around 90 per cent of an iceberg lies below the surface. For ships, icebergs are therefore more dangerous than they look.

Auguste Piccard also built the submersible **Trieste**. It had a large float filled with petrol, which is lighter than water and provided buoyancy. In 1960 his son Jacques Piccard and Don Walsh dived in it to the deepest point of the world’s oceans in the Mariana Trench. For the 1964 national exhibition in Lausanne, Jacques Piccard built the tourist submarine Mésoscaphe, which dived in Lake Geneva.

begriffe.erklaerung: The upward force on a body in a liquid or a gas.
The total mass of a body divided by its whole volume, including hollow spaces.
A tank in a submarine that can be filled with water or air.
A gas-filled organ with which many fish control their buoyancy.

gewusst: Ships have a mark on the hull that shows how deep they may sink at most in salt or fresh water.
A person with air breathed in floats more easily in water than after breathing out.
The water level in a glass does not rise when an ice cube floating in it melts.

teile.einleitung: Observing means looking at something carefully and closely and recording what you notice. In science, observation is the first step towards understanding the world. A good observer describes honestly what really happens, not what they expect.
wichtigste: In an observation you notice something with your senses or with measuring instruments.
An observation describes what you see, for example “The water turns blue.”
It is important to record exactly and honestly what happens.
A drawing or a photo helps to record an observation precisely.
Observation and explanation are two different things.
In experiments you must not put anything in your mouth, because it could be poisonous.
Aids such as a magnifying glass, microscope and telescope extend our senses.

abschnitte.text: In an **observation** you notice something deliberately and attentively. Usually this is done with the eyes, but hearing, smelling and touching also count. In physics, chemistry and biology it is the start of every investigation. You find out what happens without immediately explaining why. A sentence such as “The water turns blue.” is an observation; a sentence such as “The colour has dissolved because the water is warm.” is already an explanation.

So that you do not forget an observation, you write it in a **record**. It includes the date, what you did and what you saw. A **drawing** or a photo often captures shapes and colours better than many words. If possible, you also measure, for example with a ruler, a clock, scales or a thermometer. Measurements make observations more precise and comparable.

A good observer writes down what she actually sees, even if she expected something else. Anyone who only notes what they want to see distorts the result. That is why experiments are often repeated several times and the observations of different people compared. Our senses can be deceived, as you notice with **optical illusions**. Unexpected observations in particular have often led to new discoveries in science.

With a **magnifying glass** you see things enlarged several times, such as the legs of a beetle. A **microscope** shows tiny cells that you would never see with the naked eye. Around 1610 the Italian Galileo Galilei was one of the first to observe the moons of Jupiter through a telescope. Thermometers, stopwatches and cameras help to record changes precisely. In this way researchers can also observe things that are too small, too far away or too fast.

Fixed safety rules apply to experiments. You never put anything in your mouth, because a substance could be **poisonous**. To smell a substance, you carefully waft the smell towards you with your hand instead of sniffing it directly. You never look straight at the sun, and certainly not with a telescope or magnifying glass, because that can badly injure your eyes. Safety glasses are worn for many experiments.

You can observe a lot outdoors too, such as birds at a bird table, tadpoles in a pond or the weather. From 1960 the Briton **Jane Goodall** observed chimpanzees in Africa for years and discovered that they use tools. In Switzerland volunteers count birds every year and so help research. It is important not to disturb animals and to keep your distance. A notebook and a pair of binoculars are enough to start with.

begriffe.erklaerung: Noticing something attentively and describing exactly what happens.
A report in which you write down an experiment and its results.
A guess that can be tested with observations.
An observation with a measuring instrument that gives a number.

gewusst: In the 17th century the Dutchman Antonie van Leeuwenhoek was one of the first to observe bacteria, with microscopes he had built himself.
On his voyage round the world Charles Darwin observed, among other things, finches and tortoises on the Galápagos Islands, and later developed his theory of evolution from this.

teile.einleitung: Archimedes’ principle explains why ships float and stones sink. It says: a body in a liquid experiences a buoyant force that is as great as the weight of the liquid it displaces. It was discovered by the Greek scholar Archimedes more than 2200 years ago.
wichtigste: The buoyant force equals the weight of the displaced liquid.
It is calculated as the density of the liquid times g times the displaced volume.
Archimedes described the law in his work “On Floating Bodies”.
Archimedes lived in the 3rd century BC in Syracuse on Sicily.
A floating body sinks until buoyancy and weight are equal.
The principle also applies in gases, for example in air.
The principle can be used to find the density of bodies and liquids.

abschnitte.text: **Archimedes** was a Greek mathematician, physicist and inventor. He lived from about 287 to 212 BC in Syracuse on Sicily. He invented, for example, the Archimedean screw for raising water and studied levers. He wrote down his law about buoyancy in the work **“On Floating Bodies”**. According to a well-known legend he shouted “Eureka!”, I have found it, when the idea came to him in the bath.

When a body is put into a liquid, it pushes part of the liquid aside. This **displaced liquid** has a weight. The **buoyant force** that pushes the body upwards is exactly as great. As a formula: buoyancy = density of the liquid · g · displaced volume. A cube with sides of 10 cm, completely submerged, displaces 1 litre of water and experiences about 10 N of buoyancy.

An aluminium cube with a volume of 1 dm³ weighs 27 N. In water it experiences 10 N of buoyancy, so a spring balance only shows 17 N. A ball with a volume of 2 dm³ that is half submerged displaces 1 dm³ and experiences 10 N of buoyancy. A block of wood with a density of 0.6 g/cm³ is 60 per cent submerged when it floats. If a stone with a mass of 600 g displaces 200 ml of water, it has a **density** of 3 g/cm³.

A famous story tells of King Hiero II of Syracuse. He wanted to know whether his new crown was made of pure gold or whether the goldsmith had mixed in silver. Archimedes is said to have measured the volume of the crown with water and compared it with a bar of gold of the same weight. Silver has a lower density than gold and would have displaced more water. Whether the story really happened exactly like this, nobody knows.

The principle explains why a ship made of steel floats: its hull displaces a great deal of water. A **hydrometer** is a small glass tube that floats in a liquid and shows its density on a scale. This is used, for example, to check the sugar content of grape juice in winemaking. Air also produces a small buoyancy. A very precise balance therefore shows a slightly smaller value for a large block of polystyrene in air than in a vacuum.

begriffe.erklaerung: The force with which a liquid or a gas pushes a body upwards.
The pushing aside of liquid by a body that is put into it.
Mass per volume; it tells you how heavy a substance is for the same size.
A floating instrument for measuring the density of liquids.

gewusst: Archimedes is said to have said: “Give me a fixed point and I will lift the world off its hinges.”
In Switzerland the hydrometer for the sugar content of grape must is also called an “Öchslewaage”.
In water a person can carry a friend much more easily than on land, because buoyancy helps.

teile.einleitung: The Carnot efficiency is the highest efficiency a heat engine can reach at all. It depends on only two temperatures: the hot side, from which the heat comes, and the cold side, to which it is given off. No steam engine, car engine or power station can beat this limit.
wichtigste: The Carnot efficiency is the upper limit for every heat engine.
It is calculated as 1 minus T_c divided by T_h.
The temperatures must be given in kelvin.
Between 500 K and 300 K it is 40 per cent, between 800 K and 300 K 62.5 per cent.
It rises if the hot side gets hotter or the cold side colder.
Real engines never reach it because of friction and heat losses.
It is named after the French physicist Sadi Carnot.

abschnitte.text: A **heat engine** takes in heat from a hot source, turns part of it into work and gives off the rest to cold surroundings. Examples are steam engines, car engines, steam turbines and nuclear power stations. The **efficiency** tells you what share of the heat becomes usable work. The Carnot efficiency is the greatest value that is physically possible.

The Carnot efficiency is 1 minus T_c divided by T_h. Here T_h is the temperature of the hot side and T_c that of the cold side, both in **kelvin**. Between 500 K and 300 K this gives 1 minus 0.6, that is 40 per cent. Between 800 K and 300 K it is 62.5 per cent, and at 427 °C and 27 °C, that is 700 K and 300 K, about 57 per cent.

The formula only works with the **absolute temperature**, which starts at 0 at absolute zero. Only this is proportional to the amounts of heat that an ideal engine takes in and gives off. With degrees Celsius you would get nonsense, and you could even divide by zero. That is why you always convert first: kelvin equals degrees Celsius plus 273.15.

The efficiency becomes greater if the hot side gets hotter or the cold side colder. That is why modern power stations work with very hot steam at high pressure. If you want to reach an efficiency of 60 per cent with a cold side of 280 K, the hot side needs 700 K. An efficiency of 100 per cent never exists, because for that the cold side would have to be at **absolute zero**.

Real engines always stay below the Carnot value. Reasons include **friction**, heat escaping unused through walls, and the temperature differences needed for heat to flow fast enough at all. An ordinary petrol engine uses only about a third of the energy in the fuel for movement. Combined-cycle gas power stations, at around 60 per cent, are among the best heat engines.

The French engineer and physicist **Sadi Carnot** lived from 1796 to 1832. In 1824 he published a work on the motive power of fire. In it he imagined an ideal engine, the **Carnot cycle**, and showed that its performance depends only on the temperatures. His ideas laid the foundation for **thermodynamics**, the science of heat and energy.

begriffe.erklaerung: The share of the energy put in that is turned into useful work.
A machine that turns heat partly into movement or work.
A unit of temperature that starts at 0 at absolute zero.
The part of physics that deals with heat, temperature and energy.

gewusst: Sadi Carnot was only 28 years old when he published his ground-breaking work.
A heat pump is a heat engine run in reverse and can supply more heat than the electricity it uses.
Because the waste heat from power stations cannot be turned into work any more, it is often used for district heating to warm houses.

teile.einleitung: A kite is a light flying object made of a frame and fabric or paper, which you fly on a string in the wind. It does not fly with an engine, but only with the force of the wind. In Switzerland many children fly kites in autumn.
wichtigste: To fly a kite, you need wind.
You hold the kite with a string.
Kites were probably invented in China.
A long tail makes the kite fly more steadily.
A stunt kite has two strings and can be steered.
You must not fly a kite near power lines.
Near airports it is forbidden, because kites can endanger aeroplanes.

abschnitte.text: A kite usually consists of light sticks, in the past of bamboo or wood and today often of carbon fibre. Paper, fabric or plastic film is stretched over them. At the front there is a **bridle**, strings to which the flying line is tied. Classic shapes are the diamond kite and the box kite. Many children make their first kite themselves at school.

The kite stands at a slant in the wind; this angle is called the **angle of attack**. The wind presses against the surface and is deflected downwards. This creates a force that pulls the kite upwards and backwards, **lift**. The string holds against it so that the kite is not blown away. Without a string a kite would simply drift with the wind and crash.

A long tail at the bottom brakes a little and keeps the kite straight in the wind. That way it flies more steadily and does not spin round in circles. A **stunt kite** has two strings, which you hold with both hands. If you pull the left string, it flies to the left; if you pull the right one, to the right. With stunt kites you can fly loops and tricks.

Kites were probably invented in **China** more than 2000 years ago. There they were used not only for play but also for signalling. Later they spread throughout Asia, where there are still large kite festivals today. In the 18th century Benjamin Franklin used a kite to study the electricity of thunderstorms, a very dangerous experiment. Researchers also used kites to lift measuring instruments for weather observations high into the air.

You must never fly kites near **power lines**, because that is extremely dangerous. In a thunderstorm you must bring the kite down immediately.
