Around airports flying kites is forbidden or strictly controlled, because kites can endanger aeroplanes. Roads and railway lines are also unsuitable places. Wide meadows, fields or hills with a steady wind are best.

begriffe.erklaerung: A force that pushes a flying object upwards.
The angle at which a surface stands at a slant in the wind.
Strings on the kite to which the flying line is attached.
A kite with two strings that can be steered.

gewusst: In kitesurfing a large stunt kite pulls a person on a board across the water.
In the past kites were even used to pull weather instruments up to great heights.
In parts of Asia there are kite festivals at which thousands of kites are in the sky at the same time.

teile.einleitung: Beta radiation is a kind of radioactive radiation. It consists of fast electrons or positrons that are flung out of a decaying atomic nucleus. It penetrates further than alpha radiation, but can easily be shielded with a few millimetres of aluminium.
wichtigste: Beta-minus radiation consists of fast electrons.
In beta-minus decay a neutron in the nucleus turns into a proton.
In beta-plus decay the nucleus gives off a positron.
In air beta radiation travels up to a few metres.
A few millimetres of aluminium shield beta radiation well.
Carbon-14 turns into nitrogen-14 through beta-minus decay.
In 1930 Wolfgang Pauli, then a professor at ETH Zurich, predicted the neutrino to explain beta decay.

abschnitte.text: Some atomic nuclei are unstable and change by themselves; they are called **radioactive**. In beta decay the nucleus flings out a very fast particle. Usually it is an electron, and then it is called **beta-minus radiation**. Less often it is a positron, the antiparticle of the electron, and then it is called beta-plus radiation.

In beta-minus decay a neutron in the nucleus turns into a proton, an electron and a tiny particle, an antineutrino. The proton stays in the nucleus, so it becomes a different chemical element. Carbon-14, for example, becomes nitrogen-14. In **beta-plus decay** it is the other way round: a proton becomes a neutron, and a positron flies out.

Beta particles are light and electrically charged, so they are quickly slowed down in matter. In air they travel up to a few metres, in the body only a few millimetres. A sheet of paper is not quite enough, but a few millimetres of **aluminium** or Perspex stop them reliably. If beta emitters get into the body, for example with food, they can damage cells.

In 1899 the physicist **Ernest Rutherford** distinguished two kinds of radiation and called them alpha and beta. It soon turned out that beta rays are electrons. What was puzzling was that the electrons had different amounts of energy. In 1930 **Wolfgang Pauli**, a professor at ETH Zurich, therefore proposed an invisible particle that carries off part of the energy: the neutrino.

In factories beta radiation is used to measure the **thickness** of paper, film or sheet metal, because the thicker the material, the less radiation gets through. In medicine beta emitters are used against certain kinds of cancer, and positrons are used for examinations with a PET scanner. Researchers use the decay of carbon-14 to work out the age of old bones or wood. In the past the hands of some Swiss watches glowed with tritium, a weak beta emitter.

begriffe.erklaerung: The property of some atomic nuclei to break down by themselves and give off radiation.
A tiny, negatively charged particle.
The positively charged counterpart of the electron, an antiparticle.
An almost massless particle that passes through almost everything unhindered.

gewusst: Billions of neutrinos fly through your body every second without you noticing anything.
Bananas also contain a tiny amount of radioactive potassium-40, which among other things gives off beta radiation.

teile.einleitung: The braking distance is the distance a vehicle travels from the moment it starts braking until it stands still. It depends strongly on the speed and the road surface. If you understand it, you know why even a few km/h more can be dangerous in traffic.
wichtigste: The braking distance is the distance from the start of braking until standstill.
At twice the speed, the braking distance becomes about four times as long.
At three times the speed it becomes about nine times as long.
The formula is: braking distance = speed squared divided by twice the deceleration.
On ice the braking distance is much longer, because the tyres grip badly.
Together with the reaction distance, the braking distance makes up the stopping distance.

abschnitte.text: The **braking distance** begins at the moment the brake starts to work and ends when the vehicle stands still. Before that, however, the **reaction time** passes, during which the driver spots the danger and puts their foot on the brake pedal. During this time the car carries on without braking; this is the reaction distance. The reaction distance and the braking distance together are called the **stopping distance**.

If a vehicle brakes evenly: braking distance s = v² / (2·a). Here v is the speed in m/s and a the **deceleration** in m/s². A car at 20 m/s that brakes at 8 m/s² has a braking distance of 25 m. A bike at 10 m/s with a deceleration of 5 m/s² needs 10 m. You get the braking time with t = v / a, so a car at 20 m/s braking at 5 m/s² stops after 4 s.

abschnitte.titel: Twice as fast, four times as far
abschnitte.text: Because the speed is **squared** in the formula, the braking distance grows much faster than the speed. If you go twice as fast, it becomes about four times as long; at three times the speed, about nine times. If a car has a braking distance of 4.5 m at 30 km/h, then under the same conditions it is already 18 m at 60 km/h. The reason is the kinetic energy, which also grows with the square of the speed and has to be turned into heat by the brakes.

How well a vehicle can brake depends on the **grip** of the tyres on the road. On dry tarmac it is high; on a wet road, on leaves, snow or ice it is much lower. On ice the braking distance can therefore become several times as long. Worn tyres, bad brakes or a heavy load also make the braking distance longer.

In residential areas in Switzerland there is often a 30 km/h limit, because children are out and about there. At 30 km/h the stopping distance is much shorter than at 50 km/h, and a car can often still stop in time. At driving school you learn a rule of thumb: the braking distance in metres is roughly the speed in km/h divided by 10, multiplied by itself. For children this means: cars can never stop immediately, so always wait until a car has stopped before crossing the road.

begriffe.erklaerung: The time until you react to a danger, usually about one second.
The reaction distance and the braking distance together.
How much slower a vehicle gets each second, measured in m/s².
How well the tyres stick to the road and do not slip.

gewusst: At 50 km/h a car travels almost 14 metres in one second of reaction time without braking at all.
With ABS the wheels do not lock when braking, so the car stays steerable.
A car at 60 km/h has a braking distance four times as long as one at 30 km/h.

teile.einleitung: The asynchronous or induction motor is the most common electric motor in the world. It drives pumps, fans, conveyor belts, lifts and even locomotives. Its trick: a rotating magnetic field drags the rotor round with it, without any current having to flow to it through contacts.
wichtigste: An induction motor usually runs on three-phase current, which produces a rotating field.
The rotor always turns a little more slowly than the rotating field.
The relative difference between the speed of the rotating field and the rotor is called slip.
The most common type of rotor is the squirrel-cage rotor.
Galileo Ferraris and Nikola Tesla developed the principle at about the same time.
If you swap two of the outer conductors, the motor turns the other way.
With a frequency converter the speed can be adjusted continuously.

abschnitte.text: An induction motor consists of two main parts. The fixed part is called the **stator** and contains copper coils. The turning part is called the **rotor**. In the most common type, the **squirrel-cage rotor**, the rotor contains bars of aluminium or copper joined at the ends by rings. It looks like a hamster wheel or a cage.

The three-phase current in the stator coils produces a **rotating field**, a magnetic field that goes round in a circle. This field cuts across the bars of the rotor and induces a current in them. The current forms its own magnetic field, and the rotor is dragged round by the rotating field. If the rotor turned exactly as fast as the field, no more current would be induced. That is why it always lags a little behind; it runs asynchronously.

At 50 hertz the rotating field turns, depending on the design, at 3000 or 1500 revolutions per minute, for example. The difference from the rotor is called **slip**. If the field turns at 1500 and the rotor at 1440 per minute, the slip is 60 : 1500 = 4 per cent. If the motor is loaded more heavily, the slip rises a little. With a **frequency converter** you change the frequency of the current and can thus adjust the speed continuously.

When an induction motor is switched on directly, a very high starting current flows briefly. It is around five to eight times the rated current. Larger motors are therefore often started with a **star-delta starter**, which lowers this current. If you want to reverse the direction of rotation, you simply swap two of the three outer conductors.

The Italian **Galileo Ferraris** and the inventor Nikola Tesla developed the principle of the rotating-field motor at about the same time in the 1880s. Around 1889 Mikhail Dolivo-Dobrovolsky built the first practical squirrel-cage motor at AEG in Berlin. In 1891 three-phase current was transmitted over a long distance for the first time, from Lauffen am Neckar to Frankfurt. The Oerlikon engineering works near Zurich took part in this. In the same year Charles Brown and Walter Boveri founded the company BBC in Baden, which later became ABB.

Induction motors are robust, cheap and need hardly any maintenance, because they have no sliding contacts. You find them in washing machines, pumps, ventilation systems, machine tools and ski lifts. Many modern locomotives and trams run on induction motors. A large part of the electricity used in industry is consumed by motors like these.

begriffe.erklaerung: Alternating current from three wires whose voltages are offset in time.
A magnetic field that turns in a circle.
The creation of a current in a conductor by a changing magnetic field.
How much more slowly the rotor turns compared with the rotating field.
A device that changes the frequency of the current and so controls the motor speed.

gewusst: The rotor of a squirrel-cage motor has no electrical connection at all.
Induction motors can also work as generators if you drive them faster than the rotating field.
An induction motor can run for many decades; often only the ball bearings need replacing.

teile.einleitung: Auguste Piccard was a Swiss physicist and adventurer from Basel. In 1931 he became the first person to rise into the stratosphere in a balloon, and later he built submersibles for the deep sea. So he explored both the sky and the sea.
wichtigste: Auguste Piccard was born in Basel in 1884 and died in Lausanne in 1962.
His twin brother Jean Piccard was also a scientist.
For a long time he was professor of physics in Brussels.
In 1931 he rose to a height of about 16 km with a balloon and an airtight pressurised cabin.
The balloon landed on a glacier in the Tyrol.
Later he developed the bathyscaphe, a submersible for the deep sea.
His son Jacques and his grandson Bertrand also became famous explorers.

abschnitte.text: Auguste Piccard was born on 28 January 1884 in **Basel**, together with his twin brother **Jean**. He studied at ETH in Zurich and became a physicist. From 1922 he was a professor at the university in **Brussels**. With his high forehead, his glasses and his wild hair, he became the model for the comic character Professor Calculus in “The Adventures of Tintin”.

On 27 May 1931 Piccard and his assistant Paul Kipfer set off from Augsburg in the balloon **FNRS**. What was new was a spherical, airtight **pressurised cabin** made of aluminium, in which it was possible to breathe at great heights. The two reached almost 16 kilometres and so went higher than any human had before. They landed on a **glacier in the Tyrol**, the Gurgler Ferner. A year later Piccard rose a little higher still, setting off from Dübendorf.

Piccard wanted to study **cosmic rays**, which hit the Earth from space. At great heights this radiation is stronger, because there is less air to shield it. He also wanted to show that people can travel safely to great heights in a pressurised cabin. Today’s aeroplanes also have a pressurised cabin.

After the sky, Piccard turned to the sea. He developed the **bathyscaphe**, a submersible with a large float and a thick steel sphere for the crew. The principle is like a balloon, only under water. His best-known submersible was called the **Trieste** and was built in Italy.

In 1960 his son **Jacques Piccard**, together with Don Walsh, dived in the Trieste into the Challenger Deep of the Mariana Trench, almost 11 kilometres deep. His grandson **Bertrand Piccard** flew round the Earth in a balloon in 1999 without stopping. In 2016 Bertrand and André Borschberg flew round the world in the solar aeroplane **Solar Impulse 2**. So three generations of Piccards have set records in the air and under water.

begriffe.erklaerung: The layer of air above about 10 to 15 kilometres, where there is hardly any weather.
An airtight cabin in which the air pressure stays at a level at which people can breathe.
A submersible for great ocean depths, built on the principle of a balloon.
High-energy particles that come from space.

gewusst: Auguste Piccard was the model for Professor Calculus, the absent-minded inventor in “The Adventures of Tintin”.
On his balloon flight in 1931 Piccard was one of the first people to see that the sky looks almost black at great heights.
The Piccard family achieved both the highest balloon flight and the deepest dive of their times.

teile.einleitung: A brake is a device that makes something that is moving slower or stops it. Bikes, cars, trains, lifts and even aeroplanes need brakes so that people can travel safely. In terms of physics, most brakes turn kinetic energy into heat through friction.
wichtigste: Brakes usually turn kinetic energy into heat through friction.
On a bike you usually brake with levers on the handlebars, and on some by pedalling backwards.
In a car you brake with your foot on the brake pedal, and then red brake lights come on at the back.
On a wet road the braking distance gets longer.
When braking for a long time, for example downhill, brakes get hot.
Inline skates have the brake at the back by the heel; beginner skiers brake with the snowplough.

abschnitte.text: A brake reduces the speed of a vehicle or a machine. In most brakes one part presses against a turning wheel or disc. This creates **friction**, and the **kinetic energy** is turned into heat. That is why brakes get hot on long descents, in extreme cases so hot that they work less well.

On most bikes you pull **brake levers** on the handlebars. A cable or a fluid passes the force on to the rim brake or the **disc brake**. Some bikes, especially children’s bikes, have a **coaster brake**, which you work by pedalling backwards. In Switzerland bikes must have two brakes that work well, one for the front wheel and one for the back wheel.

In a car the driver presses the **brake pedal** with her foot. A fluid passes the pressure to the brakes on all four wheels; this is called a hydraulic brake. At the same time the red **brake lights** come on at the back to warn the vehicles behind. The anti-lock braking system, **ABS** for short, stops the wheels from locking in an emergency stop, so you can still steer.

The braking distance is the distance a vehicle needs from starting to brake until it stands still. On a wet, icy or sandy road it is much longer, because the tyres have less grip. At twice the speed the braking distance even becomes about four times as long. That is why you should drive more slowly in the rain and keep enough distance.

You also have to be able to brake in sport. Inline skates usually have a rubber stopper at the back of the boot by the heel. Beginner skiers put the ski tips together and the ends apart; this is the **snowplough**. Parachutes and air brakes on aeroplane wings, on the other hand, brake with air resistance.

Electric cars, e-bikes and trains can recover electricity when braking; this is called **regenerative braking**. The electric motor works as a generator and charges the battery or feeds electricity into the grid. Many mountain railways and trains in Switzerland recover energy in this way on the way down. For emergencies, however, all vehicles also have normal friction brakes.

begriffe.erklaerung: The distance a vehicle travels while braking until it stops.
A brake in which pads press on a metal disc that turns with the wheel.
Anti-lock braking system; it stops the wheels from locking when braking hard.
Recovering energy when braking, for example as electricity.

gewusst: The brake discs of racing cars can glow red when braking.
Anyone who brakes for a long time on a bike going downhill can heat the rim so much that you should not touch it.
The reaction time before braking is about one second; in that time a car at 50 km/h travels around 14 metres further.

teile.einleitung: A bobsleigh track is an icy channel with steep bends down which bobsleighs race at well over 100 km/h. A bob run is an exciting physics experiment: potential energy turns into kinetic energy, friction and air resistance slow it down, and huge forces act in the bends. With the natural ice track of St Moritz, Switzerland has one of the most famous tracks in the world.
wichtigste: On the bobsleigh track, potential energy is mainly turned into kinetic energy.
The start is decisive, because the push-off speed carries the bob through the whole track.
After jumping in, the pushers duck down to reduce air resistance.
Narrow, polished steel runners keep the friction on the ice low.
In fast bends the riders are pressed hard into their seats.
A maximum weight stops heavier bobs from having an advantage.
The best-known bend on the St Moritz track is called Horseshoe.

abschnitte.text: A bobsleigh track is a long, iced channel of concrete or snow that leads down a slope with many bends. Modern tracks are usually between 1200 and 1700 m long and are artificially cooled. As well as bobsleighs, **luge** sleds and **skeleton** sleds also run on them. Races are held in two-man and four-man bobs, and for women also in the monobob.

At the start at the top the bob has a lot of **potential energy**. On the way down it is mainly turned into **kinetic energy**, and the bob gets faster and faster. Some of the energy is lost as heat through friction and air resistance. That is why the push at the start is so important: every bit of speed the team brings from the sprint carries the bob through the whole track.

A bob glides on narrow, polished **steel runners** so that the friction on the ice stays as low as possible. Because warmer runners would glide better, their temperature is checked before the race. After jumping in, the pushers duck low inside the bob so that the **air resistance** falls. The shape of the bob is even tested in a wind tunnel.

In the bends the bob rides up the steep wall; otherwise it would fly out. The riders are pressed into their seats with several times their body weight. This load comes from the **centripetal force**, which forces the bob onto its curved path. You feel something similar on a roller coaster, only for much longer and more strongly.

A heavy bob is slowed down less by air resistance on the descent than a light one. That is why there is a **maximum weight** for the bob and crew together. If the athletes are lighter, they may fit extra weights in the bob. In this way technique, the start and driving skill decide, not simply weight.

Bobsleigh began at the end of the 19th century in **St Moritz**, where English winter guests whizzed down the streets on sledges. The Olympia Bobrun from St Moritz to Celerina opened in 1904 and today is the only **natural ice track** in the world used for top-level sport. It is rebuilt by hand from snow and water every winter. Its most famous bend is the almost circular **Horseshoe**, and Olympic races were held here in 1928 and 1948.

begriffe.erklaerung: The narrow steel blade on which a bob glides over the ice.
The athletes who push the bob at the start and then jump in.
Energy that a body has because it is high up.
The force that keeps a body on a curved path.

gewusst: Because the St Moritz track is made of natural ice, it can only be used for a few weeks in winter and disappears again in spring.
Swiss bobsleigh riders are among the most successful in the world and have won many Olympic medals.
A four-man bob with its crew weighs around 630 kg, as much as a small car.

teile.einleitung: An oven is a kitchen appliance in which food is cooked with hot air and heat radiation. Cakes, bread, Zopf, pizza and gratins are made in it. In an oven you can observe three ways of transferring heat: heat radiation, convection and conduction.
wichtigste: A cake is often baked at about 180 degrees.
Preheating means letting the oven get hot before you start baking.
With a fan oven, a fan spreads the hot air evenly.
When grilling, the heat comes mainly from above.
Dough with yeast rises in the warm oven.
The glass in the oven door can get very hot while baking.
When you open a hot oven, hot steam comes out first.

abschnitte.text: Most ovens in Switzerland are heated electrically. Inside the oven there are metal **heating elements**, which can glow red when electricity flows through them. A **thermostat** measures the temperature and switches the heating on and off so that it does not get too hot. A cake is often baked at about 180 degrees, pizza at much higher temperatures.

abschnitte.titel: Top and bottom heat, fan, grill
abschnitte.text: With **top and bottom heat**, elements heat at the top and bottom of the oven. With the **fan setting**, a fan on the back wall blows the hot air through the whole oven, so you can bake on several trays at once. When grilling, only the grill element at the top glows, and the heat comes mainly from above. That way a gratin gets nice and crispy.

Hot heating elements give out **heat radiation**, like the sun. The warm air rises and flows through the oven; this is called convection. The hot baking tray passes its heat on to the dough through direct contact; that is conduction. That is why it is important to preheat the oven, so that everything is properly hot from the start.

When it is warm, yeast in the dough makes a gas, carbon dioxide, and the dough rises. In the hot oven the gas bubbles expand further until the dough sets. At high temperatures browning substances form on the surface, which is why a **Zopf**, a Swiss plaited loaf, turns golden brown and smells so good. The water in the dough evaporates, so hot steam pours out when you open the oven door.

abschnitte.titel: From wood oven to electric cooker
abschnitte.text: In the past bread was baked in large stone **wood-fired ovens**, which were first heated up with fire. Many Swiss villages had a shared bakehouse in which families took turns to bake their bread. Later, gas and electric cookers came into kitchens. Today there are ovens with a steam function and with self-cleaning, in which dirt burns to ash at very high heat.

Oven gloves protect against burns from trays, racks and the oven door. When opening the oven, you should keep some distance at first, because hot steam pours out. Young children should only use the oven with adults. Always switch the oven off after baking; it is safer and saves electricity.

begriffe.erklaerung: A control that measures the temperature and switches the heating on and off.
A setting in which a fan spreads the hot air in the oven.
The transport of heat by flowing air or liquid.
Tiny fungi that make gas in dough and make it rise.

gewusst: The browning of bread and cakes is called the Maillard reaction, after the French chemist Louis-Camille Maillard.
A stone pizza oven can get much hotter than a normal kitchen oven.

teile.einleitung: The refractive index is a number that tells you how strongly a material slows light down and so deflects it. The larger the refractive index, the slower the light is in the material and the more sharply a ray of light bends as it enters. That is why a straw in a glass of water looks bent, and why diamonds sparkle so beautifully.
wichtigste: The refractive index n is the speed of light in a vacuum divided by the speed of light in the material.
A vacuum has a refractive index of exactly 1, air around 1.0003.
Water has about 1.33, ice about 1.31 and ordinary glass about 1.5.
In glass with n equal to 1.5, light travels at only around 2.0·10⁸ m/s.
In the material the wavelength of the light also gets shorter by the factor n.
The refractive index of air depends slightly on pressure and temperature.

abschnitte.text: In empty space, a **vacuum**, light travels at around 300,000 km per second. In air, water or glass it is slower. The **refractive index** n tells you by how much: you divide the speed of light in a vacuum by the speed in the material. If light travels at 2.25·10⁸ m/s in a material, n equals 1.33, which is the value for water.

A vacuum has exactly the value 1, and air is only just above it at around 1.0003. Ice has about 1.31, liquid **water** about 1.33 and ordinary window glass about 1.5. In glass with n equal to 1.5, light only travels at around 200,000 km per second. The value for **diamond** is very high, at about 2.42, which is why it glitters so strongly.

abschnitte.titel: Refraction of light in everyday life
abschnitte.text: When light passes at an angle from one material into another, it bends; this is called **refraction**. That is why a straw in a glass seems bent at the surface of the water, and why a swimming pool looks shallower than it is. The law for this was discovered by the Dutchman Willebrord **Snellius** around 1620. Lenses in glasses, cameras and in the eye use exactly this refraction.

The refractive index is slightly different for each colour; blue light is refracted more strongly than red. This **dispersion** splits white light into a rainbow in a prism or in raindrops. In the material the wavelength also gets shorter: red light of 600 nm in air has only about 451 nm in water. The colour, however, does not change, because it depends on the frequency.

Air also refracts light a tiny bit, and more strongly the denser it is. Its density depends on pressure and temperature. That is why shimmering reflections appear over a hot road in summer; this is called a **mirage** or Fata Morgana. Astronomers have to take this effect into account, because it makes stars near the horizon appear a little higher.

The refractive index is crucial for spectacle lenses, camera lenses and microscopes. In **fibre-optic cables** the light is kept in the core, which has a higher refractive index, and passed along by total internal reflection. In this way internet data travels as pulses of light through cables under roads and oceans. The refractive index is also measured in laboratories, for example to find the sugar content of grape juice.

begriffe.erklaerung: The bending of a ray of light as it passes into a different material.
A completely empty space without air.
Different colours are refracted by different amounts.
Light is completely reflected back at a boundary instead of passing through.

gewusst: Because ice and water have almost the same refractive index, pieces of ice in water are hard to see.
Winemakers in Switzerland measure the sugar content of grapes with an instrument that measures the refraction of light.
Glass dipped into a liquid with the same refractive index becomes almost invisible.

teile.einleitung: The Avogadro constant is a huge number that chemists and physicists use to count atoms and molecules. It tells you how many particles there are in one mole of a substance: around 602 sextillion, that is a 6 followed by 23 zeros. With it, you can simply use a balance in the laboratory to count particles that are far too small to see.
wichtigste: The Avogadro constant gives the number of particles in one mole.
Since 2019 it has been fixed exactly at 6.02214076 times 10 to the power of 23 particles per mole.
It is named after the Italian scientist Amedeo Avogadro.
One mole of water weighs around 18 grams.
Around 3.011 times 10 to the power of 23 particles correspond to half a mole.
Before 2019 the constant was measured very precisely with ultra-pure silicon spheres.
The Faraday constant and the universal gas constant are also linked to it.

abschnitte.text: Atoms and molecules are so tiny that even a sip of water contains an unimaginable number of them. That is why they are counted in packets, rather like buying eggs by the dozen. Such a packet is called a **mole**. The **Avogadro constant** tells you how many particles there are in one mole, namely about 6.022 times 10 to the power of 23.

One mole of a substance weighs as many grams as its particles weigh in atomic mass units. A water molecule, H2O, consists of two hydrogen atoms and one oxygen atom and together has a mass of about 18. That is why one mole of water weighs around 18 grams, which is roughly one tablespoonful. So two moles of water contain around 1.2 times 10 to the power of 24 molecules.

The Italian **Amedeo Avogadro** lived in Turin from 1776 to 1856. In 1811 he put forward the idea that equal volumes of different gases at the same temperature and pressure contain the same number of particles. He himself did not yet know the number that bears his name today. In 1865 the Austrian Josef Loschmidt was one of the first to estimate how many particles there are in a gas.

In the international Avogadro project, researchers made almost perfect spheres of ultra-pure **silicon**. They measured their diameter and the distance between the atoms in the crystal extremely precisely. In this way they could calculate how many atoms there are in the sphere. Since 2019 the Avogadro constant has been fixed as an exact value in the International System of Units and no longer has to be measured.

If you multiply the Avogadro constant by the charge of a single electron, the **elementary charge**, you get the Faraday constant. It tells you how much electric charge one mole of electrons carries. If you multiply it by the Boltzmann constant, you get the universal **gas constant**. You need this, for example, to calculate how gases expand when they are heated.

begriffe.erklaerung: The unit for an amount of substance, that is a packet of around 6.022 times 10 to the power of 23 particles.
A particle made of two or more atoms firmly joined together.
The mass of one mole of a substance, given in grams per mole.
A number in science that does not change.

gewusst: A single carbon atom weighs only about 2 times 10 to the power of minus 23 grams.
If you spread one mole of grains of sand over Switzerland, the whole country would be buried under a layer of sand a kilometre deep.
Some chemists celebrate 23 October as Mole Day, because the number begins with 6.02 times 10 to the power of 23.

teile.einleitung: A ray diagram is a drawing method used to find out where an image formed by a lens or a mirror appears and how big it is. To do this, you draw just a few special light rays whose path you know exactly. In this way you can predict on a sheet of paper what a magnifying glass, a camera or the eye will show.
wichtigste: In a ray diagram you draw special light rays whose path you know exactly.
A ray parallel to the axis passes through the focal point on the image side after a converging lens.
The central ray passes through the middle of the lens without changing direction.
A focal ray runs parallel to the optical axis after the converging lens.
For one image point you need at least two of these rays.
With thin lenses, the refraction is drawn in a simplified way at the centre plane of the lens.
Depending on the distance of the object, the image becomes bigger or smaller, upright or inverted.

abschnitte.text: In a ray diagram you draw a lens, its **optical axis** and the two focal points on a sheet of paper. Then you put an object, usually an arrow, in front of the lens. From the tip of the arrow you draw a few light rays through the lens. Where these rays meet behind the lens, the image of the arrow tip is formed.

The **parallel ray** runs parallel to the axis and, after a converging lens, passes through the focal point on the image side. The **central ray** passes through the middle of the lens and does not change direction. The **focal ray** first passes through the focal point on the object side and afterwards runs parallel to the axis. Two of these rays are enough; the third is used as a check.

In reality light is refracted both when it enters the glass and when it leaves it. With a thin lens this is drawn in a simplified way just once, at the **centre plane** of the lens. The lens is often shown simply as a vertical line with small arrows. This simplification is accurate enough for school and many uses.

If the object is further away than twice the focal length, a smaller, inverted image forms between f and 2f, as in a camera. If it is between the focal length and twice the focal length, the image is enlarged and inverted and lies beyond 2f; this is how a **projector** works. If it is closer than the focal length, the rays do not meet behind the lens. Then through the lens you see an enlarged, upright **virtual image**, as with a magnifying glass.

A diverging lens is thinner in the middle than at the edge and spreads light out. After it, a ray parallel to the axis runs as if it came from the focal point in front of the lens. The rays therefore never really meet, and there is always a smaller, upright, virtual image. Such lenses are found, for example, in glasses for **short-sighted** people and in door peepholes.

With ray diagrams pupils understand how cameras, telescopes, microscopes and projectors work. Our **eye** also works like a converging lens and produces a small, inverted image on the retina. Opticians and engineers today use computer programs that calculate thousands of rays on the same principle. But the simple drawing with two rays remains the basis.

begriffe.erklaerung: The imaginary line that passes at right angles through the middle of the lens.
The point at which rays coming in parallel meet behind a converging lens.
An image that can be caught on a screen.
An image that you can only see through the lens and cannot catch on a screen.
A lens that is thicker in the middle and focuses light.

gewusst: The image on your retina is actually upside down; only your brain turns it the right way round for you.
If an object is exactly at twice the focal length, its image is the same size as the object itself.
If an object is exactly at the focal point, the rays run parallel afterwards and no image forms at all.

teile.einleitung: The eye is our sense organ for seeing. It works rather like a camera: light comes in, is focused by a lens and produces an image on the retina. The optic nerve sends this image as signals to the brain, which turns it into what we actually see.
wichtigste: The eye focuses light with the cornea and lens into an image on the retina.
The iris changes the size of the pupil and so controls how much light enters the eye.
The vitreous body fills most of the eyeball.
The tough, white outer layer of the eyeball is called the sclera.
The optic nerve carries the signals from the eye to the brain.
Where the optic nerve leaves the eye is the blind spot.
With accommodation the eye focuses on near and distant things.

abschnitte.text: The eyeball is a sphere about 2.4 centimetres across. On the outside it is protected by the white **sclera**, which at the front turns into the transparent cornea. Behind that lie the coloured **iris** with the pupil in the middle, and the lens. Most of the eye is filled with the vitreous body, a transparent, jelly-like substance.

Light first passes through the cornea, which already bends it strongly. Then it goes through the pupil, whose size the iris changes depending on the brightness. The **lens** focuses the light further so that a sharp image forms on the retina. This image is upside down, but the brain turns it the right way round again for us.

Millions of sense cells sit on the **retina**. The rods are very sensitive to light and help us see in twilight; the cones are responsible for seeing colours. The sense cells turn light into electrical signals, which the **optic nerve** carries to the brain. Where the optic nerve leaves the eye there are no sense cells, which is why this place is called the blind spot.

A camera is built rather like an eye. The camera’s aperture corresponds to the iris, the lens to the eye’s lens and the **image sensor** to the retina. A camera focuses by moving the lens. The eye, on the other hand, changes the shape of its elastic lens; this is called **accommodation**.

With **short-sightedness** you see near things clearly but distant things blurred, because the image forms in front of the retina. With long-sightedness it is the other way round. Astigmatism makes points look like lines, because the cornea is unevenly curved. Glasses and contact lenses with suitably shaped lenses correct these faults.

Eyelashes, eyelids and tears protect the eye from dust and drying out. You should never look straight into the sun or into a laser beam, because this can damage the retina. In the mountains and on snow, good sunglasses are important. Anyone who looks at screens a lot should take regular breaks and look into the distance.

begriffe.erklaerung: The black hole in the middle of the iris through which light enters the eye.
The inner layer of the eye with the sense cells for light.
The focusing of the eye on near or distant things.
The place on the retina without sense cells, where the optic nerve leaves the eye.

gewusst: We do not normally notice the blind spot, because the brain simply fills in the gap.
A newborn baby only sees blurrily at first and learns to see properly sharply in the first few months.
The pupil gets bigger not only in the dark but also when we find something very exciting.

teile.einleitung: Lightning is a huge electrical discharge in the air that happens in thunderstorms. In a fraction of a second an enormous current flows and makes the air brighter than the sun. Afterwards you hear the thunder, the crash of the suddenly heated air.
wichtigste: Lightning forms in thunderclouds, in which electric charges separate.
Lightning can jump between a cloud and the ground or between two clouds.
A lightning flash usually lasts less than a second.
The air in the lightning channel gets about 30,000 degrees hot.
All over the world, lightning strikes several times a second.
In Switzerland, most lightning strikes in the canton of Ticino.
Lightning can certainly strike the same place several times.

abschnitte.text: In a tall **thundercloud**, water drops, ice crystals and soft hail swirl wildly about. When they collide, they become electrically charged. Positive charge usually collects at the top and negative charge at the bottom. If the voltage gets too high, a conducting channel forms through the air, and the lightning evens out the charges in a single strike.

In the thin **lightning channel** the air gets about 30,000 degrees hot, around five times hotter than the surface of the sun. The air expands explosively, and a pressure wave forms that we hear as **thunder**. Light is much faster than sound, which is why you see the lightning first. If you count the seconds until the thunder and divide by three, you get roughly the distance in kilometres.

Usually you see lightning as a branching **zigzag line**, because it jerkily searches for the best path through the air. Most lightning stays inside the clouds or jumps between two clouds. When distant thunderstorms light up the sky without any thunder being heard, it is called **heat lightning**. Very rare and not yet fully understood is ball lightning, a glowing ball.

Most thunderstorms happen in summer, when warm, moist air rises quickly. In **Ticino** a particularly large amount of lightning strikes, because moist air from the south meets the Alps there. Tall buildings and mountain peaks are often hit. The Säntis with its transmission tower is a place where researchers measure lightning precisely.

A **lightning rod** leads the current safely into the ground through metal rods and wires; it was invented by Benjamin Franklin around 1752. In a car or a house with lightning protection you are fairly safe. Outdoors you should avoid summits, ridges, single trees and open spaces. Anyone caught out should crouch down in a hollow with their feet together and keep away from water.

begriffe.erklaerung: Weather with lightning and thunder, usually with heavy rain or hail.
The bang and rumble caused by the rapid expansion of the hot air in a lightning flash.
A metal installation on buildings that leads lightning currents safely into the earth.
The flashing of a distant thunderstorm whose thunder can no longer be heard.

gewusst: Tall towers such as the Empire State Building in New York are struck by lightning many times every year.
A lightning channel is often only a few centimetres thick, but kilometres long.
Lightning can also form in the ash cloud of a volcanic eruption.

teile.einleitung: Acceleration tells you how fast the speed of a body changes. When a car starts, a bike brakes or a roundabout spins you round in a circle, acceleration is involved. It is one of the most important quantities in physics.
wichtigste: Acceleration tells you how fast the speed changes.
It is measured in metres per second squared, m/s².
Average acceleration is change in speed divided by time.
Braking is also an acceleration; it is called deceleration.
Newton’s second law says: force equals mass times acceleration.
A change of direction is also an acceleration.
The acceleration due to gravity is about 9.81 m/s².

abschnitte.text: When a body gets faster, slower or changes direction, it is **accelerated**. Acceleration tells you by how much the speed changes every second. Its unit is **m/s²**, spoken as metres per second squared. An acceleration of 1 m/s² means: every second you get 1 metre per second faster.

Average acceleration is calculated with the formula a = Δv divided by Δt. A car that goes from standing to 20 m/s in 5 seconds has an average acceleration of 20 divided by 5, that is 4 m/s². A bike that brakes steadily from 8 m/s to a standstill in 4 seconds has a **deceleration** of 2 m/s². By the way, 20 m/s is 72 kilometres per hour.

In 1687 Isaac Newton described the connection between force and acceleration. His **second law** is F = m times a, that is force equals mass times acceleration. A trolley with a mass of 200 kg that is accelerated at 2 m/s² needs a force of 400 newtons. The heavier a body is, the more force it takes to accelerate it by the same amount.

Everything that falls is accelerated downwards by the Earth. This **acceleration due to gravity** is about 9.81 m/s². Without air resistance a feather and a hammer would fall equally fast. The astronaut David Scott showed this in 1971 on the Moon, where there is no air.

You can feel accelerations in your body, for example in a lift, on a roller coaster or when an aeroplane takes off. They are often given as a multiple of the acceleration due to gravity, in **g**. Fighter pilots can briefly withstand up to about 9 g. In a bend, too, you are accelerated, because the direction changes, even though the speed stays the same.

begriffe.erklaerung: How much distance you cover in a certain time.
An acceleration that makes a body slower.
The unit of force, named after Isaac Newton.
The acceleration with which things fall downwards on Earth.

gewusst: A Formula One car can reach a deceleration of over 5 g when braking.
On the Moon the acceleration of falling objects is only about a sixth of that on Earth.

teile.einleitung: A diode is an electronic component that lets electric current through in one direction only. You can imagine it as a valve or a one-way street for electricity. Diodes are found in almost every electronic device, from chargers to light-emitting diodes.
wichtigste: A semiconductor diode lets current through in one direction only.
Its two terminals are called the anode and the cathode.
Before semiconductor diodes, vacuum tube diodes with a heated cathode were used.
In the forward direction, about 0.7 volts are dropped across a silicon diode.
A photodiode turns light into a measurable current.
A Zener diode keeps a voltage constant.
A light-emitting diode, LED for short, gives off light when current flows.

abschnitte.text: A diode has two terminals: the **anode** and the **cathode**. If the anode is positive compared with the cathode, current flows; this is called the forward direction. If the voltage is reversed, the diode blocks almost completely. On the component a ring usually marks the cathode. In a circuit diagram the diode is drawn as a triangle with a line, and the triangle points in the direction in which the current is allowed to flow.

Most diodes are made of **semiconductors** such as silicon. The silicon is deliberately changed with foreign atoms so that a p-side and an n-side are formed. At the boundary, the **p-n junction**, a depletion layer forms. Only above a certain threshold voltage, about 0.7 volts for silicon, does a noticeable current flow. This produces heat: at 0.7 volts and 2 amperes, that is 1.4 watts.

The mains socket supplies alternating current, which keeps changing direction. Many devices, however, need **direct current**. With diodes, alternating current can be rectified, that is forced in one direction. Particularly common is a circuit of four diodes, the bridge rectifier. A flyback diode next to a relay coil also protects against dangerous voltage spikes when it is switched off.

The **light-emitting diode** gives off light and today replaces many light bulbs, because it needs much less electricity. The photodiode does the opposite and turns light into current, for example in light barriers. The Zener diode keeps a certain voltage constant in the reverse direction. The Schottky diode has a metal-semiconductor junction instead of a p-n junction and a particularly small threshold voltage. Solar cells also work rather like large photodiodes.

In 1874 the German physicist Ferdinand Braun discovered that certain crystals conduct electricity in one direction only. Around 1904 the Briton John Ambrose Fleming invented the **vacuum tube diode**, a glass tube with a vacuum and a heated cathode. Valves were used in radios for a long time. From the middle of the 20th century small, robust semiconductor diodes took over. In 2014 three Japanese researchers received the Nobel Prize in Physics for developing the blue light-emitting diode.

begriffe.erklaerung: A material such as silicon that conducts electricity or not depending on conditions.
The two terminals of a diode; current flows from the anode to the cathode.
A circuit that turns alternating current into direct current.
The direction in which a diode lets current flow.

gewusst: Only with the blue LED did it become possible to make white LED light for lamps.
A simple computer chip today contains billions of semiconductor components based on similar junctions.
Early radio receivers used a crystal and a fine wire point as a diode.

teile.einleitung: Dimensional analysis is a method in physics in which you calculate only with the units of quantities. With it you can check whether a formula can be right at all, and sometimes even guess new relationships. It is a popular tool of physicists, engineers and students.
wichtigste: Every physical quantity has a dimension, such as length, mass or time.
Both sides of a correct equation must have the same dimension.
That is why the expression m·v cannot be an energy.
From the pendulum length l and the acceleration due to gravity g, √(l/g) gives a time.
The Buckingham Π theorem says that equations can be expressed using dimensionless numbers.
The Reynolds number is one such number and shows whether a flow is laminar or turbulent.
Dimensional analysis cannot supply numerical factors such as 2π.

abschnitte.text: Every physical quantity can be traced back to a few basic quantities, such as **length**, mass and time. A speed, for example, is a length divided by a time. In the International System of Units, SI, there are seven base units, including the metre, the kilogram and the second. Combined units can also be broken down into base units. For example, a watt equals kg·m²/s³.

The simplest use is the **unit check**. You put only the units into a formula and see whether the same thing comes out on the left and the right. An energy has the unit kg·m²/s², a momentum m·v only kg·m/s, so m·v cannot be an energy. In exams you can find calculation mistakes quickly in this way. You can, however, only add like to like, that is quantities of the same dimension.

You can also use dimensional analysis to derive formulas. The period of a pendulum can only depend on the length l and the acceleration due to gravity g. The only combination that gives a time is √(l/g). The exact formula also contains the factor 2π, and the method cannot supply that. In a similar way it turns out that the spring constant has the unit kg/s² and the **gravitational constant** the unit m³/(kg·s²).

Especially important are **dimensionless numbers**, combinations in which all the units cancel out. In 1914 the physicist Edgar Buckingham formulated the Π theorem, according to which physical equations can be written using such numbers. A well-known example is the **Reynolds number**, named after Osborne Reynolds. If it is small, a flow runs calmly and in an orderly way, that is laminar. If it is large, the flow becomes swirling and turbulent.

Dimensionless numbers make it possible to do research with small **models**. If a model ship in a water tank has the same numbers as the real ship, the water behaves in a similar way. Aeroplanes, cars or bridges are also tested in wind tunnels in this way. This saves a lot of money, because you do not have to build the real thing every time. Swiss universities such as ETH Zurich also use such model experiments, for example for hydraulic engineering and flood protection.

begriffe.erklaerung: The kind of a quantity, for example length, mass or time.
One of the seven basic units such as the metre, the kilogram and the second.
Without a unit, because all the units have cancelled out.
A number that tells you whether a flow is calm or swirling.

gewusst: With dimensional analysis you can often guess in a few minutes what a result depends on before calculating it precisely.
In physics angles also count as dimensionless.
Engineers test the courses of rivers in large halls with models that are much smaller than the real river.

teile.einleitung: Firewood is wood that is burnt to produce heat, for example in a stove, an open fireplace or a campfire. It is one of the oldest fuels of humankind. The energy in the wood originally comes from the sun.
wichtigste: Burning wood gives off heat and light.
Firewood must be dry, because wet wood burns badly and smokes.
Freshly split wood is left to dry for about one to two years.
The energy in the wood originally comes from the sun.
In Switzerland an open fireplace in the living room is called a “cheminée”.
Wood pellets are small pressed sticks made of sawdust.
Thick pieces of wood are split with an axe.

abschnitte.text: Trees use sunlight for **photosynthesis**. In this process they build up wood from carbon dioxide from the air and water. When the wood is burnt, this stored energy is released again as **heat** and light. About as much carbon dioxide is produced again as the tree took in while it was growing.

A distinction is made between **hardwood** such as beech, oak or ash and **softwood** such as spruce, fir or pine. Hardwood burns long and evenly and gives lovely embers. Softwood catches fire more quickly, but burns down faster and crackles more because of the resin. In Switzerland beech is burnt particularly often.

Freshly felled wood is about half **water**. For it to burn well, the water content must fall below about 20 per cent. To do this, the wood is split with an axe or a log splitter and stacked in an airy place protected from the rain. After one to two years it is dry enough; wet wood, on the other hand, smokes, produces soot and creates a lot of fine dust.

Wood is burnt in wood-burning stoves, tiled stoves, wood-fired heating systems or in the **cheminée**. Modern heating systems often use **wood pellets**, small pressed sticks made of sawdust and wood shavings. Pellets can be fed into the boiler automatically and burn very cleanly. Wood chips from forest leftovers are also used in larger heating systems for school buildings or whole neighbourhoods.

About a third of Switzerland is covered with forest, so there is a lot of local wood. Firewood is often sold by the **stere**, which is one cubic metre of stacked wood with gaps of air. Wood counts as a renewable fuel, because new trees keep growing back. It is important, though, to light fires properly, because poor burning pollutes the air with fine dust.

begriffe.erklaerung: The process in which plants use sunlight to make nutrients from air and water.
One cubic metre of stacked firewood with gaps.
Small sticks of pressed sawdust used for heating.
Tiny particles in the air that can be harmful when breathed in.

gewusst: If you light a fire from the top, that is with the kindling placed on top of the thick logs, it makes less smoke.
Wood pellets are pressed without glue; the wood substance lignin holds them together.
A pile of firewood gives lizards, hedgehogs and insects a place to hide.

teile.einleitung: A boat is a small vessel in which people travel across lakes, rivers and seas. Boats are among the oldest inventions of humankind. Physics explains why they float at all with buoyancy.
wichtigste: A boat floats because it displaces water and so gets buoyancy.
The more heavily you load a boat, the lower it lies in the water.
If everyone sits on the same side, the boat tilts, because the weight is unevenly spread.
The front part is called the bow, the back part the stern.
The first boats were often made of hollowed-out tree trunks.
A canoe is driven with a single-bladed paddle.
Steamers still sail on Swiss lakes such as Lake Lucerne today.

abschnitte.text: When a boat goes into the water, it pushes water aside; it **displaces** water. In return the water pushes back from below with a force, **buoyancy**. The boat sinks in until the displaced water weighs exactly as much as the boat itself. That is why even a ship made of heavy steel can float, because its hull is hollow inside and full of air. A rubber dinghy floats because it is filled with air.

The body of a boat is called the **hull**. At the front is the **bow**, and at the back the stern. Looking forwards, the left side is port and the right side is starboard. Along the bottom in the middle many boats have a keel, which keeps the boat stable and stops it drifting sideways when sailing.

A canoe is narrow and is moved kneeling or sitting with a **single-bladed paddle**, a kayak with a double-bladed paddle. In a rowing boat you sit facing backwards and pull on oars. Sailing boats use the wind, motorboats an engine. A raft is even simpler; it consists of tree trunks tied together.

In the Stone Age people already hollowed out tree trunks and so built a **dugout canoe**. Archaeologists have also found such dugouts from the time of the lake dwellers in Swiss lakes. Later people built boats from planks, hides or reeds. With boats they could fish, carry goods and reach new areas.

Passenger boats sail on many Swiss lakes, including historic **paddle steamers** on Lake Lucerne, Lake Geneva and Lake Zurich. On the Rhine at Basel large cargo ships travel all the way to the sea. Famous rowing regattas take place on the Rotsee near Lucerne. Anyone who wants to steer a motorboat or a larger sailing boat in Switzerland needs a boat driving licence.

begriffe.erklaerung: The force of water that pushes a body in it upwards.
The front part of a boat.
The back part of a boat.
An ancient boat made from a single hollowed-out tree trunk.

gewusst: The Greek scholar Archimedes described the law of buoyancy more than 2200 years ago.
In salt water a boat lies a little higher than in fresh water, because salt water is heavier.
When rowing, you sit with your back to the direction of travel.

teile.einleitung: Balancing means keeping something in equilibrium so that it does not fall over, for example a broom on your hand or your own body on one leg. The centre of gravity plays the main role in this. Physics explains why some things are easy and others are hard to balance.
wichtigste: A body stays in equilibrium if its centre of gravity is above its base of support.
There are stable, unstable and neutral equilibrium.
A ball in a bowl is in stable equilibrium.
A pencil on its point is in unstable equilibrium.
A long broom is easier to balance than a short pencil, because it tips over more slowly.
When cycling, you steer slightly in the direction you are tipping.
A balancing bird does not fall off, because its centre of gravity is below the point it rests on.

abschnitte.text: Every body has a **centre of gravity**, a point where you can imagine all its weight is concentrated. An object stands safely if its centre of gravity is directly above its **base of support**. If the centre of gravity moves beyond it, the object tips over. That is why wide, low things such as a table stand more safely than tall, narrow ones.

In **stable equilibrium** a body returns by itself after a small push, like a ball in a bowl. In **unstable equilibrium** it tips away after the slightest push, like a pencil on its point. In neutral equilibrium it simply stays in its new position, like a ball on a level table. If the centre of gravity is below the point of support, the equilibrium is stable, as with the balancing bird.

Balancing a long broom on your hand is easier than balancing a short pencil. The reason: a long object **tips over more slowly**, because its centre of gravity is high up. That gives you more time to correct with your hand. Tightrope walkers use a long **balancing pole**, which slows down tipping even more and helps to make up for small mistakes.

When you stand on one leg, your body shifts its centre of gravity over your standing foot. Many muscles keep working in small movements as you do this. The **organ of balance** in the inner ear tells the brain how the head is tilted. The eyes and the soles of the feet also provide important information, which is why balancing with your eyes closed is much harder.

When cycling, you keep your balance by steering slightly in the direction you are tipping. That brings the wheels back under the centre of gravity. The faster you ride, the easier this is, which is why a slow bike wobbles more. Balancing is also practised on a slackline, on the balance beam in gymnastics or when juggling plates.

begriffe.erklaerung: The point where you can imagine all the weight of a body is concentrated.
The area on which a body stands, for example under your feet.
A wobbly state in which even a small push makes the body tip over.
A small organ in the inner ear that senses the position and movement of the head.

gewusst: A balancing bird can sit on a finger with the tip of its beak, because heavy wing tips move its centre of gravity downwards.
A roly-poly toy always stands back up, because its centre of gravity is right at the bottom in a heavy, round base.
If you stand on one leg with your eyes closed, you notice straight away how important your eyes are for balance.

teile.einleitung: An astronaut is a person who flies into space in a spacecraft. Astronauts do research on space stations, repair satellites and have even been to the Moon. For this they need long, hard training.
wichtigste: A person who flies into space is called an astronaut.
Yuri Gagarin became the first person in space in 1961.
Neil Armstrong became the first person to walk on the Moon in 1969.
Today astronauts often live for months on the International Space Station, ISS.
The ISS takes about an hour and a half to go once round the Earth.
A spacesuit gives astronauts air outside in space and protects them.
Claude Nicollier was the first Swiss astronaut.

abschnitte.text: The word **astronaut** comes from Greek and means star sailor. In Russia people say **cosmonaut**, and in China taikonaut. Astronauts are often pilots, engineers, doctors or scientists. Before they are allowed into space, they train for years, for example under water, in a flight simulator and on language courses.

On 12 April 1961 the Russian **Yuri Gagarin** became the first person to orbit the Earth. In 1963 Valentina Tereshkova became the first woman in space. In 1969 **Neil Armstrong** became the first person to walk on the Moon, on the Apollo 11 mission. Up to 1972 a total of twelve men landed on the Moon. In 1971 Alan Shepard even played golf there.

Since 2000 people have lived permanently on the **International Space Station ISS**. It flies at a height of around 400 kilometres and takes about an hour and a half to orbit the Earth. That is why the astronauts see many sunrises and sunsets every day. Because everything floats, they sleep in sleeping bags tied in place and drink from pouches. They do research, for example, on plants, materials and their own bodies.

In **weightlessness** muscles and bones hardly have to work and quickly become weak. That is why astronauts on the space station do around two hours of exercise every day, for example on a treadmill and an exercise bike with straps. They also get a little taller in space, because the spine stretches. Back on Earth they shrink back to their normal height. Outside in space they wear a **spacesuit**, which gives them air and protects them from cold, heat and radiation.

The astrophysicist **Claude Nicollier** from the canton of Vaud was the first Swiss person in space. Between 1992 and 1999 he flew four times on the American Space Shuttle. Among other things he helped to repair the Hubble Space Telescope. In 2022 the European Space Agency ESA chose the Swiss Marco Sieber for its astronaut team.

begriffe.erklaerung: A state in which you and everything around you float freely.
A large spacecraft that orbits the Earth and in which people live and do research.
A protective suit with an air supply for work outside the spacecraft.
The Russian name for a space traveller.

gewusst: On the ISS, sweat and urine are turned back into drinking water.
The astronauts’ footprints on the Moon are still there today, because there is no wind.
Astronauts cannot cry in space the way they do on Earth, because the tears stick to the eye as a ball.

teile.einleitung: Dispersion is the effect by which white light is split into its colours in a prism. The reason is that each colour of light is refracted by a slightly different amount in glass. This is how rainbows and the sparkle of gemstones come about.
wichtigste: Dispersion splits white light into its colours in a prism.
White light is a mixture of all the colours of the rainbow.
Blue and violet light are refracted more strongly than red.
Isaac Newton studied dispersion around 1666 with glass prisms.
A rainbow is produced by dispersion in raindrops.
In lenses, dispersion causes coloured edges that have to be corrected.

abschnitte.text: If you send a white beam of light through a triangular piece of glass, a **prism**, a band of colours comes out on the other side. This splitting is called **dispersion**. It shows that white light is made up of many colours. The series of colours from red through orange, yellow, green and blue to violet is called the **spectrum**.

Light is refracted, that is bent, when it passes from air into glass. How strongly depends on the colour, because each colour has a different wavelength. Violet and blue light, with a short **wavelength**, are refracted more strongly than red light, with a long wavelength. As a result the colours spread apart like runners in different lanes.

Around 1666 Isaac Newton carried out famous experiments with prisms in a darkened room. He showed that a second, upside-down prism can combine the colours back into white light. In this way he proved that the colours are already present in white light and are not produced by the glass. In 1704 he published his findings in the book **Opticks**.

abschnitte.titel: Dispersion in nature and everyday life
abschnitte.text: A **rainbow** forms when sunlight is refracted and reflected in many raindrops and split into colours as it does so. Diamonds sparkle in colours because they have strong dispersion. Glass crystals on lamps or in a window also throw little rainbows onto the wall. If you want to see a rainbow, the sun has to be behind you.

In simple lenses dispersion causes blurred images with coloured edges, the **colour fault**. That is why camera lenses and telescopes combine different types of glass that balance each other out. In spectrometers, on the other hand, dispersion is used deliberately. With them astronomers study the light of stars and recognise what substances they are made of.

begriffe.erklaerung: A triangular glass body that bends light and splits it into colours.
The band of all the colours into which white light breaks up.
The distance between two wave crests; it determines the colour of light.
The bending of light as it passes into a different material.

gewusst: The album cover of “The Dark Side of the Moon” by the band Pink Floyd shows a prism with a colour spectrum.
Sometimes you can see a second, fainter rainbow in which the order of the colours is reversed.

teile.einleitung: A lightning rod protects buildings from lightning strikes. It catches the lightning on the roof and leads the huge current safely into the ground through a wire. It was invented by the American Benjamin Franklin in the 18th century.
wichtigste: A lightning rod leads lightning safely into the ground.
It is at the very top of the roof of a building.
It was invented by Benjamin Franklin.
Above all, it protects a house from fire caused by a lightning strike.
Tall church towers very often have a lightning rod.
The metal rod at the very top is called the air terminal.
During a thunderstorm you should not touch the wire and should keep your distance.

abschnitte.text: **Lightning** is a huge electrical discharge between a cloud and the ground or between clouds. In thunderclouds, particles of ice and water become electrically charged until the voltage is suddenly released. For a brief moment a current of often several tens of thousands of amperes flows. The air in the lightning channel gets hotter than the surface of the sun and expands explosively, which we hear as thunder.

A lightning protection system consists of three parts. The **air terminal** or air conductors on the roof catch the lightning. Thick metal wires, the **down conductors**, run down the outside wall of the house. Finally, the **earthing** in the ground spreads the current safely into the soil.

Electric current always looks for the path with the least resistance. Metal conducts electricity much better than wood, tiles or brickwork. So when lightning strikes, the current flows through the lightning rod and not through the house. This stops beams from catching fire or walls from cracking.

Around 1750 the American **Benjamin Franklin** studied electricity and suspected that lightning was an electric spark. He suggested putting metal rods on buildings to protect them. Soon the first lightning rods were built in America and Europe. In the past many churches and gunpowder towers burnt down because of lightning strikes; with the lightning rod this became much rarer.

During a thunderstorm you should not touch the wire of a lightning rod and should keep your distance. Outdoors you should not shelter under single trees, and you should avoid summits and ridges. You are safe in houses with lightning protection and in cars, because the metal body acts as a **Faraday cage**. In Switzerland thunderstorms are especially common in the mountains in summer, so it is worth checking the weather forecast before a hike.

begriffe.erklaerung: A metal rod at the very top of the roof that catches the lightning.
A connection to the ground through which the current flows away safely.
A metal wire that leads the lightning current from the roof into the ground.
A metal shell inside which you are protected from lightning.

gewusst: A lightning flash usually lasts only a fraction of a second.
Because light is faster than sound, you see lightning before you hear the thunder; every three seconds of gap mean about one kilometre of distance.
Tall buildings such as church towers or transmission towers are hit by lightning much more often than low houses.

teile.einleitung: The atomic nucleus is the tiny centre of every atom. It is much smaller than the whole atom, but contains almost all of its mass. Inside it are enormous forces and energies that make stars shine and produce electricity in nuclear power stations.
wichtigste: An atomic nucleus consists of protons and neutrons.
The general term for the particles in the nucleus is nucleons.
Almost all the mass of an atom is in the nucleus.
The strong nuclear force holds the nucleus together, even though the protons repel each other.
The number of protons determines which chemical element it is.
In chemical reactions the atomic nucleus stays unchanged.
Ernest Rutherford discovered the atomic nucleus in 1911.

abschnitte.text: An atom consists of a shell of electrons and a nucleus in the middle. The nucleus is built of **protons** and **neutrons**, which together are called **nucleons**. Protons are positively charged; neutrons have no charge. The number of protons decides which element it is: hydrogen has one proton, carbon six and iron 26. Atoms of an element with different numbers of neutrons are called **isotopes**.

The atomic nucleus is about 10,000 to 100,000 times smaller than the whole atom. If an atom were as big as a football stadium, the nucleus would only be the size of a pea on the centre spot. Even so, almost all the mass is in it. A teaspoon of pure nuclear matter would therefore weigh around a billion tonnes. In neutron stars such unimaginably dense matter really exists.

Protons with the same charge repel each other electrically. The fact that the nucleus does not fly apart anyway is due to the **strong nuclear force**. It is much stronger than the electrical repulsion, but only acts over tiny distances. When protons and neutrons join to form a nucleus, **binding energy** is released. Some nuclei are unstable and break down by themselves; this is called radioactivity.

In 1911 **Ernest Rutherford** and his team fired alpha particles at a very thin gold foil. Most went straight through, but some bounced back. From this Rutherford concluded that an atom has a tiny, heavy nucleus. In 1932 James Chadwick discovered the neutron. In 1938 Otto Hahn and Fritz Strassmann found out that uranium nuclei can be split.

In **nuclear fission** a heavy nucleus such as uranium breaks into lighter pieces, releasing energy. This is how the Swiss nuclear power stations Beznau, Gösgen and Leibstadt work. In **nuclear fusion** light nuclei such as hydrogen fuse into heavier ones. This is how the sun shines. In stars, fusion only releases energy up to the element iron, which is why it stops there.

At EPFL in Lausanne there is the fusion research facility **TCV**, a so-called tokamak. In it extremely hot gas is held in place by magnetic fields in order to study nuclear fusion. At CERN near Geneva researchers study what protons and neutrons themselves are made of. They are in fact built of even smaller particles, the quarks. The Paul Scherrer Institute in Aargau also does research with neutrons.

begriffe.erklaerung: A positively charged particle in the atomic nucleus.
An uncharged particle in the atomic nucleus.
The general term for protons and neutrons.
Atoms of the same element with different numbers of neutrons.
The force that holds the particles in the atomic nucleus together.

gewusst: Rutherford said that the particles bouncing back was as incredible as if a shell had bounced off a piece of tissue paper.
Your body consists almost entirely of empty space, because atomic nuclei are so tiny.
All elements heavier than iron were created in huge star explosions and collisions of stars.

teile.einleitung: The CMYK colour model describes how almost all colours can be printed on paper with the four printing colours cyan, magenta, yellow and black. It is used in every inkjet printer and in newspapers, books and posters. The colours are not mixed from light as on a screen, but from pigments that swallow light.
wichtigste: CMYK stands for cyan, magenta, yellow and black; the K stands for black.
The CMYK model is used mainly in colour printing.
Values are usually given in per cent; 0 per cent everywhere gives the white paper.
Printed images consist of tiny halftone dots.
Black is printed as well, because the three colours on top of each other do not give a deep black.
The printing process with the four colours is called four-colour printing.
With CMYK fewer bright colours can be shown than with RGB on a screen.

abschnitte.text: CMYK is short for the four printing colours **cyan**, a light blue-green, **magenta**, a strong pinkish red, yellow, and key for black. The K comes from the key plate, which was used in the past to print outlines and text in black. With these four colours a great many shades can be shown. Each colour share is given in per cent, for example 100 per cent cyan and 100 per cent yellow for green.

White paper reflects all the light. Each printing colour swallows part of it; cyan, for example, swallows red light. The more colours you print on top of each other, the less light comes back and the darker it gets; this is called **subtractive colour mixing**. If all the values are 0 per cent, you simply see the white paper.

In theory cyan, magenta and yellow on top of each other would give black. In reality, though, only a murky dark brown appears, because the pigments are not perfect. That is why real **black** is printed as well. This also saves expensive ink, and black text becomes much sharper.

If you look at a printed photo through a magnifying glass, you see many tiny **halftone dots** in the four colours. The bigger the dots of a colour, the more of that colour you see. From a normal reading distance the dots merge in the eye into an even picture. This process is called **four-colour printing** and is used in printing works, for example in offset printing.

Screens mix their colours from red, green and blue **light**; this is the RGB model and an additive colour mixing. All three lights together make white. With light you can produce much brighter colours than with printing inks on paper. That is why vivid screen colours often look paler when printed, and graphic designers convert their files to CMYK before printing.

begriffe.erklaerung: A light blue-green, one of the three primary colours in printing.
A strong pinkish red, one of the three primary colours in printing.
Colours are produced by pigments swallowing parts of the light.
A tiny dot of colour of which printed images are made.
The colour model for screens, made of red, green and blue light.

gewusst: Many inkjet printers contain exactly the four CMYK colours as separate cartridges.
For especially bright colours such as neon orange or gold, printers use extra spot colours.
The colour dots in a newspaper can often be seen quite easily with a simple magnifying glass.

teile.einleitung: Biogas is a flammable gas produced when bacteria break down plant remains, manure or food waste without oxygen. It consists mainly of methane and carbon dioxide. With biogas you can produce electricity, heat and even fuel for cars.
wichtigste: Biogas consists mainly of methane and carbon dioxide.
It is produced when bacteria break down organic material without oxygen.
In agricultural biogas plants, slurry and manure are often fermented.
The digestate that is left over is used as fertiliser.
A combined heat and power plant produces electricity and heat from biogas at the same time.
A similar gas, sewage gas, is produced in sewage works.
Biogas counts as a renewable energy.

abschnitte.text: Biogas is a mixture of gases that consists of about half to three quarters **methane**. The second largest part is **carbon dioxide**. In addition there are small amounts of other gases, for example hydrogen sulphide, which smells of rotten eggs. It is mainly the methane that burns, the same substance that is also in natural gas.

Biogas is produced by **fermentation**. Tiny microorganisms break down organic material such as manure, plants or leftover food. It is important that there is no oxygen present; this is called **anaerobic**. This also happens in nature, for example in marshes, where bubbles of marsh gas rise, and in the stomachs of cows.

The heart of a biogas plant is the **digester**, a large, airtight, heated container. In it slurry, manure, green waste or food scraps are stirred again and again. The gas produced collects at the top and is kept in a store, often under a round dome. What is left over, the **digestate**, is spread on the fields as fertiliser.

Biogas is often burnt in a **combined heat and power plant**, which produces electricity and heat at the same time. The heat is used to warm cowsheds, houses or greenhouses. Biogas can also be cleaned until it consists almost entirely of methane. This **biomethane** is fed into the gas network or used as fuel for gas-powered cars.

Gas is also produced in **sewage works**, when the sewage sludge is broken down without oxygen in large digestion towers. This gas is called sewage gas. Many Swiss sewage works use it to produce their own electricity and heat. A similar gas, landfill gas, can form at rubbish tips.

In Switzerland there are many biogas plants on farms and larger plants that process green waste from the green waste collection. A process for this developed in Switzerland is called **Kompogas**. Biogas is good for the climate, because otherwise some of the methane from slurry would escape into the air, where it is a strong greenhouse gas. In addition, the plants from which the waste comes took in carbon dioxide while they were growing.

begriffe.erklaerung: A flammable gas, the main part of natural gas and biogas.
Without oxygen.
An airtight container in which the material ferments.
What is left after fermentation; it is used as fertiliser.

gewusst: More than a hundred years ago some sewage works were already using their gas to produce light and heat.
When digesting food, cows give off methane, the same gas that is in biogas.
