In some countries in Asia many families cook with biogas from small plants next to their homes.

teile.einleitung: Angular momentum is a physical quantity that describes how much momentum a turning body has. It depends on how fast something turns and how its mass is spread out round the axis of rotation. An important law of nature says that angular momentum is conserved as long as no outside forces change it.
wichtigste: Angular momentum is the measure of the momentum of a turning motion.
For a rigid body: angular momentum equals moment of inertia times angular velocity.
A wheel with 0.4 kg·m² and 10 rad/s has an angular momentum of 4 kg·m²/s.
A torque changes angular momentum; 2 N·m for 3 seconds gives 6 kg·m²/s.
Without an outside torque, angular momentum is conserved.
The direction of angular momentum is found with the right-hand rule.
Elementary particles such as the electron have an intrinsic angular momentum, spin.

abschnitte.text: In a straight-line motion, momentum describes how much momentum a body has. In a turning motion, **angular momentum** takes over this role. For a small mass on a circular path it is mass times speed times radius. So a mass of 0.2 kilograms moving at 3 metres per second on a circle with a radius of 0.5 metres has 0.3 kg·m²/s. Its unit is kg·m²/s, the same as that of Planck’s constant.

Angular momentum stays the same if nothing from outside brakes or drives it; this is called **conservation of angular momentum**. In a pirouette a figure skater first spins with her arms stretched out. If she pulls her arms in towards her body, her **moment of inertia** gets smaller. So that the angular momentum stays the same, she spins much faster. If she spreads her arms again, she slows down.

Angular momentum has not only a size but also a direction along the axis of rotation. You find it with the **right-hand rule**: the curled fingers show the direction of turning, and the thumb shows the direction of the angular momentum. Because it is conserved, a fast-spinning top keeps its axis steady. That is why a rolling bike falls over less easily, and a frisbee also flies steadily thanks to its spin. Vectors such as angular momentum are called axial vectors, because they keep their direction under point reflection.

Planets, stars and whole galaxies also have angular momentum. The Earth has been turning on its axis for billions of years, because hardly anything slows it down. When a large star collapses, it can become a tiny **neutron star** that spins many times a second. This is the same principle as in the pirouette. Kepler’s second law of planetary orbits also follows from the conservation of angular momentum.

abschnitte.titel: Angular momentum in the quantum world
abschnitte.text: In 1913 Niels Bohr put forward a model of the atom in which the angular momentum of the electrons can only have certain values. It is said that angular momentum is **quantised**. On top of this there is spin, an intrinsic angular momentum that particles such as electrons have by nature. Spin is the basis of the magnetism of many substances. Medical devices such as the MRI scanner in hospital also use the spin of atomic nuclei.

begriffe.erklaerung: How strongly a body resists a change in its rotation, depending on how its mass is spread out.
How fast something turns, measured as angle per second.
The turning effect of a force, which speeds up or slows down a rotation.
The intrinsic angular momentum of elementary particles.

gewusst: Some neutron stars spin hundreds of times a second.
When falling, cats use clever twists of their bodies to land on their paws.
Satellites are pointed in the right direction with fast-spinning flywheels inside them.

teile.einleitung: Bobsleigh is a fast winter sport in which a team races down an ice channel in a sledge-like vehicle. Many laws of physics can be seen in it: gravity, friction, air resistance and centrifugal force. The sport was invented in Switzerland, in St Moritz.
wichtigste: A bobsleigh team pushes the bob at the start and then jumps in.
At the front sits the pilot, who steers the bob.
At the back sits the brakeman, who brakes the bob after the finish.
The bends of a bobsleigh track are high and banked so that the bob does not fly out.
The oldest bobsleigh track in the world is in St Moritz and is made of natural ice.
In St Moritz a bob can reach about 135 km/h.
Bobsleigh is raced in two-man bobs, four-man bobs and monobobs.

abschnitte.text: A **bob** is a sledge with a covering and four steel runners. It is raced as a two-man bob, a four-man bob or alone as a monobob. The team with the shortest total time from several runs wins. Often just hundredths of a second decide the winner.

At the start the athletes sprint alongside the bob and push it hard. For this they wear shoes with **spikes** so that they do not slip on the ice. After a few metres they jump in and duck down. The **pilot** steers with ropes that move the front runners, and the **brakeman** only brakes the bob after the finish line.

**Gravity** pulls the bob down the slope and accelerates it. The smooth runners on the ice mean there is very little friction. The faster the bob goes, the more strongly air resistance slows it down, which is why the team ducks down. In the bends the **centrifugal force** pushes the bob outwards, so the bends are built high and banked.

abschnitte.titel: St Moritz, the cradle of bobsleigh
abschnitte.text: Towards the end of the 19th century British winter guests in St Moritz began building sledges and holding races. The **Olympia Bobrun** from St Moritz to Celerina is the oldest bobsleigh track in the world. It is the only track made of **natural ice** and is rebuilt by hand from snow and water every winter. A run takes a little more than a minute.

Bobsleigh has been part of the programme since the first Winter Olympics in Chamonix in 1924. The Winter Olympics of 1928 and 1948 took place in St Moritz, including bobsleigh races. Switzerland is one of the most successful bobsleigh nations in the world. Women have raced bobsleigh at the Olympics since 2002, and since 2022 also in the monobob.

begriffe.erklaerung: Narrow steel blades under the bob on which it glides over the ice.
The person at the front of the bob who steers.
Ice that forms only through the winter cold, without cooling machines.
The force you feel in a bend, which pushes outwards.

gewusst: Most bobsleigh tracks in the world are made of concrete and are iced artificially with cooling pipes.
In St Moritz you can ride as a guest in a taxi bob behind an experienced pilot.
In tight bends the riders are pressed into their seats with several times their body weight.

teile.einleitung: Chromatic aberration is a colour fault of lenses. Because glass refracts the colours of light by different amounts, coloured fringes appear at edges and the image becomes blurred. Opticians have been fighting this fault for centuries with clever combinations of lenses.
wichtigste: The cause is that the refractive index of glass depends on the wavelength.
With a simple converging lens, blue light has the shortest focal length.
In photos you can recognise the fault by coloured fringes along high-contrast edges.
An achromat consists of a converging lens of crown glass and a diverging lens of flint glass.
A high Abbe number means that a glass shows little dispersion.
An apochromat corrects the colour faults for three wavelengths.
Mirrors have no chromatic aberration, because reflection is the same for all colours.

abschnitte.text: White light consists of many colours with different wavelengths. Glass refracts short-wave blue light more strongly than long-wave red light; this is called **dispersion**. The same effect splits white light into a rainbow in a **prism**. In a lens it means that each colour has its own focal point.

With a simple converging lens, the focal point for blue lies closer to the lens than the one for red. If you focus on green, red and blue are slightly blurred. A biconvex lens with two radii of 10 cm each, with n = 1.51 for red and n = 1.53 for blue, has focal lengths that differ by about 3.7 mm. In photos this shows up as purple or green **colour fringes**, for example on branches against a bright sky.

In the 18th century it was found that two types of glass can be combined. An **achromat** consists of a converging lens of **crown glass** and a diverging lens of flint glass, which spreads colours more strongly. The colour faults of the two lenses almost cancel each other out for two colours. The Englishman John Dollond made such lenses well known from 1758.

Even better lenses, **apochromats**, correct the fault for three wavelengths. How strongly a glass fans out the colours is described by the **Abbe number**, named after the German physicist Ernst Abbe. A high Abbe number means little dispersion. For expensive camera and telescope lenses, special glasses with very low dispersion or crystals such as fluorite are used.

Mirrors deflect all colours equally, because the light is only reflected and not refracted. That is why the main mirror of a **reflecting telescope** has no chromatic aberration. In 1668 Isaac Newton built one of the first reflecting telescopes, partly because the colour faults of lens telescopes bothered him. The world’s large research telescopes today are all reflecting telescopes.

begriffe.erklaerung: The dependence of the refraction of light on its colour, that is its wavelength.
The distance between a lens and the point at which parallel light rays meet.
A pair of lenses made of two types of glass that greatly reduces colour faults.
A figure that shows how little a glass pulls colours apart.

gewusst: The human eye also has chromatic aberration, but the brain cleverly makes up for it.
Modern cameras and image programs can automatically remove colour fringes afterwards.
The rainbow is produced by dispersion in raindrops, that is by the same cause.

teile.einleitung: Curling is a winter sport in which heavy granite stones are slid across a sheet of ice into a target. With brooms the players sweep in front of the stone to influence its path. Behind the calm game there is a lot of physics: friction, meltwater and spinning movements.
wichtigste: Curling comes from Scotland.
A curling stone weighs about 20 kg and is made of granite.
The stone touches the ice only with a narrow ring on its underside.
On the sheet there are small frozen droplets of water, the pebbles.
Sweeping warms the ice slightly, and the stone slides further.
A stone released with a slight spin travels in a curve.
A Swiss men’s team won Olympic gold in Nagano in 1998.

abschnitte.text: Two teams of four players each play against each other. Taking turns, each team slides its stones along the sheet, around 45 m long, towards the target circle, the **house**. After each round, the **end**, only the team whose stone is closest to the centre scores. It gets one point for each of its own stones that is closer than the opponents’ best stone.

A curling stone weighs about 20 kg and is made of particularly dense **granite**. The granite from the small Scottish island of Ailsa Craig is famous. On top the stone has a handle, and underneath it is slightly hollowed out. So it touches the ice only with a narrow ring, which keeps the friction low.

Before the game the ice is sprinkled with fine droplets of water that immediately freeze into little bumps, the **pebbles**. When the players sweep hard in front of the stone, the ice is warmed slightly by friction. As a result the stone slides on with less **friction** and travels straighter. In this way they can control the length and, a little, the direction of a throw.

The stone is released with a slight spin. As a result it does not travel straight ahead, but in a curve to the left or right. This curved path is called the **curl** in English and gave the sport its name. In this way a stone can even be played round other stones lying in the way into the house.

Curling comes from **Scotland**, where people were already sliding stones across frozen lakes and ponds in the 16th century. From the 19th century the sport spread to Canada and the Alpine countries. Curling was already played at the first Winter Olympics in Chamonix in 1924. Since the Winter Games in Nagano in 1998 it has been a permanent part of the Olympic programme.

Switzerland is one of the strongest curling nations in the world. In **Nagano in 1998** the Swiss men’s team, with skip Patrick Hürlimann, won Olympic gold. Swiss women’s teams have also won many world championship titles and Olympic medals. In many places, for example in Bern, Basel, Geneva or mountain villages, there are curling halls where children and teenagers also play.

begriffe.erklaerung: The circular target at the end of the curling sheet.
A round in which each team plays all its stones.
Small frozen droplets of water on curling ice.
The captain of a curling team.

gewusst: Because you have to aim curling stones so calmly and precisely, curling is sometimes called “chess on ice”.
With a good throw a curling stone can glide over the ice for half a minute.
Most Olympic curling stones are cut from the granite of the uninhabited Scottish island of Ailsa Craig.

teile.einleitung: CO2 emissions are the amount of carbon dioxide that people, vehicles, heating systems and factories release into the air. CO2 is produced mainly when crude oil, natural gas and coal are burnt. Because it warms the Earth like a blanket, CO2 emissions are a main cause of climate change.
wichtigste: CO2 holds back heat radiation in the atmosphere and so warms the Earth.
Burning one litre of petrol produces about 2.3 kilograms of CO2.
Before industrialisation the CO2 content of the air was about 280 ppm.
In Switzerland, transport causes the largest share of domestic greenhouse gases (as of 2023).
Since 2008 Switzerland has charged a CO2 levy on heating fuels such as heating oil and natural gas.
In the Paris climate agreement of 2015, countries aim to limit warming to 1.5 °C if possible.
A growing forest is a carbon sink, because it takes in more CO2 than it gives off.

abschnitte.text: Carbon dioxide, CO2 for short, is a colourless gas made of one carbon atom and two oxygen atoms. We breathe it out, and plants take it in for **photosynthesis**. The air contains only a small amount of it, which is given in ppm, parts per million. Even so, it has a strong effect on the climate, because it holds back the Earth’s heat radiation; this is the **greenhouse effect**.

Crude oil, natural gas and coal are the remains of ancient plants and animals and contain a lot of carbon. When they are burnt, the carbon combines with oxygen to form CO2. One litre of petrol produces about 2.3 kg of CO2 in this way, because the oxygen from the air is added. So a car that uses 5 litres on a journey gives off around 11.5 kg of CO2. Making cement also releases a lot of CO2.

Before industrialisation the air contained about 280 ppm of CO2; today it is over 420 ppm (as of 2024). As a result the Earth has already become noticeably warmer. In Switzerland this shows especially in the **retreat of the glaciers**, which have melted a great deal. Heatwave summers, heavy rain and less snow at low altitudes are becoming more frequent.

Since 2008 Switzerland has charged a **CO2 levy** on heating fuels such as heating oil and natural gas; part of it is returned to the population through health insurance premiums. In June 2023 voters approved the Climate and Innovation Act. It provides for Switzerland to reach **net zero** by 2050, that is to emit no more CO2 overall. Transport has the largest share of domestic emissions, followed by buildings and industry.

A person’s **carbon footprint** can be reduced with many small steps. Bikes, trains and buses cause much less CO2 per person than a car or an aeroplane. Seasonal and regional food usually needs less energy for transport and greenhouses. Switching off lights, not heating too much and repairing things instead of buying new ones also helps.

begriffe.erklaerung: The warming of the Earth because gases in the air hold back heat radiation.
Short for “parts per million”.
A natural system such as a forest or a bog that takes in more CO2 than it gives off.
The total of all the greenhouse gases caused by a person or a product.

gewusst: Part of the CO2 emitted is absorbed by the oceans, which become more acidic as a result.
Many products that Switzerland imports cause their CO2 emissions abroad.
A litre of petrol weighs less than a kilogram, but produces more than twice that weight of CO2 when burnt.

teile.einleitung: The dioptre is the unit for the refractive power of lenses, for example spectacle lenses or contact lenses. It tells you how strongly a lens focuses or spreads out light rays. Anyone who wears glasses can find the number of dioptres on their prescription.
wichtigste: The refractive power of a lens is given in dioptres (D).
The refractive power is the reciprocal of the focal length in metres: D = 1 / f.
A converging lens with a focal length of 0.5 m has 2 dioptres.
Negative dioptres mean a diverging lens.
The refractive powers of thin lenses lying directly on top of each other can be added.
The human eye has about 60 dioptres in total.
Most of this comes from the cornea.

abschnitte.text: A lens bends light rays; this is called **refraction**. A **converging lens** focuses parallel rays at one point, the focal point. The distance from the lens to the focal point is the **focal length** f. The refractive power D in dioptres is the reciprocal of the focal length in metres, that is D = 1 / f. The shorter the focal length, the stronger the lens.

A converging lens with a focal length of 0.5 m has 1 / 0.5 = 2 dioptres. The other way round, a lens with 4 dioptres has a focal length of 1 / 4 m, that is 25 cm. A **diverging lens** has a negative focal length; at −0.25 m it is −4 dioptres. If you put two thin lenses of 3 and 2 dioptres directly on top of each other, together they make 5 dioptres. That is exactly why the dioptre is so practical: you can simply add.

With **short-sightedness** you see blurred in the distance, because the eye refracts the light too strongly. A diverging lens with negative dioptres helps against this, for example −2 D. With **long-sightedness** it is the other way round, and the glasses have positive values. Eye doctors and opticians work out the right dioptres with eye tests and measuring instruments.

The human eye has a total refractive power of about 60 dioptres. Most of this comes from the curved **cornea** at the front of the eye. The **lens** behind it can change its shape and so switch between near and distance vision. With age the lens becomes stiffer, which is why many people need reading glasses from about the age of 45.

The name comes from the ancient Greek word **dioptra**, an instrument for looking through and measuring. The French eye doctor Ferdinand Monoyer introduced the dioptre as a unit for lenses in the 19th century. Before that, spectacle lenses were awkwardly described by their focal length in inches. Today the dioptre is used worldwide in eye medicine.

begriffe.erklaerung: The distance between a lens and the point at which the light rays meet.
A lens that is thicker in the middle and focuses light, like a magnifying glass.
A lens that is thinner in the middle and makes light spread out.
You see close things clearly but distant things blurred.

gewusst: With a magnifying glass you can focus sunlight so strongly that paper starts to burn, which is why the point where it is focused is called the focal point, the “burning point” in German.
Divers see blurred under water without a mask, because the cornea has almost no refractive power in water.
Contact lenses and spectacle lenses for the same person often have slightly different dioptre values, because they are at different distances from the eye.

teile.einleitung: A wind-up toy moves without any batteries at all. You turn a small key, which tightens a spring, and the spring slowly gives the energy back. In this way cars drive, frogs hop and music boxes play a tune.
wichtigste: A wind-up toy gets its energy when you turn the key.
The energy really comes from your muscles and is stored in a spring.
When the spring unwinds, the toy moves.
Small gearwheels pass the movement on to wheels or legs.
When the spring’s energy is used up, the toy stops.
A wind-up toy does not need batteries.
Music boxes and mechanical clocks also work by being wound up.

abschnitte.text: When you wind it up, you turn a key or a little wheel. Inside, a long, thin metal spring coils up tighter and tighter. The strength of your muscles is now stored in the spring as **elastic energy**. It is similar to a stretched rubber band that snaps back as soon as you let go.

The coiled spring is called the **mainspring** or spiral spring. When it unwinds, it turns an axle. Several **gearwheels** pass this turning on to wheels, legs or arms. Often a small fan wheel or an escapement slows the movement down so that the spring does not run down in a second.

The energy in the spring is gradually turned into movement. Friction also produces a little heat. When the spring has completely unwound, there is no energy left and the toy stops. If you wind it up far too tightly, the spring can be overstretched or break.

Mechanical figures driven by springs already existed at royal courts centuries ago. In the 19th century many wind-up **tin toys** were made in Germany, especially around Nuremberg. Cars, railways, animals and dancing figures were popular. Today old wind-up toys are sought-after collector’s items.

abschnitte.titel: Music boxes and watches from Switzerland
abschnitte.text: A **music box** is also wound up: a cylinder with pins turns and plucks the teeth of a metal comb. The village of Sainte-Croix in the Vaud Jura was famous for its music boxes and automata. At the Museum of Music Automatons in Seewen in the canton of Solothurn you can marvel at many such treasures. Mechanical wristwatches, a Swiss speciality, also run on a wound-up spring.

begriffe.erklaerung: A coiled metal spring that stores energy and drives a toy or a watch.
Energy stored in an object that has been stretched or squeezed.
A wheel with teeth that fits into another and passes movement on.
A force that slows movement down when things rub against each other.

gewusst: Many mechanical wristwatches wind themselves while being worn, because a small rotor tightens the spring with every movement of the arm.
Wind-up toys show the law of conservation of energy nicely: the energy is not lost, it is only changed into another form.

teile.einleitung: Reactive power is a special part of electrical power in alternating current networks. It swings back and forth between the power station and the device without doing any work. Even so, it puts a load on cables and transformers and is therefore important for electricity companies.
wichtigste: Reactive power is caused by coils and capacitors in alternating current circuits.
It is measured in the unit var, apparent power in VA and active power in watts.
Active power is the part that really produces light, heat or movement.
In a coil the current lags 90 degrees behind the voltage; in a capacitor it leads by 90 degrees.
The power factor cos phi shows how much of the apparent power is active power.
The inductive reactive power of large motors is balanced out with capacitors.
Too much reactive power loads the lines without doing any useful work.

abschnitte.text: In the alternating current network, current and voltage change direction 50 times a second. In a kettle both run exactly in step, and all the energy becomes heat. Coils and capacitors, however, store energy briefly and give it straight back to the network. This power that swings back and forth is called **reactive power**; in German it is called “blind power”, because it stays “blind” and drives nothing.

A coil builds up a magnetic field, a capacitor an electric field. In an ideal **coil** the current lags a quarter of a period, that is 90 degrees, behind the voltage. In an ideal **capacitor** it leads by 90 degrees. Coils are found in electric motors, transformers and ballasts, which is why these cause inductive reactive power.

Active power P, reactive power Q and **apparent power** S together form a right-angled triangle. That is why, as in Pythagoras’ theorem: S squared equals P squared plus Q squared. If a device has 3 kW of active power and 4 kvar of reactive power, the apparent power is 5 kVA. The **power factor** cos phi is the ratio of P to S, so with 8 kW and 10 kVA it is 0.8.

Factories with many large motors draw a lot of inductive reactive power from the network. To balance this out, cabinets full of capacitors, a **compensation system**, are installed. Because capacitors and coils have exactly opposite effects, their reactive powers partly cancel each other out. Many electricity companies charge large customers extra if their power factor is too low.

The swinging reactive power also needs current to flow through the lines. This current heats cables and transformers and so causes losses. The lines therefore have to be built thicker than would be needed for the active power alone. On the other hand, network operators use reactive power deliberately to keep the **voltage** in the network stable.

begriffe.erklaerung: The part of the power that really does work, measured in watts.
The total power with which the network is loaded, measured in volt-amperes (VA).
Short for volt-ampere reactive, the unit of reactive power.
A number between 0 and 1 that shows how much of the apparent power is useful active power.

gewusst: With direct current there is no reactive power; it only occurs with alternating current.
A kettle has a power factor of almost exactly 1.
Whole power stations sometimes help to supply reactive power so that the network voltage is right.

teile.einleitung: Equations of motion are mathematical formulas that describe where a body is at any moment and how fast it is moving. With them you can work out in advance how far a car rolls when braking, how high a ball flies or how long a stone takes to fall. They are among the most important tools of mechanics.
wichtigste: Equations of motion describe the position and speed of a body depending on time.
For uniformly accelerated motion: s equals s0 plus v0 times t plus one half times a times t squared.
The speed increases steadily: v equals v0 plus a times t.
The equation v squared equals v0 squared plus 2 times a times s does without time.
A freely falling body falls around 19.6 metres in the first 2 seconds.
Without air resistance, a ball thrown straight up at 20 metres per second rises 20 metres.
They are based on the laws of Galileo Galilei and Isaac Newton.

abschnitte.text: An equation of motion links **position**, **velocity**, **acceleration** and time. If you know the starting values and the acceleration, you can work out the whole motion in advance. The simplest is uniform motion, in which the speed stays the same; then distance equals speed times time. More important and more exciting is uniformly accelerated motion.

With uniform acceleration a, the speed is: v equals v0 plus a times t. The position is: s equals s0 plus v0 times t plus one half times a times t squared. If you do not know the time, the third equation helps: v squared equals v0 squared plus 2 times a times s. With these three formulas almost all problems about accelerated motion can be solved.

A body starts at 3 metres per second and accelerates for 4 seconds at 1.5 metres per second squared; afterwards it is going 9 metres per second. A car at 10 metres per second that accelerates for 5 seconds at 2 metres per second squared covers 75 metres in that time. A locomotive that brakes from 30 to 10 metres per second at 4 metres per second squared needs 100 metres to do so. When braking, the acceleration is simply **negative**.

Without air resistance all bodies fall equally fast, with the **acceleration due to gravity** g of about 9.81 metres per second squared. So in the first 2 seconds a stone falling from rest drops around 19.6 metres. If you throw a ball straight up at 15 metres per second, with g equal to 10 it reaches its highest point after 1.5 seconds. At 20 metres per second it rises 20 metres.

Around 1600 the Italian **Galileo Galilei** studied how bodies fall using balls on sloping ramps and found the laws of falling. In 1687 **Isaac Newton** published his laws of motion, according to which force equals mass times acceleration. In the 18th century the Basel mathematician **Leonhard Euler** wrote this law down as an equation in the form usual today. In this way you can set up the equation of motion of a body from the force acting on it.

Equations of motion are used to calculate the paths of rockets, satellites and planets. Engineers use them to plan roller coasters, the braking distances of trains and the safety of cars. Computer games also use them so that characters and balls jump and fall realistically. In reality you often have to include **air resistance** and friction too, and then the equations become harder.

begriffe.erklaerung: How fast the speed changes, measured in metres per second squared.
The acceleration with which bodies fall on Earth, about 9.81 metres per second squared.
The speed a body has at the start of the observation.
Motion at a constant speed.

gewusst: In 1971 the astronaut David Scott dropped a hammer and a feather on the Moon, and both reached the ground at the same time, because there is no air there.
Without air resistance, a ball thrown up takes exactly as long to go up as to come back down.

teile.einleitung: Buoyancy is a force that pushes objects upwards in liquids and gases. It makes ships float and balloons rise. The force that keeps an aeroplane in the air is also called lift.
wichtigste: Buoyancy is an upward force in liquids and gases.
A body experiences as much buoyancy as the water or gas it displaces weighs.
This rule is called Archimedes’ principle.
If the buoyancy is greater than the weight, a body floats or rises.
Hot-air balloons rise because warm air is lighter than cold air.
The force that keeps an aeroplane in the air is called lift.
Aeroplanes get lift from the shape and angle of their wings.

abschnitte.text: When you get into the bath, you feel lighter. The water presses harder against your body from below than from above, because water pressure increases with depth. This difference produces an upward force, **buoyancy**. It acts in all liquids and gases, and so also in air.

The Greek scholar Archimedes lived in the 3rd century BC in Syracuse. He recognised that a body experiences as much buoyancy as the displaced liquid weighs. This rule is called **Archimedes’ principle**. According to legend he shouted “Eureka!” when he came up with it in the bath.

If an object is heavier than the water it displaces, it sinks. If it is lighter, it floats and partly sticks out. A steel ship floats because its hull is hollow and displaces a lot of water. A **submarine** can fill tanks with water or empty them with air and so dive, hover or surface.

There is buoyancy in air too, but it is much smaller, because air is very light. A **hot-air balloon** rises because the heated air in the envelope is less dense than the cold air outside. Balloons filled with helium rise because helium is much lighter than air. Every January a well-known international balloon festival takes place in Château-d'Oex in the canton of Vaud.

An aeroplane is much heavier than the air it displaces. It therefore needs a different kind of upward force, **dynamic lift**. The curved wings, tilted slightly, deflect the air flowing past them downwards. This creates lower pressure above the wing and higher pressure below it, which pushes the aeroplane upwards. The faster an aeroplane flies, the greater this lift.

begriffe.erklaerung: A force that pushes upwards in water or air.
The amount of water or air that a body pushes aside.
How much mass there is in a certain volume.
The specially shaped wing of an aeroplane that produces lift.

gewusst: In the Dead Sea the water is so salty and dense that people lie on top of it like a cork.
A large cruise ship displaces many tens of thousands of tonnes of water and still floats.

teile.einleitung: An expansion joint is a gap built in deliberately between two parts of a structure, for example in bridges, roads or large concrete floors. It gives the materials room when they expand in the heat and contract in the cold. Without it, structures would crack or bend.
wichtigste: Almost all substances expand in the heat and contract in the cold.
Expansion joints give room for these movements.
A concrete slab without expansion joints could bulge or crack on hot days.
A long bridge needs wider joints than a short one, because it expands more.
On road bridges, an expansion joint device bridges the gap.
In buildings expansion joints are often filled with elastic material.
In the past you heard a “da-dum” when travelling by train because of the gaps between the rails.

abschnitte.text: When a substance is heated, its smallest particles move more strongly and need more room. That is why a steel girder gets a little longer on a hot summer’s day than in winter. This effect is called **thermal expansion**. Steel expands by about 0.012 millimetres per metre for every degree of warming. That sounds like very little, but in long structures it adds up.

A steel bridge 500 metres long gets about 240 millimetres longer when warmed by 40 degrees. So that it does not push against the abutments, it needs a wide joint at the end. Over it lies an **expansion joint device**, so that cars can drive over it safely. You often see interlocking metal teeth or rubber profiles there, and you feel a slight rumble as you drive over. Bridges also rest on movable bearings so that they can expand.

Large concrete floors in halls, car parks or squares also have expansion joints. You can recognise them as straight lines that divide the floor into sections. The joints are often filled with an **elastic** material such as a plastic sealant, so that no water or dirt gets in. Without such joints, cracks form in an uncontrolled way because the concrete moves. Tiles in the bathroom also need small movement joints at the edges.

In the past railway tracks were made of individual lengths of rail with small gaps between them. Every time a wheel rolled over a gap, you heard a “da-dum”. Today rails are usually welded into long strings; this is called **continuous welded rail**. So that they do not buckle in the heat, they are firmly anchored to the sleepers and stressed when they are laid. In this way the rails can withstand the forces without bending.

How much a part expands depends on three things: the material, the length and the change in temperature. You multiply the length by the expansion coefficient and by the change in temperature. Concrete and steel expand by similar amounts, which is why they work well together in reinforced concrete. Aluminium expands about twice as much as steel. Engineers calculate these values precisely before they build a bridge.

begriffe.erklaerung: A substance gets bigger when heated and smaller when cooled.
A part that covers the gap at the end of a road bridge.
A number that tells you how much a material expands per degree.
Rails welded into long strings without gaps.

gewusst: Because of the heat, the Eiffel Tower in Paris is a few centimetres taller in summer than in winter.
Because of their shape, the metal teeth on bridge joints are also called finger joints.
Power lines also sag more in summer than in winter, because the wires get longer.

teile.einleitung: Doping means deliberately putting tiny amounts of foreign atoms into a semiconductor such as silicon. This changes its electrical conductivity greatly. Without doping there would be no computer chips, solar cells or light-emitting diodes.
wichtigste: Doping is the deliberate introduction of foreign atoms into a semiconductor.
With phosphorus, silicon becomes n-type.
With boron, silicon becomes p-type.
Foreign atoms that give up an extra electron are called donors.
An n-doped semiconductor stays electrically neutral, because for every free electron there is a positive foreign atom.
The stronger the doping, the higher the conductivity.
In chip manufacturing, foreign atoms are fired into the silicon wafer by ion implantation.

abschnitte.text: A **semiconductor** conducts electricity worse than a metal but better than an insulator such as glass. The most important example is **silicon**, which is obtained from sand. Each silicon atom has four outer electrons and is firmly joined to four neighbours. In pure silicon there are therefore hardly any free charge carriers, and at room temperature it conducts only very poorly.

If a **phosphorus atom** is built into the silicon, it brings five outer electrons with it. Four of them are needed for the bonds, and the fifth can move almost freely. Such foreign atoms are called **donors**, that is givers. The semiconductor is then called n-type, because negative electrons carry the current. Even so, it stays neutral overall, because the phosphorus atom is positively charged after giving up its electron.

A **boron atom** has only three outer electrons, so one bond remains incomplete. This gap is called a **hole**. Neighbouring electrons can jump into the hole, so that it moves through the crystal like a positive charge. Such foreign atoms are called **acceptors**, that is takers, and the semiconductor is called p-type.

Even a single foreign atom among many millions of silicon atoms changes the conductivity enormously. In the past the foreign atoms were made to travel into the crystal at high temperature; this is called **diffusion**. Today **ion implantation** is often used, in which accelerated foreign atoms are fired precisely into the surface of a silicon wafer. In this way you can decide exactly which doping goes where on tiny areas.

Where a p-region meets an n-region, a **p-n junction** forms. It lets current through in one direction only, which is how a diode works. Transistors in computer chips, light-emitting diodes in lamps and screens, and **solar cells** on house roofs are all based on doped semiconductors. A modern mobile phone chip contains billions of such doped components.

begriffe.erklaerung: A material that conducts electricity moderately well and whose conductivity can be controlled deliberately.
A foreign atom that gives up an extra electron.
A foreign atom that can take in an electron and so creates a hole.
A thin, round disc of silicon on which chips are made.
The boundary between a p-doped and an n-doped region, the basis of diodes and solar cells.

gewusst: The name Silicon Valley for the technology centre in California comes from the semiconductor silicon.
For chips, silicon must be so pure that there are only a very few foreign atoms for every billion silicon atoms before it is deliberately doped.
The word doping comes from the Latin dotare via German “dotieren”, meaning to equip.

teile.einleitung: A tin can telephone is a simple toy telephone made of two cans or cups and a tight string. You speak into one can, and the other person hears your voice in the second can. It works without any electricity, just with the physics of sound.
wichtigste: For a tin can telephone you need two cans and a string.
Yoghurt pots also work instead of cans.
When you speak into it, the bottom of the can starts to vibrate.
The sound travels through the tight string to the other cup.
If someone holds the string in the middle, you can hardly hear anything any more.
The listener holds the second can to their ear.
A tin can telephone needs no electricity.

abschnitte.text: Take two empty, clean cans or **yoghurt pots** and make a small hole in the middle of the bottom of each. With cans, adults should help, because sharp edges can cut. Thread a long string through the holes and tie a thick knot inside or tie a matchstick to it. That way the string does not slip out. Then two people move apart until the string is pulled tight.

Sound consists of **vibrations** that spread out. When you speak into the cup, the sound waves of your voice make the bottom vibrate. These vibrations travel through the string to the other cup. There the string makes the second bottom vibrate, and it passes the sound on to the air. In this way the other person hears the voice, even though no cable or electricity is involved.

The string must be pulled tight, otherwise the vibrations are passed on badly. If someone holds the string in the middle, the vibrations are damped and you can hardly hear anything. If the string touches a corner, the sound also gets weaker. A thin, strong string such as builder’s line or fishing line usually works well. A thin wire often carries the sound even better.

With a tin can telephone only one person speaks at a time. The speaker holds the can in front of their mouth, and the listener holds the other can to their ear. Then you swap, rather like with a walkie-talkie. With several strings you can even try out conversations between three or four people. Through a wall or round a corner, however, it hardly works.

The principle of a string telephone was known long before the electric telephone. It is also called a mechanical or **acoustic telephone**. In the 19th century there were even string telephones with which you could talk over several hundred metres. The electric telephone, which Alexander Graham Bell patented in 1876, on the other hand turns the vibrations into electric current. Today the tin can telephone is a popular experiment in lessons and on the playground.

begriffe.erklaerung: Vibrations that travel through air, water or solid materials and that we hear.
A fast back-and-forth movement.
A thin, vibrating surface, like the bottom of the can.
When vibrations get weaker because they are slowed down.

gewusst: Sound travels much faster in solid materials than in air.
With a well-tightened tin can telephone you can talk across the length of a school playground.
Doctors also use the transmission of sound through tubes rather than electricity in the stethoscope.

teile.einleitung: A ballast tank is a container in a ship or submarine that can be filled with water or emptied. In this way the weight of the vessel and its position in the water are changed. Cargo ships become stable, and submarines can dive and surface again.
wichtigste: Ballast tanks are filled with water or emptied to change the weight of a ship.
Empty cargo ships take on ballast water so that they lie steadily in the water.
Submarines flood their ballast tanks to dive and blow them out with compressed air to surface.
Smaller trim tanks set the position and hovering of a submarine precisely.
Ballast water can carry foreign animal species into other seas.
The international Ballast Water Management Convention came into force in 2017.
If you fill a tank on one side only, the ship tilts to that side.

abschnitte.text: A fully loaded cargo ship lies low and steady in the water. When it is empty, it rolls a lot and the propeller can even stick out of the water. That is why **ballast water** is pumped into tanks in the hull. This makes the ship heavier, lowers its centre of gravity and makes it more stable.

Every body in water experiences a **buoyancy** as great as the weight of the water it displaces. The Greek scholar Archimedes already recognised this. If the vessel is lighter than the displaced water, it floats on top. If it is exactly as heavy, it hovers, and if it is heavier, it sinks.

In many submarines the ballast tanks lie between the **pressure hull**, in which the crew lives, and the outer hull. When valves are opened, sea water flows into the tanks and the boat sinks. To surface, the water is blown out again with compressed air. An example: if a submerged submarine displaces 1200 tonnes of water and weighs 1000 tonnes without ballast, it must take on 200 tonnes of water to hover.

As well as the big tanks, submarines have smaller **trim tanks** at the front and back. With them you set whether the boat is level and hovering exactly. Ships are balanced in the same way, because if you fill only one tank on one side, the ship tilts that way. Sailing boats often have heavy lead in the **keel**, so that the low centre of gravity stops them capsizing.

Cargo ships take on ballast water in one port and often release it again in a port far away. Larvae, mussels, crabs and algae travel along with the water. In foreign seas such species can spread widely and drive out native animals. That is why the international **Ballast Water Management Convention** has applied since 2017, under which ships must treat their ballast water.

The Swiss scientist Auguste Piccard developed the deep-sea submersible known as the bathyscaphe. In 1960 his son Jacques Piccard dived in the bathyscaphe Trieste to the deepest point of the oceans in the Mariana Trench. Iron pellets served as ballast and were dropped to surface. For the national exhibition Expo 64, Jacques Piccard built the tourist submarine Mésoscaphe, which took visitors down into the depths of Lake Geneva.

begriffe.erklaerung: Extra weight that makes a vessel more stable or makes it sink.
The force with which water pushes a body upwards.
The thick inner hull of a submarine that withstands the water pressure.
A foreign animal or plant species that spreads widely in a new area and causes damage.

gewusst: Large cargo ships can take tens of thousands of tonnes of ballast water on board.
Fish also have a kind of ballast tank: with their swim bladder many fish can hover in the water.

teile.einleitung: The Coriolis force is a force that arises from the rotation of the Earth. It deflects winds and ocean currents to the right in the northern hemisphere and to the left in the southern hemisphere. Without it there would be no swirling areas of low pressure and no tropical storms.
wichtigste: The Coriolis force arises because the Earth rotates.
It is a fictitious force or inertial force that only appears in rotating frames of reference.
In the northern hemisphere it deflects movements to the right, in the southern hemisphere to the left.
At the equator its effect on winds is zero; towards the poles it becomes stronger.
It is the reason why air swirls round areas of low pressure.
It is far too weak to cause the whirlpool in the bath.
It is named after the French physicist Gaspard-Gustave de Coriolis.

abschnitte.text: The Earth turns once a day on its axis, and we turn with it. When something moves over long distances, such as a wind, it seems to be deflected from its straight path. This deflection is explained by the **Coriolis force**. It is a **fictitious force**: from outside, for example from space, you can see that the body is moving straight ahead and only the Earth is turning away beneath it. It is named after Gaspard-Gustave de Coriolis, who described it precisely in 1835.

Imagine two children sitting on a turning roundabout and rolling a ball to each other. The ball actually rolls straight ahead. But because the roundabout keeps turning beneath it, it does not reach the other child. To the children it looks as if an invisible force is pushing the ball to the side. The Coriolis force works in exactly this way on the rotating Earth.

Air always flows from high to low air pressure. The Coriolis force deflects it as it does so, and it starts to circle round an **area of low pressure**. In the northern hemisphere air turns **anticlockwise** round a low, in the southern hemisphere clockwise. Right at the equator the horizontal Coriolis effect is zero, which is why practically no tropical storms form there. The steady **trade winds** are also deflected by the Coriolis force.

You often hear that in the northern hemisphere water always drains out of the bath in a particular direction. That is not true. The Coriolis force is far too weak for such small amounts of water and short times. The direction of the swirl depends much more on the shape of the bath and small currents in the water. Only in very careful laboratory experiments with completely still water has the effect been shown.

The Coriolis force always acts **at right angles** to the direction of movement. That is why it only changes the direction of a body, not its speed. Its strength depends on the **Coriolis parameter** f = 2Ω sin φ, where Ω is the angular velocity of the Earth, around 7.29 times 10 to the power of minus 5 per second. The parameter grows with the sine of the latitude φ. At a latitude of 45 degrees, roughly level with northern Italy, it is around 1.0 times 10 to the power of minus 4 per second.

In 1851 the French physicist **Léon Foucault** hung up a long, heavy pendulum in Paris. Over the hours the plane in which the pendulum swung slowly turned. In this way the rotation of the Earth could be seen directly. Such pendulums hang today in many museums and universities. Experts on rockets, long-range shells and flight routes also have to take the Coriolis force into account.

begriffe.erklaerung: A force that only an observer who is turning or accelerating notices.
The point of view from which a movement is observed and described.
An area with low air pressure round which the air circles.
Steady winds in the tropics that blow all year round.

gewusst: A Foucault pendulum at the North Pole would turn its plane of swing right round in about a day.
At the equator the plane of swing of a Foucault pendulum does not turn at all.
The jet stream, a fast band of wind at a height of around 10 kilometres, is also shaped by the Coriolis force.

teile.einleitung: Daniel Bernoulli was a mathematician, physicist and doctor from Basel who lived in the 18th century. He studied how water and air flow, and in doing so discovered a law that still explains aeroplanes and sprayers today. He came from a famous family of scholars in Basel.
wichtigste: Daniel Bernoulli lived from 1700 to 1782 and worked mainly in Basel.
His father Johann Bernoulli was also a famous mathematician.
He studied mathematics and medicine and became a doctor of medicine in Basel in 1721.
For some years he worked at the Academy in Saint Petersburg.

abschnitte.text: Daniel Bernoulli was born on 8 February 1700 in **Groningen** in the Netherlands, where his father was teaching at the time. The family soon moved back to **Basel**. His father **Johann Bernoulli** and his uncle Jakob Bernoulli were important mathematicians. Daniel first studied medicine and gained his doctorate in Basel in 1721, but he was always interested in mathematics too.

From 1725 to 1733 Bernoulli worked at the new Academy of Sciences in **Saint Petersburg** in Russia. There he also got to know the young Basel mathematician **Leonhard Euler**. After that he returned to Basel and taught anatomy, botany, physiology and finally physics at the university. He died in Basel on 17 March 1782.

In 1738 Bernoulli published his main work, **Hydrodynamica**. In it he described how water moves in pipes and containers. Best known is **Bernoulli’s law**: where a liquid or a gas flows faster, the pressure is lower. In a narrow section of pipe water flows faster, so the pressure there is lower.

If you blow between two hanging sheets of paper, they move **towards each other**, because the pressure between them falls. In a **sprayer** a fast stream of air over a small tube lowers the pressure, so that liquid is sucked upwards. On an aeroplane a **pitot tube** uses this relationship to measure the speed. The lift on aeroplane wings is also connected with the different pressures above and below the wing.

Bernoulli imagined gases as many tiny particles flying about and bumping against the walls of the container. With this he explained **gas pressure** and is regarded as one of the founders of the **kinetic theory of gases**. He also worked on probability, for example on the question of how much a game of chance is worth. He won prizes from the Paris Academy of Sciences several times for his work.
